International Security at Fifty Years
abstract: Fifty years ago, the founders of this journal hoped that its creation would help revitalize the academic study of international security. Their ambitions have been fulfilled: International Security is now one of the most widely cited journals in the field of international relations and there is a robust community of scholars studying different aspects of the subject. The contents of the journal constantly evolve in response to world events, new scholarly developments, and its contributors’ particular interests, but it remains a vital resource for scholars and students alike. By facilitating active debates on important scholarly questions, International Security and other academic journals help educate each new cohort and contribute to robust discussions of critical policy questions.

title: The Return of Nationalist Geopolitics: Liberal Backsliding and Armed Conflict
authors: Lars-Erik Cederman, Paola Galano Toro, Luc Girardin, Andreas Juon, Julian Wucherpfennig
abstract: The post-Cold War decline in violent conflict has given way to rising instability both within and between states. While many attribute this shift to intensified great power competition, we argue that nationalist geopolitics, manifested through conflict driven by grievances reflecting the political exclusion of ethnic groups and their kin, offer a more accurate explanation. We explain how endogenous and exogenous factors weakened the liberal international order, which allowed ethnic nationalism to resurge in the early twenty-first century. This erosion of broader liberal norms, particularly what we call liberal backsliding, has started to undermine the inclusive policies that ultimately helped to stabilize the post-Cold War peace. Using newly updated global data on ethnic power relations (1946–2023), we document a reversal of inclusionary trends that began in the early 2010s. These findings challenge power-centric explanations of global instability and highlight how liberal institutional erosion, particularly in the domain of ethnic inclusion, creates fertile ground for identity-based violence. The return of nationalist geopolitics is thus rooted in not only shifting power relations but also retreating institutional safeguards.

title: The Iron Cage of International Anarchy
abstract: Great power competition has been endemic to the modern system of industrialized nation-states that began emerging in Europe around 1800. This article seeks to describe and explain the principal features of that competition over the past 226 years, paying special attention to how it has evolved during the fifty-year history of International Security (1976–2026). The focus is on both security competition, which is a constant feature of great power politics, and war, which is not. The article shows that although security competition is pervasive, the shape of that competition has varied markedly over time, depending largely on the polarity of the system—the number of great powers—and the distribution of power among them. Those same two factors, coupled with the coming of nuclear weapons, have had a pronounced effect on the likelihood of great power war, including conflicts that involved all the great powers, such as the Napoleonic Wars, World War I, and World War II. Finally, the article considers the likely contours of great power competition in the next fifty years, focusing on determining which countries are likely to be great powers, what is the likely distribution of power among them, and what are the prospects for a future great power war.

title: Seeing Through “Transparent Oceans”: Emerging Technology, Submarine Vulnerability, and the Future of MAD
abstract: Ballistic missile submarines (SSBNs) are widely believed to be invulnerable to disarming strikes because of their weak detectable signatures and the large areas within which they can threaten an adversary. SSBNs are therefore considered secure second-strike forces and thus a strong deterrent against nuclear war and nuclear coercion. Many analysts now believe that various emerging technologies could render SSBNs vulnerable to disarming strikes. This study surveys key sensing and signal processing technologies featured in the “transparent oceans” debate (i.e., quantum sensors, artificial intelligence [AI], space-based sensors, and advanced acoustic sensors) and analyzes their potential to enhance SSBN detection. Findings indicate that states can enhance SSBN detection by applying AI algorithms to passive sonar signal processing. But the capabilities that have been demonstrated by the relevant AI algorithms in the unclassified literature suggest that these advances in SSBN detection are evolutionary rather than revolutionary. This study finds that the other technologies do not meaningfully improve SSBN detection; it is therefore highly unlikely that a threat to SSBNs that are presently survivable will materialize in the coming decades.

title: Correspondence: The Challenge of Studying What China Wants
authors: Rush Doshi, Andrea Ghiselli, Todd H. Hall, Jamie Gruffydd-Jones, Arash Heydarian Pashakhanlou, David C. Kang, Jackie S. H. Wong, Zenobia T. Chan

title: Consistency, not waste aversion, explains apparent sunk‐cost effects in politics
abstract: Do sunk costs shape how voters judge political leaders, or do reputational signals carried by current choices dominate? Across three preregistered experiments (total N = 1462) using vignettes about a national rail project, we orthogonally manipulated sunk costs (high vs. absent), leaders' decisions (continue vs. abandon), campaign commitments (pro, anti, none), and reminders of prior voting behavior. In Experiment 1 ( N = 346), Bayesian ANOVA showed that evaluations (vote likelihood, perceived honesty, competence) were reliably higher when leaders continued rather than abandoned a project, with no main effect of sunk costs and no interaction. Experiment 2 ( N = 719) replicated the null sunk‐cost effect and further found no effect of campaign commitments once the leader's current decision was known. Experiment 3 ( N = 397) used a structural equation model to test mediation: perceived commitment—but not perceived sunk costs—robustly predicted evaluations, and abandonment sharply reduced perceived commitment; prior‐vote cues were weak and did not mediate effects. Together, the studies indicate that people take continuation to signal commitment and view it positively, whereas abandonment stopping signals a breach of commitment and is penalized. Apparent sunk‐cost sensitivity in politics may often reflect a premium on consistency rather than waste aversion. We discuss implications for designing “face‐saving” off‐ramps and reframing evidence‐based reversals as fidelity to higher order commitments.

title: Power Through Visibility: How Policy Narratives Matter in Climate Change Debate on X
authors: Simon Bulian, Anne‐Marie Parth, Maria Becker, Lars Tapken
abstract: Research on policy narratives has shown that political actors employ certain narrative strategies in their competition for attention. Although we know that actors' narrative strategies coincide with existing power constellations (e.g., government vs. opposition), the ways in which they influence public attention remain largely unknown. In this paper, we ask whether different narrative strategies laid down by the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) vary in the attention they create on social media. To do so, we identify policy narratives within the German debate on climate change on X with Large Language Models (LLMs) and estimate their impact on attention through statistical analysis. Our results suggest that tweets with a policy narrative on climate change tend to be more visible than tweets on climate change without such a narrative. In particular, tweets that link policy solutions on climate change with the narrative characters villains or heroes tend to receive more attention on social media. This suggests that using both heroic and villainous policy narratives in public debate may be an effective way of generating public attention. The results challenge the widely held assumption in NPF research that devil‐ and angel‐shift narrative strategies influence agenda‐setting dynamics in the policy process differently.

title: Time's Sentimental Tale: Operationalizing Plot Within the Narrative Policy Framework
authors: Rachel McGovern, Crystal Soderman, Alex Osei‐Kojo, Michael D. Jones, Kristin L. Olofsson
abstract: The Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) has proven to be a successful analytical tool for examining the role of narratives within the policy process; however, the analysis of plot is still understudied. This gap persists due to difficulty in developing valid and reliable measures of plot and a lack of plot operationalizations using longitudinal data. Inspired by Kurt Vonnegut's thesis on the shape of stories, this study explores the extent to which policy narratives assume a generalizable shape and how that shape can contribute to our understanding of the policy process. Using 2014–2020 news media coverage of Ghana's energy crisis, we reconceptualize plot as a temporal story arc captured through the media's affective evaluations of policy events, reflecting how the policy problem is framed across time. To achieve this, we apply sentiment analysis to news media coverage of policy events and aggregate them into a sentiment score. This score is then plotted over time to visually depict the shape of Ghana's energy crisis story. Our results reveal that this shape closely mirrors Vonnegut's Man in Hole story, suggesting that policy narratives may adhere to generalizable story arcs. Theoretically, these results contribute to our understanding of time and sentiment within the NPF, opening avenues for future research. Methodologically, this paper provides an empirical blueprint for capturing and coding plot variables in a reliable and replicable manner.

title: A Narrative Walks Into a Forum: Bridging the Narrative Policy and Ecology of Games Frameworks
authors: Rachel McGovern, Danielle M. McLaughlin, Jack Mewhirter, Michael D. Jones
abstract: Policy process research has expanded rapidly, yet many frameworks still develop in silos, limiting dialogue and leaving complementary mechanisms underused. In an effort to bridge these silos, we bring together two influential frameworks that have largely developed in parallel: the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) and the Ecology of Games Framework (EGF). We integrate them across three levels of analysis: actors at the micro level, forums at the meso level, and interconnected systems of forums at the macro level. At the actor level, we connect the EGF and NPF through learning, showing how narrative learning clarifies the mechanisms behind EGF learning processes, while the EGF helps the NPF specify the conditions under which learning is more or less likely. At the forum level, we develop concepts of narrative convergence and divergence to explain cooperation and conflict within collective‐choice venues. At the system level, we show how both frameworks help explain policy spillovers and ultimately, system performance. In doing so, we aim to begin a conversation between two seemingly disparate frameworks, offering preliminary but intentionally non‐exhaustive set of propositions and ideas about where the frameworks align, diverge, and where their integration is most theoretically and empirically productive.

title: Supply‐Side Policy Feedback
abstract: The scholarship on policy feedback has been among the most plentiful and successful of the policy sciences. Much of it has focused on the demand‐side, or on the political relationship between a public policy and its recipients. Less attention has been paid to the supply‐side: the political relationship between a public policy and its providers. Parents may care about education, patients about health care, and prisoners about criminal justice—but an emerging literature shows that teachers, hospital employees, and the police care just as, if not more, about these areas. This article builds on new work to introduce a theory of supply‐side policy feedback and outline a research agenda for its further investigation.

title: Elite Interactions and Social Bonds: How Partisan Cooperation Shapes Perceptions of Cross-Party Friendships
Words with Consequences: The 2016 Election and International Student Visa Demand in the United States
abstract: This paper examines whether the 2016 US presidential election altered international student mobility by transforming campaign rhetoric into a credible signal of future policy and social risk. Using country–year data on F-1 visa issuances and active international student enrollments, the analysis studies how international students from countries explicitly targeted during the campaign responded to the election outcome. Two-way fixed effects models and event study specifications are used to trace both average post-election effects and their dynamic evolution. The results indicate a sharp post-election reversal in new international student inflows among targeted countries. Event study estimates show that, prior to 2016, F-1 visa issuances from Muslim-majority and Arab World countries grew faster than those from a plausibly less-affected comparison group. This upward trajectory reverses in FY2017, with visa issuances falling and remaining persistently lower in subsequent years. In contrast, active international student enrollments exhibit substantially more muted responses, reflecting the stock nature of enrollment outcomes and the continued presence of cohorts admitted prior to the election. Together, these findings indicate that the election primarily affected entry decisions rather than inducing immediate exits among enrolled students.

title: The Quest for Freedom and Migration Aspirations: Evidence from the MENA Region
abstract: This article develops and empirically tests a theory of migration under repression. It argues that migration aspirations are shaped by perceived freedom repression and that such perceptions can make exit more attractive when voice appears blocked, risky, or ineffective. The theoretical framework yields four hypotheses, which we test using Arab Barometer data from 2021 to 2024 covering about 34,000 respondents in 12 Middle East and North Africa (MENA) countries. Empirically, we construct a Freedom Repression Index and examine how perceived repression shapes migration aspirations across different freedom dimensions and migration routes. Four findings stand out. First, perceived repression significantly increases migration aspirations, with substantive effects comparable to standard economic push factors. Second, the association is strongest for personal liberties, especially freedom of expression and freedom of religion, whereas restrictions on collective political rights such as protest are less strongly associated with migration aspirations. Third, repression shifts intentions toward irregular rather than regular migration routes. Fourth, this relationship is context-dependent; it is strongest in stable yet restrictive settings and weakens in conflict-affected contexts where insecurity dominates. By disaggregating freedom dimensions and distinguishing regular from irregular intentions, the article connects exit-voice theory to micro-level evidence and clarifies when, which, and how perceived repression shapes migration aspirations in the MENA region.

title: Who deserves protection? Deservingness, intergroup contact, and public support for gig workers’ rights
authors: Anna Wilson, Carlo Dimitri, Juliana Chueri
abstract: The rapid expansion of platform-mediated gig work has intensified debates over whether gig workers should receive social and employment rights comparable to those of standard employees. Yet, despite its high political salience, we know little about how citizens evaluate gig workers’ entitlement to such protections. Gig work, especially in ride hailing and food delivery, is often precarious, with a lack of control at work, weaker contribution records, and overrepresentation of migrant workers—aspects that previous research has identified as central to welfare deservingness judgments. This makes deservingness a particularly relevant lens for analysing public support for gig workers’ rights. With a pre-registered factorial vignette experiment in a six-country survey (Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom), we examine the general population’s willingness to pay for ride-hailing gig workers’ improved rights. We find that support for improved rights closely follows core deservingness dimensions: workers perceived as in need, showing effort on the job and lacking control receive higher support, whereas migrant status and low reciprocity reduce it. Yet, deservingness cues explain only part of the variation. Exploratory analyses show that frequent use of gig services and personal ties with gig workers associate with a higher willingness to pay, showing the relevance of intergroup contact.

title: Does citizen deliberation inside representative institutions enhance legitimacy among non-participating publics?
authors: Adele Webb, Max Grömping, Marlene Mauk
abstract: Claims that citizen deliberation can strengthen public confidence in democracy rest on the assumption that it enhances the perceived procedural legitimacy of democratic governance. We test this assumption by examining whether integrating deliberative constituent forums into electoral-representative institutions increases perceived legitimacy among non-participating publics and which specific features of such forums drive these diffuse effects. We extend existing experimental research on democratic innovations by theorising that the deliberative norms of consequentiality and listening shape legitimacy judgements. Drawing on a nationally representative survey vignette experiment in Australia, we show that even minimal, realistic exposure to information about a deliberative citizens’ panel informing a parliamentary committee produces a modest but statistically significant increase in perceived procedural legitimacy. These gains depend on signals that citizens’ input is taken seriously and that participants are sincerely listened to. While legitimacy declines when deliberative input is ignored, the strongest positive effects arise when processes visibly communicate high-quality listening by political representatives. Moreover, legitimacy gains are strongest among respondents with low institutional trust. The findings demonstrate that the legitimacy-enhancing potential of deliberative innovations hinges not only on institutional design but also on the perceived relational quality of engagement between constituents and decision-makers. This contributes to ongoing debates in democratic theory and political behaviour about when and why deliberative innovations can rejuvenate representative democracy.

title: The winner–loser gap in democratic attitudes among politicians: Individual and collective outcomes
abstract: Rooted in concerns about losers’ consent to electoral outcomes, a vast literature documents a winner–loser gap in democratic attitudes among voters, with winners displaying systematically more positive attitudes than losers across a range of indicators. Surprisingly, we know much less about whether this gap extends to politicians. This paper addresses this question both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we distinguish between politicians’ reactions to electoral outcomes at the individual level – whether candidates secure a seat in parliament – and the party level – whether their party enters government, and theorise about their interaction. Empirically, we present comprehensive observational evidence from 27 elections showing that losers systematically report lower satisfaction with democracy, weaker support for representative institutions, and lower perceptions of citizens’ trust. The gap is present at both levels, but the individual-level gap is conditioned by party outcomes: it is most pronounced within winning parties and disappears within losing parties. A complementary analysis leveraging close races and administrative data from Iceland provides plausibility that these associations are, at least in part, causal. Taken together, the findings reveal that democratic attitudes among rank-and-file politicians are, like those of voters, highly malleable and responsive to electoral outcomes. While politicians maintain overall positive attitudes towards democracy, this malleability raises questions about when and how such contingency might translate into anti-democratic behaviour.

title: PRRP identity and sense of understanding for citizens who engage in political violence
authors: Fernando Feitosa, Bjarn Eck, Jean-Benoit Pilet
abstract: This research note extends existing knowledge on anti-pluralism among identifiers of a populist radical right party (PRRP) by investigating their sense of understanding for citizens who engage in two key forms of political violence: threatening and spreading false information about political opponents. Building on methodological advances in political science research, we estimate a series of Bayesian zero-inflated regression models using original Flemish data ( N = 2,963). Results reveal a positive correlation between PRRP identity and sense of understanding. Results further indicate that this correlation diminishes with higher levels of education in the case of spreading false information, but remains equally strong in the case of threatening. This research note offers new insights into anti-pluralism among PRRP identifiers.

title: Moderation or Amplification? Mapping Speech Distinctiveness Among Green Parties Using a Machine Learning Approach
authors: Clint Claessen, Denise Traber, Martijn Schoonvelde
abstract: How do issue‐owning parties adapt their rhetoric when transitioning from opposition to government? Focusing on the Green parties in Germany and Ireland, we analyze legislative debates to trace how these parties seek to maintain ownership of environmental issues. Using more than 1.7 million parliamentary speeches from the German Bundestag (1991–2018) and the Irish Dáil (1992–2013), we apply a fictitious prediction problem approach implemented as a multiclass text‐classification task to measure distinctiveness in parties' legislative speeches. Our findings show that both parties increased their rhetorical distinctiveness on environmental issues during their first time in government, but with key differences: the Irish Greens maintained a distinct profile throughout their term, while the German Greens' distinctiveness increased as elections neared. No such patterns emerge for welfare, a non‐owned issue. Our study offers a framework and a transferable method for studying how smaller parties navigate between coalition influence and visibility through the issues they own.

title: The Legislative Effectiveness of Congressional Oversight Reports
abstract: This article assesses the linkage between the House and Senate oversight committees' reports and subsequent legislative efforts in those policy areas from the 106th to the 116th Congresses (1999–2020). The analysis finds support for the three proffered hypotheses. First, the policy topics covered in the reports spur the referral of bills on those topics to the oversight committees. Second, the oversight reports on topics that the majority staff releases are more reflected in downstream legislative activity than the topics covered in the minority staff reports. Finally, the majority's advantage in pushing legislation related to its oversight reports' topics is greater in the House than it is in the Senate. These initial findings substantiate the importance of gathering and coding congressional oversight reports for not only how Congress conducts oversight, but also how it legislates.

title: Love in a “hopeless” place? Courtship, intimacy, and romance in displacement
abstract: Even in the midst of war and displacement, love persists. Yet, these lived realities remain mostly absent from refugee studies and from the vast body of literature on mass internal displacement and encampment in northern Uganda specifically. In this article, I document different narratives of romance, intimacy, love, and compassion in the context of Ugandan IDP camps and situate those accounts alongside a recognition of the harms caused by a decade of mass forced displacement, including their profound disruption of social-moral-intimate orders. Drawing on ethnographic insights, the article offers two key observations and arguments: I show that relations of love can be remarkably resilient, resistant, and adaptive, even in the face of adversity and despite divergences between lived realities and idealized notions. I also demonstrate how love and intimacy in the midst of violence can facilitate hope, perspective, and survival for displaced people, attesting to the power of love.

title: ‘Duty-bearers’ in the governance of durable solutions for internally displaced persons in Ethiopia: an actor-oriented approach
abstract: The notion of duty-bearers in forced displacement research is often confined to states. Yet, the responsibilities of humanitarian organizations in the governance of durable solutions for internally displaced persons remain scant in academic scholarship. This study goes beyond a formal and legalistic understanding of duty-bearers’ responsibilities and explores affected communities’ perspectives in the displacement context in the Tigray region, Ethiopia. Based on ethnographic interviews and focus group discussions conducted in Tigray and Addis Ababa in 2024 and 2025 and grounded in an actor-oriented approach, the study argues for moving from the top-down imposition of norms to value the affected community’s agency in shaping duty-bearer norms from below. This is in opposition to commonly held notions that duty-bearer norms are merely a top-down imposition by formal state-sanctioned rules and instead advances a multiple duty-bearer framework, with empirical evidence from the ground where accountability of duty-bearers is claimed and contested.

title: ‘It felt wrong’: emotional labour and the everyday reconfiguration of refugee governance in Cameroon
abstract: This article examines how emotional labour shapes the everyday implementation of forced migration governance. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in Cameroon, it explores how refugee aid providers’ emotional responses—including frustration, empathy, and ethical discomfort—inform situated forms of judgement in their daily work. Building on the emotional turn in the social sciences, emotions are conceptualized as epistemic dispositions through which actors interpret institutional tensions and, in some cases, act upon them. The analysis identifies three pathways through which emotional labour contributes to reconfiguring refugee assistance from within: pragmatic adaptations that soften bureaucratic rigidity; improvised forms of inclusion and relational alliances that challenge categorical boundaries; and structural engagements that support alignment with state institutions. These findings show how emotional labour makes visible institutional contradictions and informs practical adjustments, while remaining shaped by organizational constraints and unequal power relations, offering a more situated and embodied understanding of refugee governance in practice.

title: The Bureaucratic Paradox of Citizen Agency: Institutional Crowding‐Out in Government‐Catalyzed Co‐Production in Shanghai, China
authors: Huanming Wang, Xiaoyun Sun, Bing Ran
abstract: Public service co‐production is often framed as a means of creating public value, yet its dynamics are complex when citizen‐led participation is catalyzed by strong public institutions. This mixed‐methods study examines government‐catalyzed, citizen‐centric co‐production in Shanghai, China, where the state provides institutional support, policy legitimacy, and infrastructure while citizens undertake much of the work of deliberation, coordination, and implementation. Drawing on 246 interviews and survey data from 1476 residents involved in community new infrastructure projects, we examine how citizen trust, public‐service‐oriented motivation, and perceived co‐production efficacy are associated with process and outcome value creation, and how perceived institutional settings condition these relationships. The findings show that citizen cognitive factors are positively associated with value creation, while stronger perceived institutional settings can negatively moderate these relationships. Recursive qualitative analysis suggests two mechanisms that help interpret this pattern: formal rigidity may crowd out citizen agency in the co‐production process, while informal social density may generate lock‐in effects that weaken the translation of trust into substantive outcomes. The study contributes to co‐production and institutional theory by specifying the boundary conditions under which institutional support becomes over‐institutionalization. Effective co‐production requires not less government, but strong enabling support at the initiation stage combined with greater local discretion, participatory rule revision, and flexible enforcement.

authors: Amnon Cavari, Asif Efrat, Omer Yair
abstract: The norm against conquest—a central tenet of the international order—is eroding. This study is among the first to examine public support for this norm, using a real-world case: Israel’s seizure of Syrian territory following the collapse of the Assad regime in December 2024. Our survey experiment in Israel reveals that citizens are sensitive to the prohibition on conquest. They demonstrate greater support for an occupation that involves only military control of the forcibly seized territory and weaker support for civilian settlement in or annexation of the foreign territory: policies that amount to conquest. Our finding—a stronger preference for legally acceptable occupation over illegal settlement or annexation—sends a positive signal for the constraining power of norms.

title: Institutional Amnesia and Public Administration: Does History Repeat?
authors: Alastair Stark, Hridesh Gajural, Jack Corbett, Dennis C Grube, Heather Lovell, Rodney Scott
abstract: Existing research suggests that a lack of institutional memory causes history to repeat in problematic ways within public administration agencies. However, this claim has not been well supported by theory or data that illuminates the process and effects of history repeating. To remedy this, the nascent concept of institutional amnesia is presented here as a means of theorizing repetitions of public administrative history. A sequential explanatory mixed method research design uses quantitative survey data (n=1608) and qualitative interview data (n=75) generated in the public services of Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom to show how institutional amnesia can lead to the recycling of ideas and practices, the inefficient relearning of information seeking processes and the delivery of conducive decision-making environments that can help address historical problems. These findings draw attention to the fact that administrative history does indeed repeat in public agencies because of institutional amnesia, but that it does so in positive as well as negative ways.

The exact variance of the average treatment effect estimator in cluster randomised controlled trials
abstract: In cluster randomised controlled trials (CRCTs) with finite populations, the exact design-based variance of the Horvitz-Thompson (HT) estimator of the average treatment effect (ATE) depends on the joint distribution of unobserved, cluster aggregates of potential outcomes and is therefore not point-identified. We study a two-stage sampling design in which clusters are sampled at random, units are then sampled within selected clusters, and treatment is assigned at the cluster level. We first derive the exact design-based variance of the HT estimator of the ATE, accounting for cluster sampling, within-cluster sampling, and treatment assignment. We then extend Aronow et al. (2014) to derive sharp bounds for an estimated variance based on estimated cluster totals and propose a feasible consistent estimator of the upper bound. In simulations and an empirical application, confidence intervals based on the proposed upper-bound estimator are typically narrower than those based on conventional cluster-robust standard errors.

title: The long shadow of the past: How Irish history shapes attitudes towards the Israel–Palestine conflict
abstract: Why do some publics engage deeply with distant conflicts absent direct ethnic or strategic ties? Existing explanations emphasise geopolitical ties, demographics, or elite cues, but these cannot account for the Republic of Ireland’s consistent pro-Palestinian stance, exceptional in Western Europe and central in shaping Irish state behaviour, international coalitions, and bilateral relations. We argue that historical narratives – particularly those rooted in anticolonial struggle – provide cognitive and affective mechanisms that shape public attitudes to foreign conflict. Using novel survey measures and open questions on a representative sample of Irish respondents (1547), we find that sympathy for Palestinians is broad-based, deeply held, and closely tied to perceptions of Irish historical oppression and unity. These results hold after accounting for ideology and party cues. Given its prominence in public debate, we also test antisemitism as an explanation. We find low levels of antisemitism and higher levels of Islamophobia, indicating that general pro-Palestinian sympathy is driven neither by prejudice toward Jews nor particular affinity toward Muslims. Open-ended responses show Irish respondents spontaneously draw analogies between Ireland’s colonial past and the Palestinian experience. Our findings highlight the long shadow of national history in shaping contemporary foreign policy attitudes.

title: Representations of nuclear risk in the UK Parliament: Understanding the role of political discourse in the development of preparedness activity for nuclear accidents
abstract: This article argues that despite a prevailing national preparedness imperative, significant vulnerabilities persist in the UK’s emergency arrangements for a nuclear accident. While such an imperative may drive legislation and the legitimation of emergency planning, its integrity can be compromised by other institutional and discursive factors. We propose that social representations of nuclear risk in UK parliamentary debates play a key role in shaping the conditions for anticipatory action. Through a discourse analysis of debates following three major nuclear accidents, Windscale (1957), Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011), we identify the emergence of a dominant nuclear energy metanarrative, which frames nuclear power as safe, necessary and nationally beneficial. We argue this metanarrative has contributed to the marginalisation of central government preparedness by shifting responsibility to local authorities and regulators and fostering potential overconfidence in structural mitigations, thereby narrowing the conditions under which nationally coordinated anticipatory action becomes possible.

title: Algorithmic imaginaries: Definition and critical questions
authors: Andreas Schellewald, Ellenrose Firth, Hui Lin
abstract: Algorithmic systems play an increasingly central role across a variety of social domains. Over the last few years, various concepts have been developed in the interdisciplinary field of algorithm studies to understand how people make sense of these systems and interact with them – including mental models of algorithms, folk theories of algorithms, or algorithmic imaginaries. This theoretical article engages with the concept of the algorithmic imaginary in particular. It argues that the concept of the algorithmic imaginary occupies a unique position in literature, foregrounding questions of affect and emotion in human-algorithm interaction, and theorising the dynamics of sense-making about algorithms in such terms. Critically examining work that has explicitly applied and developed the concept, we synthesise the scholarship, offer an updated definition, and pose critical questions for future research, including on emergent artificial intelligence phenomena.

title: Posting under pressure: Politicians active on social media are more stressed
abstract: While social media has become an indispensable tool for politicians’ communication with citizens and other stakeholders, emerging qualitative evidence suggests that its use may be associated with diminished well-being and reduced performance within the parliamentary arena – potentially undermining democratic processes. Combining insights from a representative survey study of politicians in Denmark ( n = 1233) with data on their observed social media usage (Facebook: 24,625 posts; Instagram: 13,019 posts), this study is the first to test the generalizability of this emerging evidence and advance our theoretical understanding of the conditions under which politicians’ social media usage is connected to stress. The study demonstrates a significant, positive correlation between politicians’ social media usage and self-reported stress symptoms and points to excessive usage as the primary explanation behind the association. Furthermore, exposure to online harassment is a crucial mediating factor in the association.

title: Rendering the whole world blank: Precarity, totalising fear and digital scrolling
abstract: This article explores the connection between structurally induced precarity and the material practice of digital scrolling in the global north. It argues in favour of an expanded definition of precarity and that precarity, as a generalised affective condition, results in a state of totalising fear (fear which relates, at once, to discrete objects as well as the world itself). In that context, this article advances the claim that scrolling can be understood as an affective attachment (of the kind outlined by Lauren Berlant), developed in response to totalising fear, and which enables the subject to suspend time and to escape from conscious experience of precarity. In establishing this conclusion, the article also explores how the form of scrolling engenders an absorbing, passive and essentially ‘blank’ experience of the world, and how the attainment of this state is an expression of a limited, precarious mode of agency.

title: Care, competence, or control? The evolution of parental supervision tools on social media platforms: A cross-platform comparison
authors: Amanda Cipriani, Tama Leaver, Michele Willson
abstract: Interaction with social media constitutes a significant part of children’s online experiences, with the potential for both positive and negative experiences. Social media platforms provide parental “supervision tools” as a mechanism for balancing children’s autonomy with safeguards, promoting this function to parents to ensure safer digital practices for their children. This research adopts a constructivist framework to investigate the evolution and operationalisation of parental supervision across Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok. Utilising qualitative methodology, this study combines archival data from an ethnographic walkthrough conducted in 2024, simulating a child’s and parent’s account for each platform. The cross-platform comparison reveals how platforms construct parental responsibility through their discursive and interface supervision mechanisms, expressed through macro-narratives, meso-contexts, and micro-practices. In doing so, platforms shift responsibility for regulation to parents as the accountable supervisory actors, while ultimately also controlling the supervision practices of these parents through the affordances and constraints offered through supervision tools.

title: Success and failure in complex collective decision making: The Random Exchange Decide model
authors: Frans N Stokman, Jelmer Draaijer, Jacob Dijkstra, Marcel ALM van Assen
abstract: We present the Random Exchange model, an extension of the bilateral exchange model of collective decision-making of Stokman and Van Oosten. Compared to more elementary models, the Random Exchange model generates predictions of the process leading to the outcome and enhances understanding of deadlock or difficulties in the negotiation process. After explaining its logic, the Random Exchange model is applied to collective decision-making in the international setting of two climate agreements, chaired by the European Union; the 2009 Climate Conference of Parties (COP) in Copenhagen, and the 2015 COP in Paris. The applications show how Random Exchange model not only may be used to predict collective decision-making outcomes but also deadlock when powerful actors attach high relative saliences to at least two issues on which they have opposite positions.

title: State debtcraft under illiberalism: rethinking financial repression and (de)financialization in Orban’s Hungary
abstract: How do states practicing financial repression balance orthodox and heterodox macro-financial policies while staying solvent? The article focuses on post-2010 Hungary as a critical case of financial repression, where an illiberal government reasserted state control over financial markets and actors, challenging the literature on subordinate financialization and financial nationalism in the semi-periphery. Introducing the concept of “state debtcraft,” the article highlights a politicized approach to sovereign debt management based on forging mutually beneficial, long-term relationships with market actors. Drawing on interviews and policy documents, we argue that the government domesticated foreign banks with bespoke policies favoring primary bond dealers. In turn, the foreign creditors consented to Hungary’s heterodox policies and financial repression, valuing fiscal stability and profits over liberal norms and refraining from penalizing the government in the bond market. This strategy hinged on favorable external conditions like low inflation and EU fund inflows, which eroded post-COVID-19.

title: “The Amazon warehouse within my store”: e-commerce adoption and conflicted industrialization in Southern California’s grocery industry
abstract: The growth of grocery e-commerce has commodified tasks previously done by customers. Scholars have studied the labor conditions of new e-commerce jobs in Amazon warehouses, dark kitchens, and delivery platforms. Yet little is known about how these technologies are impacting working conditions in grocery stores, where consumers still shop alongside employees. This article uses a case study of two grocers to understand how e-commerce is shaping working conditions and what factors impact the implementation of technology in the workplace. I first find that grocery store employees are experiencing the industrialization of work, where work can be rationalized and routinized, and high labor costs reduced accordingly. Second, this industrialization creates conflict in the use of space, time, and the meaning of work. Third, contradictory factors, including high costs, competition, and stalled automation shape the adoption of e-commerce. I reflect on how organizational context and imagined futures impact technological adoption and working conditions.

title: Redistribution through services? The case of childcare provision in Germany
abstract: Over the past two decades, public childcare services have grown to comprise a larger share of family-related benefits than cash transfers in Germany. Using German Socio-Economic Panel data and administrative expenditure records, we apply a microsimulation model to integrate public childcare expenditure into household incomes. For families with children aged 0–6, childcare services reduce the Gini-coefficient by 2 percentage points, though absolute benefits are skewed toward higher-income households: the top quintile receives over 34 per cent more than the bottom quintile. Regional disparities remain pronounced. In West Germany, the top income quintiles received the highest benefit increase between 2010 and 2019, while in East Germany the first quintile gained most. Counterfactual estimations show that increasing average hours of use and attendance for under 3-year-old children among lower income quintiles leads to a more uniform distribution of childcare benefits. These findings highlight the inequality-reducing potential and regressive distributional patterns of childcare expansion.

title: Elective affinities: growth models as structured sector–demand configurations
abstract: This article conceptualizes growth models as structured sector–demand configurations, extending existing approaches that focus primarily on aggregate demand components. Using OECD input–output data for thirty-four countries across two periods (1995–2007 and 2009–19), we create new measures of growth contributions by aggregate demand component, sector, and their intersections. Combining comparative mapping of selected countries, principal component analysis, and regression analysis, we identify two dominant demand patterns—domestic demand-led and export-led—and three sectoral patterns, centered on construction and domestic services, high-tech manufacturing, and low-end services. Demand and sectoral patterns are systematically linked: domestic demand-led growth is strongly associated with construction and domestic services, while export-led growth is positively associated with high-tech manufacturing and low-end services—representing “high” and “low” roads to export-led growth—but negatively associated with construction and domestic services. These findings suggest that understanding growth models requires examining the “elective affinities” linking sectors and demand.

title: Explaining inequality: economic elite narratives across Latin America
abstract: Drawing on 130 in-depth interviews with economic elites in Mexico, Uruguay, and Honduras, this paper analyzes how elites understand economic inequality by examining two distinct but related dimensions: their explanations of poverty and of wealth. The findings reveal cross-national variation informed by perceptions of institutional capacity. In Uruguay, elites primarily justify inequality through meritocratic narratives; in Honduras, the visibility of state failure renders individualistic explanations less plausible, leading the wealthy to acknowledge structural constraints. Mexican elites occupy a middle ground, acknowledging structural constraints on poverty while defending the merit of wealth. The analysis suggests that perceptions of robust institutions “free” elites to invoke meritocratic arguments. Conversely, in low-capacity contexts, the visibility of corruption and institutional weakness makes structuralist views more salient in elite reasoning. These findings challenge the notion that elites hold uniform meritocratic views, showing instead how they draw on local realities to frame their interpretations of inequality.

title: Colorism, Descriptive Representation, and the Representation of African Americans in the United States House of Representatives
authors: Danielle Casarez Lemi, Jennifer R. Garcia, Christopher T. Stout
abstract: Previous research overlooks how certain ascribed characteristics, such as skin tone, correlate with the representation of marginalized groups. Yet research also demonstrates how colorism shapes candidate evaluations and life experiences. We theorize that colorism, the systemic privileging of lighter skin, structures the motivations and electoral incentives of Black lawmakers. We hypothesize that darker-skinned Black members of Congress will better represent Black Americans on racialized issues than lighter-skinned Black members, depending on the form of representation: rhetorical or legislative. We test this hypothesis with a combination of human and computer-assisted content analyses of 204,806 press releases and 18,025 bill introductions from the 114th, 115th, and 116th Congresses and a crowdsourced measure of skin tones. We find that on average, darker-skinned Black members of Congress provide more representation in press releases, but not in legislation. Our findings highlight the need to examine diversity among descriptive representatives.

title: The War on Universities: Illiberal Tactics in Turkey, Hungary, and the United States
abstract: Illiberal governments increasingly target universities as sites of political dissent and ideological opposition. This paper compares three illustrative cases—Boğaziçi University under Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Central European University under Viktor Orbán, and elite US universities under Donald Trump—to examine how illiberal governments deploy state power against autonomous, high-profile, liberal-aligned institutions of higher education, and how students and faculty respond. Although universities are not always bastions of pluralism, tolerance, and democracy, attacks on universities are often concurrent with illiberal governance. We argue that illiberal governments perceive universities as vanguards of hegemonic liberalism and as partisan opponents in certain contexts, and that state repression operates along a continuum of coercion, legal displacement, and discursive delegitimation. These attacks on academic autonomy trigger varied responses—from mobilization, to fragmentation, to withdrawal—shaped by domestic political opportunity structures, the intensity of state repression, and campus culture. By conceptualizing the university as a contested political institution rather than a neutral educational space, this article contributes to broader debates on democratic backsliding, populism, culture wars, and higher education.

title: Reconciliation, Decolonization of Relationships, and Egalitarian Bi-nationalism: A Praxis for the Israeli–Palestinian Impasse?
abstract: In this article, I interrogate the theoretical architecture that underpins three increasingly influential normative prescriptions for a just political configuration in Israel–Palestine: reconciliation, decolonization of relationships, and egalitarian bi-nationalism (RDB-N). Although recent scholarship has attempted to integrate them into a shared framework, they remain insufficiently articulated, delaying the emergence of a transformative praxis. Here, I argue that the core impasse lies in the dominant “top-down” conception of reconciliation, which, by presuming that a postconflict political order is a prerequisite for implementation, produces a dependency that obstructs the normative potential of RDB-N as a coherent framework for structural transformation. In response, I advance a “bottom-up” conception of reconciliation that is both theoretically plausible and normatively desirable. This reimagines reconciliation as an implementation-driven and grassroots dynamic capable of initiating decolonial transformation and prefiguring an egalitarian binational future, rather than a postconflict process led by the state and its institutions. In proposing this theoretical rearticulation, I set the groundwork for a new praxis of RDB-N grounded in localized political agency. The analysis culminates in the Palestinian Community of Israel (PCI), whose liminal position and situated political condition potentially make it a particularly fertile site for developing such a praxis. Although largely theoretical, this contribution has practical implications for conflict resolution, settler-colonial critique, and political transformation in asymmetric contexts. It also opens avenues for future empirical and normative research into both justice in non-ideal conditions and collective action.

title: I Read the News Today, but Why? Media Consumption, Socialization, and Autocracy
abstract: Dominant models of news consumption in political science treat citizens as rational individuals, gathering information to make materially or politically consequential choices. This assumption, developed largely in democratic contexts, risks obscuring other incentives that may be equally or more influential—particularly in authoritarian regimes, where the informational value of news is often constrained. This article advances the concept of social rationality: the incentive to consume news to sustain conversations, reinforce social bonds, and participate in communities of shared meaning. Drawing on original survey data from Belarus and Russia—two highly authoritarian states with divergent approaches to media control—the analysis shows that social motivations are powerful predictors of both the intensity and breadth of media consumption, while decision-rational considerations also help to explain breadth. Divergent interactions between social motivations and intrinsic prosocial orientations in the two cases further complicate theories of “informational autocracy.” These findings challenge classical models and underscore the need to place social incentives at the center of explanations of media use.

title: Grounding Hope in Trust: The Case of Climate Activism
abstract: According to the standard definition of hope, for one to be hopeful, the desired outcome must be considered at least possible. The literature on climate activism has incorporated this notion of hope, but we argue that this notion alone cannot fully account for hopeful attitudes in situations where collective action is demanded. For hope to be justified in the case of climate activism, it must be supported by some form of trust. We then outline different forms of trust that can be found in activist practices to ground hopeful attitudes, including procedural and moral trust in institutions and in fellow citizens or activists. We finally argue that mistrust represents a democratic equilibrium between the activists’ duty to exercise vigilance and critique toward institutions and the need for institutions to be perceived as trustworthy by activists and citizens more broadly.

title: The Victory Trap: Endogenous Opposition Coalition Weaknesses in Reversing Autocracy
abstract: After opposition parties and alliances defeat dominant autocratic incumbents, what challenges do they encounter in reversing autocracy and what are the consequences? We argue that long-neglected endogenous weaknesses in opposition coalitions undermine re-democratization efforts, easily opening the door to autocratic comebacks. First, coalition intra-elite conflicts post-victory result in fractured and ineffective governance, generating mass disappointment with the new political elites. Second, coalition intra-supporter divergence pressures the new coalition government into implementing pro-democratic reforms at haphazard speeds and fluctuating scopes. Swift actions in reversing autocracy alienate supporters of the ex-autocrat, elicit accusations of partisan revenge, and fuel counter-mobilization against the new government. A most-different case comparison between the recent autocratic reversal experiences of Poland and Malaysia demonstrates our argument. We show in both cases that ideological and distributional conflicts among diverse coalition elites undermined governance after victory, and different supporter bases prioritized different policy agendas. Counter-mobilization by the autocratic ex-incumbents was highly successful in undermining public support for the new government. These findings suggest that profound challenges in reversing autocracy and rebuilding democracy lie within opposition coalitions themselves, in addition to authoritarian legacies.

title: José Carlos Mariátegui’s Archaic Developmentalism: Utopia, the Incan Empire, and Peruvian Reality
abstract: “Developmentalism” refers to the idea that human societies progress through a series of historical stages, along one path or multiple paths, which allows for the comparison and hierarchization of different populations. As numerous works have shown, developmentalism was often called upon to justify Europe’s domination of non-European populations, which were figured as backward or barbaric. To complicate the commonplace equation of developmentalism and empire, I analyze José Carlos Mariátegui’s political thought as a stratigraphic history in which different temporalities—especially archaic temporality, or the remnants of Incan communalism, and developmental temporality—were vertically stacked and in tension, and I elaborate a conception of what I call “archaic developmentalism.” For Mariátegui, while the past temporality, institutions, and practices of the Incan Empire persisted into the present, he did not perceive them as hurdles to be cleared on the upward march of progress. Rather, as I argue, Mariátegui recognized the political potency of Incan communalism’s remnants—particularly, the ayllu , or Incan communal form—and he conjectured that the collision of temporal-historical layers could open an alternative developmental trajectory by which the ayllu would be reactivated as a stage in the process of creating modern communism, skipping over the developmental stage of mature capitalism that was required by Soviet orthodoxy. In other words, Mariátegui thought that the friction generated by the convergence of Peru’s different telluric strata opened a new developmental trajectory in which remnants of Incan archaism could spark socialist struggle and be reconfigured as an arsenal of possibilities in the present.

title: The Returns to Viral Media: The Case of US Campaign Contributions,
authors: Johannes Böken, Mirko Draca, Nicola Mastrorocco, Arianna Ornaghi
abstract: Social media has created new, highly competitive markets for attention. But to what extent does attention on social media generate tangible economic returns and how are these returns characterized? Using a daily dataset of Twitter activity and campaign contributions for US Members of Congress (2019-2020), we show that attention on Twitter, as measured by likes, increases small donations. However, the effect is highly skewed: only a few members benefit substantially, consistent with a winner-takes-all market. These results are confirmed using a geography-based causal design tracking donation patterns across counties, showing that the increase in donations from attention on Twitter comes disproportionately from high Twitter usage areas.
journal_full: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Coupling Labor Supply Decisions: An Experiment in India,
abstract: Joint household decision-making becomes more common as economies develop. Can external intervention advance this transition? We study this question in the context of female employment in India. We randomized which spouse was given a ticket enabling enrollment in a women’s weaving job, and cross-randomized the other to receive no information about the ticket, information, or information and discussion with their spouse. Academic and local experts predict information and discussion should raise enrollment. Instead, information had no effect, and discussion reduced enrollment by 50%. We do not find an effect of giving the wife the job ticket rather than the husband. Our results show that interventions toward joint decision-making about an opportunity can lower take-up.
journal_full: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Homes for Ukraine: Understanding the Geography of Ukrainian Refugees and Hosts in Great Britain
abstract: The escalation of conflict in Ukraine in March 2022 triggered the mass displacement of Ukrainian people. In response, the UK government launched the Homes for Ukraine scheme, a private hosting initiative that urged members of the public to temporarily host refugees in their homes. As of December 2024, around 194,800 Ukrainian refugees had been issued visas through the scheme. Despite the significance of the scheme, little is known about the geography of refugees and hosts, factors that have influenced this geography, and how this geographical distribution shaped the temporary integration of Ukrainian refugees. This paper employs a mixed‐methods design, integrating qualitative interviews with Ukrainian refugees and those hosting them, with spatial mapping and regression modelling, to examine the geography of the Homes for Ukraine scheme. Our findings demonstrate that while hosting was geographically widespread, there were distinct regional trends, with more Ukrainian refugees being hosted in southern England. Various factors were associated with this distinct geography, including average income levels, as well as the availability of spare rooms. Finally, we show that many areas home to higher rates of Ukrainian refugees pose challenges for their temporary integration due to higher housing costs, as well as limited availability of social housing. These findings contribute to wider understandings of migration and refuge by demonstrating the significance of place‐based attributes in not only determining where displaced people are able to move but also in shaping their temporary integration into hosting areas.

title: From Integration Deficit to Imbalanced Integration: Digital–Social Mechanisms Across Places and Migrants' Mental Health
abstract: Migrants' mental health has become an increasing public health concern amid persistent social and cultural displacement. Although social integration is widely recognised as a key determinant of mental health, existing research has largely focused on integration deficits, while overlooking imbalanced forms of integration. We address this gap by examining superficial integration, in which frequent face‐to‐face interactions outpace migrants' sense of belonging. Using original survey data from Wuhan and multigroup structural equation modelling (MG‐SEM), we investigated how social integration influences migrants' mental health through digital‐social processes across generations. We found that the mental health consequences of social integration depend not on social interaction or belonging alone, but on their social asymmetries. Frequent interactions become psychologically detrimental when they are not accompanied by a corresponding sense of belonging, revealing the adverse effects of superficial integration. We further identified two complementary mechanisms underlying this relationship. First, social media engagement intensifies the health consequences of social integration by strengthening both the benefits of belonging and the psychological costs of interaction. Second, a stronger destination‐city belonging reduces perceived relative deprivation with respect to migrants' places of origin, thereby improving mental health, particularly among younger migrants. By moving beyond the deficit‐based view of migrant integration, this study highlights the importance of examining how integration unfolds unevenly across social, digital, and spatial contexts. Our findings call for policies that go beyond increasing social contact and instead promote meaningful, emotionally supportive, and locally embedded forms of integration.

title: A Biographical Approach to Understand Long‐Term Occupational Trajectories of Immigrants in the UK Labour Market
abstract: This study adopts a biographical approach to examine migrants' integration experiences within the UK labour market. It employs monthly retrospective data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (UKHLS) and the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) to identify distinct occupational trajectories experienced by migrants who arrived in the UK between 1927 and 2016. We identified five representative trajectories capturing labour market stability (i.e. stable paid employment, stable self‐employment, and stable family care), precarity (transitional unemployment) and enhancement (investing in education). Overall, these trajectories evidence that a high proportion of UK migrants experienced successful integration, characterised by fast and sustainable labour market entry, while only a small percentage (2.36%) experienced transitional unemployment. EU nationals were substantially more likely than non‐EU migrants to experience this success, despite being less educated on average and entering without prior job offers. Our analysis also revealed that gender, education, age at arrival, and ethnicity all significantly influence the integration process. They interact in unique ways to influence the probability of immigrants embarking on one of the identified trajectories. High national unemployment during migrants' year of arrival was identified as a consistent factor of labour market exclusion, indicating that initial inactivity significantly increased migrants' vulnerability to future economic scarring.

title: Imagined Majorities: Perceived Group Size and Population Replacement Beliefs in Turkey
authors: Evren Balta, Ezgi Elçi, Deniz Sert
abstract: Population‐replacement beliefs are often treated as an intensified form of demographic misperception. This article instead argues that they comprise three distinct layers: perceptions of the current migrant population size, expectations of future growth and the attribution of deliberate political agency. Using an original nationally representative survey in Turkey ( N = 1136), we test whether these layers form a single attitude or operate independently. Respondents overestimate the migrant population and expect further growth, yet current misperception does not independently predict belief in deliberate replacement. Projected growth is more strongly associated with replacement belief, while partisanship structures the attribution of hostile intent. Overestimation is concentrated among far‐right voters, whereas replacement belief extends more broadly across opposition constituencies. Socio‐demographic effects are weaker and less consistent. The findings show that replacement belief is not simply a mistaken assessment of present demography. It is a future‐oriented political interpretation that links anticipated group change to intentional agency. By demonstrating this layered structure in a majority‐Muslim refugee host, the article also shows that replacement belief is not confined to Western white‐majority settings.

title: A Duty to Care or a Duty to Comply? Gambling Operators' Interpretation of the Legal Concept of Duty of Care and Their Responsibility for Preventing Gambling‐Related Harm
authors: Maria Persson, Therese Reitan, Jenny Cisneros Örnberg
abstract: From the perspective of negotiated governance, this study examines how companies respond to regulatory measures that combine hard and soft elements, assigning them greater responsibility for addressing social problems. Focusing on the Swedish gambling market, the study analyzes gambling operators' interpretation of the legal concept of duty of care. While this duty obliges operators to protect gamblers from excessive gambling, what it entails in practice and how responsibilities are understood are largely left to operators to define. Guided by the concept of responsibility, the analysis shows that interpretations vary and it is unclear what duty of care aims to prevent. Despite variations, duty of care is often framed in terms of responsible gambling, thereby individualizing responsibility for gambling‐related harm, and the action plans largely describe compliance with other legal requirements. In conclusion, the findings suggest a need for greater regulatory clarity regarding the normative foundations of duty of care regulation.

title: Does Corruption Increase Inequality? Evidence From a European Fact‐Based Assessment
abstract: This paper examines whether government favoritism in public procurement generates negative social costs, even within redistributive institutional frameworks such as the European Union. Rather than relying on perception‐based corruption indicators, we employ an objective proxy of corruption risk—the share of awarded public contracts which received only one bid. This measure captures non‐competitive allocation and mitigates reverse causality concerns. Using static and dynamic fixed effects panel models, we find that procurement favoritism is systematically associated with adverse social outcomes across EU member states. Specifically, we document robust, statistically significant negative effects on educational attainment, income inequality, and poverty. Our results suggest that governance quality—and not merely the volume of public expenditure—is a critical determinant of social development, and that distortions in procurement processes can undermine the effectiveness of public spending even where formal cohesion commitments exist.

title: Rectifying injustices against humanity: communitarianism, Ubuntu, and restoration
abstract: How should we assess and judge the harm inflicted by egregious wrongdoing and how should we respond to such wrongdoings after they have occurred? These are the questions this contribution tackles from an African communitarian Ubuntu worldview that centres the humanity of everyone impacted in both its understanding of wrongdoing and remedy. It argues that restoration of shared humanity is regarded as the primary and ultimate function of justice in the African systems of political thought.

title: Pan-Africanism or Black internationalism? Evoking African political thought as political activism
abstract: The article examines the ideas of Pan-Africanism and Black internationalism as African political thought and core concepts in African International Relations. They acquire significant meaning through their framing as political activism or as theoretical frameworks aimed at advancing social and political change. Pan-Africanism has been understood as an idea and a movement for African peoples’ self-determination and solidarity worldwide and has been linked to the concept of internationalism, specifically Black internationalism. Both concepts call for solidarity between Africa and its diasporas worldwide, and they both evoke the ideals of self-determination and Black liberation. The article argues that the two concepts are deployed not as problem-solving theories but rather as intellectual activism. They are central pillars of African intellectual exercises that seek to change or transform the international system to reflect the experiences of Africans and Black people, who have historically been marginalized in both scholarship and practices of international politics.

title: International Relations in Africa: not without Indigenous knowledge systems
abstract: The field of International Relations (IR) has come under increasing and sustained criticism for producing and disseminating a particular reading of European history, one rooted in violence, as if it were universal knowledge. Generations of students, academics, practitioners, and policymakers have been taught and socialized into accepting this violent historical experience as the norm and, implicitly, as a reflection of human nature. As a result, the dominant accounts of IR tend to foreground competitive, conflictual, domineering, power-seeking, and exploitative behaviours as defining features of international life. This understanding of IR marginalizes and often ignores Indigenous ways of knowing that emphasize relationality, solidarity, mutual care, and cooperative forms of social organization. In this article, we argue that centring Afrocentric Indigenous Knowledge Systems (AIKS), particularly their conceptualizations of persons in IR scholarship, has the potential to move the field beyond its bleak and violent roots towards a more humane and relational epistemology. The AIKS-centred approach to IR is better suited to capturing the nuances of contemporary global life while speaking to the lived experiences of Africans and potentially other Indigenous peoples around the world.

title: Strategic desecuritization under asymmetry: from security opportunity to security trap
abstract: Why do actors that use security framing to elevate an urgent issue later soften, narrow, or recalibrate that framing, even when the threat remains acute? This article develops a theory of strategic desecuritization under asymmetry. We argue that securitizing moves can generate both security opportunities and security traps. They create opportunities by raising salience, securing recognition, and attracting resources. Yet under power asymmetry and geopolitical competition, they may also draw in stronger external actors whose security logics reshape governance and erode initiators’ agenda control. Security opportunities can thereby become security traps. To mitigate these traps, weaker actors may pursue strategic desecuritization: a discursive and institutional strategy that preserves urgency while narrowing security framing, limiting external strategic intrusion, and reasserting authority over issue governance. The article illustrates this mechanism through Pacific climate diplomacy, tracing the trajectory from the 2018 Boe Declaration to the 2025 Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration and the Pacific Resilience Facility. The argument contributes to securitization theory by distinguishing securitizing moves, full securitization, and security effects; reconceptualizing desecuritization as a strategic response to security framing’s autonomy-eroding consequences; and showing how institutional substitution enables weaker actors to reassert agency under geopolitical competition.

title: African systems of thought and IR: the road to epistemic justice
authors: Thomas Kwasi Tieku, J. Andrew Grant, Karolina Werner
abstract: International Relations (IR) has come under increasing and sustained criticism for marginalizing Africa’s intellectual traditions, rich history, Indigenous knowledge systems, and lived experiences. Several scholars of IR have argued that meaningful engagement with African contexts and thought would lead to better theory and pedagogy, more robust concepts, sharper analysis, and the study of issues that have greater relevance to contemporary global life. Despite the seriousness and widespread nature of the criticism, it is rare to find manuscripts in major IR journals that move beyond critique to demonstrate concretely how centring Africa in IR scholarship could transform the discipline or substantially enhance its analytical tools. This symposium takes up that difficult task by showing how a focus on African systems of thought can enrich IR’s conceptual vocabulary, reorient core assumptions, and expand the range of questions the discipline is equipped to address.

title: African feminisms in International Relations
abstract: Scholars of Africa’s International Relations (IR) have criticized how the continent is studied in IR and its positioning on the margins of the field. Though a significant portion of the IR literature on Africa focuses on gender, and women, African feminist thought has not been centred in this literature. In this paper, I examine how African feminisms can contribute to IR. I show that by drawing on African feminist thought, IR can address weaknesses in how Africa is studied in the field. Specifically, I discuss how African feminists’ understanding of the complexity of context, and attention to history and intersectionality, provide direction on how to study African states and societies and their interaction with the international.

title: IR Resource Bank: a tool for diversifying and decolonizing the curriculum
abstract: Spurred on in part by the large social justice mobilizations that began in 2020, recent years have seen growing calls for diversifying and decolonizing the disciplinary practices in the field of International Relations (IR). In response to these calls within the field and across academia more broadly, faculty and students in the Department of Political Studies at Queen’s University embarked on a project to produce a ‘Resource Bank’ highlighting and centring alternatives to Euro-American epistemologies, pedagogies, and ontologies that have thus far dominated the IR field. Drawing on our experiences as project managers of this Resource Bank project since its inception in 2021, we discuss some of the most salient issues and important challenges that emerged in the course of this work. We employ a postcolonial theoretical framework to tease out and problematize the Eurocentric foundations of the IR field and utilize the Resource Bank to reimagine research and teaching in the IR field.

title: Contrapuntal reading of ‘Africa rising’: seeing Africa in International Relations beyond the exceptional
abstract: How can we read International Relations from the perspective of Africa in a way that does not perpetually put the continent in a permanent state of exception vis-à-vis global politics? What strategies are available to study Africa without overhyping narratives of its rise or demise? This article contends, drawing on Edward Said, that adopting contrapuntal reading enables reading Africa’s place in international politics beyond narratives and counter-narratives of Africa moving from one exceptional state of despair to an exceptional state of prosperity with nothing in between. The article uses the ‘Africa Rising’ narrative and its counter-narrative of Africa as a place of perpetual lack, deviance, and demise to illustrate how to practically adopt contrapuntalism as a method and as an ethos when engaging African perspectives in IR. It argues that contrapuntalism is a commitment to practicing critical thinking and questioning Eurocentric modes of thinking when approaching mainstream accounts of the history, origin, or interpretations of any political event. Contrapuntalism acknowledges that dominant narratives need to be read side-by-side with narratives of resistance and that non-Western concepts do not always need to be translated or rendered legible by creating (forced) Eurocentric equivalents for them to be legitimate or valid.

title: Voting for populism? How ‘populist’ labels affect support for candidates
abstract: Many consider the rise of populism to be a major threat to liberal democracy today. At the same time, voters have given considerable support to such parties and politicians, with their average vote-share quadrupling in the last thirty years. Thus, while research realizes the potential hostility populism poses to the polity at large, it is unclear what connotations of the ideology exist to voters. Do voters recognize they are voting for a politician considered to be averse to democracy? Do they simply not care? I field a randomized survey experiment of 2099 respondents in the United Kingdom to measure (1) the effect labeling a politician ‘populist’ may have on their level of support, and (2) voters’ perception of the link between populism and democracy. Results suggest voters’ perception of ‘populist’ labels are largely dependent on the candidate’s left-right ideology, as well as the level of populist ideology of the voter.

title: Affective, but not ideological, polarization increases tolerance for undemocratic behavior
authors: Jordi Muñoz, Francesc Amat, Albert Falcó-Gimeno, Marc Guinjoan, Toni Rodon
abstract: Over the last years, there have been frequent claims that democracy may be endangered by polarization, which has the potential to push voters and elites to embrace undemocratic practices and hence pave the way for democratic backsliding. But what is more decisive to generate tolerance to such practices: ideological or affective proximity? This article examines the effect of ideological vis-à-vis affective polarization on support for undemocratic practices.
