By using a conjoint experiment fielded in Catalonia in a sample of citizens and politicians, we find that both voters and elites overall reject politicians with undemocratic attitudes in a sizable and consistent way. Among citizens, while ideological proximity does not mitigate punishment of undemocratic attitudes, affective polarization does: individuals with a more intense affection toward their candidate’s party are less prone to punishing him/her for eroding the losers’ consent. The article has important implications for our understanding of the relationship between affective and ideological polarization, and support for democratic undoing.

title: Macrodiscontent across countries
authors: Haofeng Ma, Jeongho Choi, Yuehong Cassandra Tai, Yue Hu, Frederick Solt
abstract: Public discontent with the political system has become an increasingly salient concern in recent years, with the argument that it undermines democratic stability and effective governance. Nevertheless, the understanding of the nature, trends, and drivers of political discontent remain debated, largely reflecting the constraints from available survey data and items in the construction of measurement. This article takes advantage of state-of-the-art latent-variable modeling to aggregate survey responses and a comprehensive collection of survey data to generate dynamic comparative estimates of public political discontent (PPD) for 136 countries and regions over 56 years (1968–2023). These PPD scores are validated with responses to the individual source-data survey items that were used to generate them as well as the democratic evaluation survey item that was not used in our estimation. Next, a cross-national and longitudinal analysis of PPD in advanced democracies (i.e., OECD countries) highlights that PPD has been on a rising trend, rather than merely trendless fluctuations. Our results reveal that these increased discontents are largely attributable to worsening economic conditions, including low average income, slow growth, and high unemployment rates.

title: Federalism and citizen preferences: a vignette experiment on policy-making in Germany – CORRIGENDUM
authors: Johanna Schnabel, Antonios Souris, Christoph Nguyen, Lena Masch

title: The State of Environmental-Economic Statistics: Puzzle Pieces Waiting to Be Assembled
authors: Eli P. Fenichel, Angel Hsu, Silvia Landa, Yating Ru, Mariana Camacho
abstract: Environmental changes and challenges, such as climate change and nature loss, are increasingly relevant to economic decisions. Evidence-based economic decisions require organized data. So, environmental data need to be organized in a way similar to, and connected with, existing economic data and statistics. Current approaches to environmental-economic statistics and data remain fragmented, despite a variety of efforts to unify them. We review environmental-economic concepts to provide a high-level framework for addressing the primary challenge of organizing existing environmental data within the economic statistical system. We connect environmental-economic statistics to a variety of use cases, focusing on uses aside from benefit-cost analysis and sustainability assessment. We then review and assess the state of existing efforts to organize environmental-economic data and statistics. We conclude with a discussion of emerging tools that can enable a next-generation approach to environmental-economic statistics and ideas about how to accelerate the process or organizing and integrating environmental data into economic statistics.

title: Innovation and the Governance of Outer Space as a Commons
abstract: The commercialization of outer space has accelerated faster than any other global commons, yet governance remains tethered to static frameworks designed by twentieth-century global institutions and national governments. This article examines how technological innovation endogenously reshapes commons attributes at a pace that destabilizes existing institutional models. Through comparative analysis of six technological domains (space transportation, in-space manufacturing, bioproduction, agriculture, nuclear propulsion and disposal, and satellite services), we identify sector-specific dynamics of congestion, market concentration, and undersupplied public goods. Our framework demonstrates that governance challenges arise less from fixed resource characteristics than from feedback loops between innovation development and institutional design. The findings advance three contributions: a conceptual model of shifting commons attributes, sectoral diagnoses of emerging coordination failures, and prescriptions for adaptive governance architectures, including modular treaties, polycentric arrangements, and public-private partnerships.

title: Air Quality in Sub-Saharan Africa: Measurement Issues and Empirical Challenges
abstract: Air pollution imposes large and uneven health and productivity costs in sub-Saharan Africa, yet evidence remains limited by severe data constraints. This review synthesizes what economists know about particulate matter exposure in the region, with a focus on measurement, sources, and implications for applied research. I review ground-based, satellite, reanalysis, and hybrid data products, emphasizing how spatially structured measurement error shapes empirical identification. I then assess evidence on health, agriculture, labor, and human capital, highlighting both credible designs and remaining gaps. The review concludes by outlining research strategies that integrate exposure uncertainty into applied economic analysis.

title: What Every PhD Student Should Know About Adam Smith
abstract: Widely known as the father of economics, Adam Smith lived in the eighteenth century. Smith was a polymath, and his magnum opus, The Wealth of Nations , is 250 years old this year. In this article, I suggest the nature of Smith's contribution to economics, moral philosophy, and political science. Scholars participating in these fields today tend to see them as separate domains of inquiry. Not so for Smith. I study three main aspects of Smith's political economics. First is his economics; second is his fresh understanding of the political and economic problems confronting the nations of Western Europe when they were developing; and finally (and more briefly) is his moral theory. As I show, the problems facing developing countries of early modern Europe were not unlike those problems facing today's developing countries. Smith approaches these problems from an integrated perspective.

title: The Macroeconomics of Market Power
abstract: This review surveys the literature on the macroeconomics of market power. Since 1980 various aggregate measures of market power, such as markups, profit rates, and market capitalization, have increased in the United States and around the globe. We find that the rise of markups is due in large part to the reallocation of market shares and to the rise of the inverse expenditure share on variable inputs, whereas output elasticities have not risen. We analyze the macroeconomic causes and consequences of this process and use a model to evaluate the potential mechanisms. Key is the underlying heterogeneity in the distribution of parameters, which passes through to heterogeneity in the distribution of outcomes such as output, the labor share, profits, and welfare. Focusing on aggregate measures of market power is misleading, as the same aggregate markups can be associated with different output and welfare. We conclude with a discussion of how competition policy can be a tool not only for restoring economic efficiency but also for redistribution, depending on how the markups and underlying parameters are distributed.

title: Monetary Policy, Bank Fragility, and the Modern Financial Intermediation
authors: Gregor Matvos, Tomasz Piskorski, Amit Seru
abstract: This article reviews recent research on monetary policy transmission through banks and the broader financial intermediation sector, and its implications for financial stability. Traditional banks remain fragile due to high leverage and maturity transformation, making them vulnerable to interest rate, credit, and liquidity shocks. Meanwhile, the rise of nonbank intermediation—now involved in most lending—has reshaped how credit is originated, funded, and distributed, complicating policy transmission and regulation. We examine evidence on six key adjustment margins of monetary policy transmission through banks and the financial intermediation sector: ( a ) balance sheet valuation, ( b ) loan retention, ( c ) securities holdings, ( d ) shadow bank lending substitution, ( e ) deposit substitution, and ( f ) bank-to-nonbank lending. These channels often reallocate credit in response to monetary and capital shocks rather than just altering its aggregate level, highlighting the need for a system-wide perspective that reflects the adaptive, interconnected nature of modern financial intermediation.

title: Navigating the Battlefield: How Social Media Platforms Respond to Governance Demands From Legitimacy Communities in Geopolitical Conflicts
authors: LeTian Cheng, Diyi Liu, Le Yang
abstract: Social media platforms have become central actors in governing online speech during geopolitical conflicts, navigating complex governance demands from diverse stake‐holding communities including states, civil society, and users. This paper explores these dynamics through an analysis of Meta, X (formerly Twitter), and TikTokduring the recent Russia–Ukraine war and Israel–Palestine conflict. We develop a framework categorizing platform strategies along two dimensions: activeness and alignment, leading to five response types: proactive, accommodation, avoidance, defiance, and disregard. Through analysis of 126 interaction events, we found three platforms’ distinct strategic approaches. Meta adopted the most proactive measures with clear inclinations to the Western states and calculated defiance against others. X's strategy shifted dramatically after Musk's takeover: from accommodation to defiance and disregard, though it made pragmatic accommodations under severe pressure. TikTok, risk‐averse, and geopolitically vulnerable, frequently employs cautious and ambivalent avoidance and disregard strategies. The findings shed light on how corporate strategy, institutional background, and geopolitical positioning shape how platforms construct their legitimacy in content governance.

title: Drops in confidence precede symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder
authors: A. A. Marzuki, L. A. Kosina, L. Dome, S. R. C. Hewitt, T. U. Hauser
abstract: Mental health symptoms, like those in obsessive-compulsive disorder, show pronounced fluctuations over time. However, little is known about the underlying factors driving these fluctuations. Whilst theoretical accounts propose that cognitive processes drive symptom variability, cross-sectional work is unable to effectively probe these mechanisms. Based on prevailing notions of doubt and underconfidence being cognitive hallmarks of the disorder, we investigate whether metacognitive processes correspond to obsessive-compulsive disorder symptoms. We employ a smartphone-based momentary assessment design wherein participants with obsessive-compulsive disorder ( N = 137) log instances of experiencing symptoms across 2-weeks. Participants also complete daily scheduled assessments and play a perceptual metacognitive task every two days. Our results reveal that metacognition is associated with obsessive-compulsive symptoms. Concretely, we find directional effects whereby reductions in both self-confidence and task-based metacognition precede occurrences of obsessive-compulsive symptom logs, but not vice versa. Moreover, confidence during perceptual decision-making is significantly related to self-reported confidence on a moment-to-moment basis, indicating that distinct metacognitive modalities may be interrelated. Results remain robust in the face of several sensitivity analyses targeting possible imbalances and missingness in the data. Thus, our micro-longitudinal study design provides evidence for cognitive distortions (both self-reported and task-based) preceding symptom escalations, signifying the potential for designing just-in-time interventions.

title: Public institutions for cleantech commercialization in the United States
authors: Em Finkelstine, Laura Diaz Anadon, Jonas Meckling
abstract: The United States has been building public institutions to promote cleantech commercialization since the 1970s oil crisis. The ascent of new industrial policy has accelerated this process substantially since 2020, resulting in a doubling of the total number of institutions by 2024. Introducing a dataset of 122 institutions, we show how institutions perform five functions: goal setting, coordination, derisking, imposing discipline, and external engagement. Further, we demonstrate how post-2020 institutions extend and diverge from historical trends, highlighting the recent buildout of planning capacity, the widespread use of conditionalities, and the pivot toward engagement with local and non-firm actors. We conclude with an analysis of how the second Trump administration is transforming the cleantech commercialization system through retrenching, redesigning, repurposing, and maintaining institutions. We offer a bottom-up, institution-level examination of the emergence and evolution of state capacity for green industrial policy in the United States, its functions, and current developments.

title: How sovereign control, decarbonization and energy costs shape public support for data centers
Strategic objectives underpin national climate pledges
abstract: Emissions-reduction pledges under the Paris Agreement are commonly understood as expressions of domestic preferences. Recent scholarship, however, suggests that governments may also use climate pledges strategically to shape the behavior of other political actors. Here, we provide an empirical account of these strategic objectives based on in-depth interviews with 40 policymakers and experts. We identify six key strategic objectives: attracting international climate finance, setting standards for others, enhancing status, preserving credibility, facilitating domestic action, and pre-committing future governments. International actors emerge as the primary target audience. These objectives have distinct implications for ambition. While most encourage stronger pledges, concerns about credibility can constrain ambition. In an exploratory analysis, we also examine how strategic objectives vary across countries. The findings suggest that higher emitters and states with lower levels of democratic institutionalization place greater emphasis on long-term credibility, while countries eligible for climate finance seek to attract it regardless of income or vulnerability. Our findings have implications for ratcheting up international climate commitments.

title: Measuring racial attitudes pre-treatment in survey experiments
authors: Leah Christiani, Nathan Kelly, Jana Morgan
abstract: Experimental researchers often need to assess the moderating effect of racial attitudes. However, it is unclear whether the racial attitude battery deployed may bias treatment effects. Less subtle batteries could bias treatment effects toward zero if measuring racial attitudes primes these attitudes for subjects assigned to all conditions, including the control condition. We assess whether bias is introduced across four conditions, pre-treatment: not measuring racial attitudes, using stereotype endorsement measures, using the American National Election Study racial resentment battery, or using the simplified Cooperative Election Study racial resentment battery. We do not uncover widespread instances of treatment bias. However, we do identify bias when the stereotype endorsement measures are used pre-treatment. We conclude with recommendations for researchers.

title: Debriefings in misinformation research should include fact-checks to correct misperceptions and increase perceived learning
abstract: Debriefings are a cornerstone of ethical research, especially when deception is used. In misinformation experiments, debriefings both disclose the deception and warn participants about misinformation. Unlike other misinformation interventions, they reveal that researchers deliberately introduced the falsehoods, raising concerns about trust and skepticism. In a preregistered U.S. experiment (N = 896), we compare no debriefing, a general debriefing, and a specific debriefing with fact-checks and source links. Only the specific debriefing reduced belief in false claims participants saw, not in novel ones. The general debriefing slightly reduced belief in true news, suggesting warnings may heighten skepticism. Both improved attitudes toward the study and perceived transparency, supporting the use of specific debriefings as an ethical and effective practice in misinformation research.

title: Right-wing terrorism and far-right support: evidence from anti-Roma attacks in Hungary
authors: Gabor Simonovits, Attila Gaspar, Bekes Gabor, Marton Vegh
abstract: How do ethnically motivated terrorist attacks shape electoral support for the far right? We study a unique case: a coordinated series of anti-Roma murders in Hungary in 2008–2009, the most severe episode of anti-minority violence in the country since World War II. Combining difference-in-differences and synthetic control methods, we compare attacked settlements to multiple counterfactuals, including planned-but-unrealized targets. We find that Jobbik, Hungary’s radical right party, gained 11–14 percentage points more support in attacked villages than in comparable controls in the 2010 election—an increase 53–70% larger than baseline trends. The effect persisted for several years and spilled over to nearby settlements. In contrast to some research from Western Europe suggesting that right-wing terrorism can reduce far-right appeal, our findings highlight how deep-seated prejudice can reverse this pattern. The results underscore the importance of antecedent inter-group relations in conditioning political reactions to ethnic violence.

title: Data-usage descriptors as search metadata: the case of food security data and the National Data Platform
authors: Lauren Chenarides, Rafael Ladislau, Natasha Noy, Manish Parashar, Simon Porter, Julia Lane

title: A survey dataset of 1,000 battery industry professionals with LLM-assisted free-text categorization
Make Campaigns Dance Again: The Trumpdance and the Memeaesthetic Logic of TikTok
authors: Cristopher Cepernich, Alice Fubini, Antonio Martella
abstract: TikTok’s mimesis-oriented affordances invite users to ‘perform’ politics through embodied, replicable templates. This article examines the Trumpdance – Donald Trump’s recurrent YMCA dance at campaign rallies – as a case of how offline events become a platform-native trend. Using the TikTok Research API, we collected 6799 Trumpdance-related videos posted during the final month of the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign. We extracted a stratified sample of the top 20% most-viewed videos per day and content-analyzed 1130 posts. Through Multiple Correspondence Analysis and hierarchical clustering, we identified six participation modes and modeled views and comments with negative binomial regression. Findings show that TikTok visibility concentrates on event-based remediation: clips of Trump dancing at rallies generate the highest expected views and comments, while supporter reenactments and playful appropriations circulate more narrowly. Discursive reframing and satirical remediation attract comparatively fewer views but can elicit intensive commenting, underscoring a split between algorithmic visibility and conversational engagement. We argue that ‘imitation publics’ support meaning-making and production but do not automatically translate into algorithmic visibility. Overall, the Trumpdance exemplifies what we label memeaesthetic: a communicative logic in which political performance becomes a shared aesthetic template for production and participation on TikTok.

title: Negotiating the Influencer Imaginary: How Everyday Professionals Construct Legitimacy on Social Media
abstract: This article examines how professionals in diverse fields create content on social media as part of their efforts to establish professional legitimacy. Existing scholarship has primarily focused on influencers and creators whose work relies financially on digital content production. Instead, we analyze the experiences of what we call everyday professionals: individuals who pursue full-time occupations while selectively adopting elements of the influencer “toolbox” to complement their practices. Drawing on 20 interviews conducted in Costa Rica, we show that performing legitimacy in the contemporary media environment requires professionals to increasingly grapple with the “influencer imaginary,” a framework that organizes ideas of subjectivity around notions of authenticity and commerciality. Our findings reveal that everyday professionals negotiate this imaginary in three interrelated ways: by engaging with the influencer identity itself, by reflecting on the motivations behind creating content, and by confronting the increased labor required for content production. This study highlights the normative weight of influencer culture across professional domains by extending the influencer imaginary beyond issues of subjectivity to encompass motivations and labor. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for understanding current transformations of professional legitimacy.

title: How far will citizens go for transborder ethnic kin? Public support for kin-state policies in Serbia
Museums of Eurowhiteness or museums of migration? Exploring the geographies of racialization through migration museums
abstract: This article explores the opportunities and challenges of Migration Museums as sites of knowledge-production and representation. Building upon contemporary debates that connect migration studies with research on race and ethnicity, I first provide an overview of which museums exist worldwide that are explicitly framed as ‘museums of migration’, meaning that their mission and permanent expositions concern migration (be it emigration or immigration), and that receive some kind of public funding or support. After tracing the emergence of 15 museums that respond to these criteria, I look at how these institutes understand and narrate migration and migrants, and how such narrations have changed over time. I employ a global blackness framework as a tool to reflect on the entanglements of race, racism, colonialism and migration, and on the existing absences in the representation of migration narratives. One pattern that emerges is that most migration museums worldwide have so far mainly centered the experiences of white European migrants, leaving other migration narratives and experiences untold. Yet a second pattern testifies to a shift in focus over the past decades, with museums acknowledging that many communities have been traditionally invisibilized, and increasingly taking some remedial actions to incorporate the lived experiences of indigenous, racialized and migranticized populations in their permanent exhibitions.

title: Men’s Labor-Market Decline and the Rising Correlation between Spouses’ Earnings in the United States
Open practices across science, software, education and other domains
authors: John Meluso, Cassandra Chambers, Richard Littauer, Nerea Llamas, Elizabeth Long Lingo, Marlene Mhangami, Beck Pitt, Violetta Splitter, Huajin Wang

title: Hierarchical resource rationality explains human reading behaviour
authors: Yunpeng Bai, Xiaofu Jin, Shengdong Zhao, Antti Oulasvirta
abstract: Reading is a pervasive and cognitively demanding activity that underpins modern human culture. It is a prime instance of a class of tasks where eye movements are coordinated for the purpose of comprehension. Existing theories explain either eye movements or comprehension during reading, but the critical link between the two remains unclear. Here we propose resource-rational optimization as a unifying control principle governing adaptive reading behaviour. Eye movements are selected to maximize expected comprehension while minimizing cognitive and temporal costs, organized hierarchically across nested time scales: fixation decisions support word recognition; sentence-level integration guides skipping and regression; and text-level comprehension goals shape memory construction and rereading. A computational implementation successfully replicates an unprecedented range of findings in human reading, from lexical effects to comprehension outcomes. Together, these results suggest that resource rationality provides a general mechanism for coordinating perception, memory and action in knowledge-intensive human behaviours, offering a principled account of how complex cognitive skills adapt to limited resources.

title: Homophily in grant evaluations
abstract: Funding agencies play a central role in science by awarding grants to researchers. Grant review can be influenced by bias, including preferences for applicants who share reviewers’ gender, country or citizenship. Using 37,073 applications for European Research Council grants with multiple reviews per proposal, we show that reviewers who share an applicant’s country of work or citizenship award higher scores than reviewers with no such match. This effect is strongest when both country and citizenship align. Shared gender increases scores to a smaller extent. Further analyses indicate that these findings are unlikely to be driven by shared tastes or informational advantages. At the panel level, correlational evidence shows that applicants are more likely to advance past the first stage when the chair or more panel members share their country of work or citizenship. Country of work and citizenship may therefore be relevant sources of bias in international grant review.

title: Human ticklishness is a widespread, culturally shared and bodily organized sensory experience
abstract: Human ticklishness is one of the oldest yet unresolved scientific puzzles. As early as the time of Aristotle and Socrates, scholars have speculated on its origins and function, but fundamental questions remain. Is ticklishness culturally shared or specific? Does it follow a structured bodily topography, and how does it relate to other bodily sensations? Here we analysed data from three cultural groups (Chinese, Dutch and Greek) and reveal consistent behavioural patterns and social dynamics. We extracted a high-resolution bodily map of ticklishness and show that it generalizes across cultures and individuals, and is distinct from maps of touch sensitivity, pain and pleasure. When tested against predictions from five historical and contemporary theories, we show that no single theory can fully explain the ticklishness topography. Although ticklishness is stronger in rarely touched regions, supporting Darwin’s hypothesis, its topography relies on a psychophysiological mechanism that is more complex than previously assumed.

title: Space for people, not cars: a large-scale visual choice experiment on urban street redesigns
authors: Michael Wicki, Claudia Sinatra, Aura Huang, David Kaufmann
abstract: Urban street reallocations and redesigns are central to sustainable mobility transitions, yet public acceptance remains a major challenge. While previous research has examined general attitudes toward transport policy, little is known about how specific design features shape support across diverse user groups. We conducted a large-scale stated choice experiment ( N = 5991) embedded in a nationally representative mobility panel in Switzerland. Respondents evaluated navigable 360° and static visualizations of redesigned fictional urban streets, varying in infrastructure, greenery, and social space. We examine effects on three outcome dimensions: acceptance, willingness to live nearby, and willingness to cycle. Greenery consistently increases support across both formats. How the redesigns are visualized shapes which features become salient: the 360° condition increases sensitivity to social features, while the static condition increases sensitivity to environmental and infrastructural features. Subgroup analyses reveal substantial cleavages by gender, age, transport behavior, and political ideology. The results show that design-sensitive, visually supported planning strategies can build broader public coalitions for urban street transformations. Our findings inform participatory planning and policy design for more inclusive and context-sensitive urban transitions.

title: Pupil Responses in Healthy Aging: Task Demands Shape Age-Related Differences
authors: Eszter Ágnes Kiss, Gábor Gesztesi, Peter Pajkossy
abstract: The locus coeruleus-noradrenerg (LC-NA) system plays a crucial role in optimizing performance in different information processing domains and changes in its function plays an important role in age-related cognitive decline. Because pupil responses are linked to LC-NA activity, we investigated whether the expression of age-related differences in pupil responses depends on the interplay between age-related LC-NA decline and compensatory cognitive effort. To this aim, we measured pupil responses during two tasks differing substantially in their demands on compensatory cognitive effort: an n-back task and an auditory detection task. We found decreased pupil dilation of elderly participants during the high-demand n-back task, whereas no age differences were evident in the lower-demand auditory detection task. These findings are consistent with the idea that age-related differences in pupil responses emerge primarily under high cognitive demands, whereas under more modest task demands compensatory cognitive effort may partially offset the effects of age-related LC-NA decline. The pattern of our results also suggests that no general age-related differences can be shown for pupil responses accompanying cognitive processing. In contrast, age-related differences are determined by the exact nature of the involved tasks, and the emerging pattern of selective deficits can be informative regarding the underlying neural background. Keywords: pupil dilation, aging, cognitive control, n-back task, uncertainty, LC-NA system

title: Who Works from Home, and Who Enjoys It? Gender, Parenthood, and Affective Well-Being in Britain Before, During, and After the Covid-19 Pandemic
authors: zhuofei lu, Matthew Henglong Luo, Yucheng He, Man-Yee Kan
abstract: Policy discourse in the United Kingdom presents flexible working as a remedy for work–family conflict, with mothers and carers as its principal beneficiaries. We ask who actually works from home, and who enjoys it, using UK Time Use Sur- vey diaries collected before (2014–2015), during (2020–2021), and after (2023) the Covid-19 pandemic. Uptake is measured as daily minutes of home-based paid work and as the share of paid work performed at home; affective experience is measured as episode-level enjoyment, modelled with two-way (person–diary) fixed effects among non-manual employees on weekday diaries. Working from home rose sharply during the pandemic and remained elevated in 2023, but mothers are not its principal users: in 2023 they record the lowest uptake of the four gender × parenthood groups. The affective evidence is period-dependent. Before the pandemic, women report lower enjoyment when working at home than on-site, whereas men report higher. In 2021, under lockdown, this pat- tern inverts: mothers show the largest positive home-working association of any group. By 2023 the lockdown pattern is gone: mothers, fathers, and childless women all report significantly lower enjoyment when working at home, and only childless men report higher. The one period in which mothers benefited was thus the period in which home-working was a universal mandate rather than a statutory entitlement. Flexible-working rights alone appear insufficient to deliver the affective benefits promised to mothers and carers; complementary care and workplace-norm interventions are required.

title: A qualitative analysis of the construction of responsible dog ownership in UK stakeholder policy and educational literature.
abstract: A variety of campaign and policy messages in the field of dog ownership and canine welfare centre upon the fundamental concept of ‘responsible’ ownership. However, what this is perceived to entail is unstudied, and important if the design of interventions to promote it are to be effective. Therefore, this study aimed to explore the meaning and stipulations of ‘Responsible Dog Ownership’ (RDO) within UK stakeholder literature focused on education of dog owners and the animal professionals who manage them. Primary literature concerning RDO and canine codes of practice in the UK was collected (10 documents), along with a google search for UK hits for ‘responsible dog ownership’ (16 documents). An inductive thematic analysis was performed on the 26 documents. Owners were described as having a duty, requiring commitment, to provide personalised care for the dog, by seeking out the advice of qualified professionals. Actions were required to keep the dog under control, healthy (physically and behaviourally), in a suitable environment, with appropriate identification, and not allowing the dog to foul. Perceived responsibility of the owner extended to carefully considering where and how they source a dog. Clarity of current guidance on RDO is challenging due to the advice to do different things depending on the dog and context. Owners and the professionals they seek advice from are also failing to meet the clear stipulation to use reward-based training techniques and not use aversive, punishment-based methods. This study for the first time distils multiple varied guidance into one clear set of recommendations, including a suggested ‘Are you a responsible dog owner?’ checklist. This can be used as a framework by policymakers and educators to construct more detailed localised guidance around the duties and expected behaviours of dog owners in regard to UK law and wider societal perceptions.

title: From National Accounting to Macroeconomic Flows
abstract: This study develops a macroeconomic framework that integrates the household, business, government, and foreign sectors. At the center of the analysis is the circulation of value and funds across the economy through cash flows associated with issuer-holder financing. The framework clarifies the relations among major macroeconomic aggregates. In particular, by treating money creation as part of value supply, it provides a systematic basis for analyzing how monetary operations affect transactions across sectors.

title: Firm Optimization across Capital Forms
abstract: This study derives a model of firm optimization across capital forms and incorporates the resulting optimality conditions into asset pricing. The structure of the problem depends on how profitability is modeled. When profitability is endogenous, optimization is grounded in production decisions; when profitability is exogenous, it is organized around operating profit. These alternative assumptions yield two asset pricing frameworks, each with a factor representation derived from the firm’s decision margins. By relating these representations to established pricing factors, the study provides a structured economic basis for reinterpreting established factors through firm optimization.

title: A General Framework for Equity Valuation
abstract: This study develops a general framework for equity valuation that unifies a wide range of valuation models within a coherent structure. It is built on a reformulation of key equity-related variables that preserves their economic functions, together with three exact identities that capture the fundamental links among them. These identities make it possible to derive valuation models under both fixed and revising expectations. The resulting models include not only familiar formulations but also new ones, underscoring the value of this approach for analyzing equity valuation.

title: A General Framework for Tax Shield Valuation
abstract: This study develops a general valuation framework that delivers internally consistent valuations for all forms of firm capital and for the tax shield associated with their combination. This consistency is achieved by incorporating the interdependence among the components of a levered firm’s cash flows. The study reexamines classical tax shield valuation models within the same framework and clarifies the conditions under which each arises as a special case. A central finding is that these models depend not only on stated assumptions but on an implicit assumption that debt is risk-free. This hidden assumption is more restrictive than it may appear.

title: Price Setting, Free Riding, and Equilibrium
abstract: We analyze strategic interaction among investors by distinguishing between price taking and price setting. The analysis shows that as price setting becomes more prevalent, equilibrium prices fall. Because this lower price benefits price takers as well as price setters, price taking can be understood as free riding on price setting. The gains from the lower price are distributed more heavily toward price takers. This asymmetry creates relative-comparison concerns, which can distort incentives and discourage price setting even when it would increase aggregate utility. We examine this problem through a pricing game and derive implications for strategic behavior and equilibrium outcomes.

title: A Macroeconomic Theory of Value Conversion
abstract: This study develops a theory of value conversion in which conversion depends on realized consumption growth. By governing value conversion over time, consumption growth becomes a key determinant of output’s market value and a driver of broader economic expansion. The theory differs from conventional macroeconomic frameworks in two respects. First, it redefines production as an internal technological process combined with an external valuation process, so market-valued output depends not only on production but also on converting latent value into market value. Second, it reinterprets macroeconomic relations by treating household consumption as the starting point of causality.

title: Ethical Influence of Behaviourally Targeted Political Advertising on Young Adults in Edo State, Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Yamah Abdul, Faith Ozikor Amah
abstract: The study was designed to investigate the ethical implications of behaviourally targeted political advertisements on young adults in Edo State, Nigeria, within the context of the rising trend of digital platforms and personal data use in political communications. The study was guided by Privacy and Surveillance Theory, which explains how personal data are gathered, tracked, and exploited, often against personal autonomy, privacy and democratic choice. The study used survey research as its design, and data were collected from young adults between the ages of 18 and 35 from Etsako West Local Government Area of Edo State, Nigeria. Using the Taro Yamane formula, the study established a sample size of 399, from which 396 valid copies of questionnaire were retrieved for analysis using SPSS. The findings revealed that behaviourally targeted political advertisements are not effective in promoting political participation and that the influence of the advertisements on political opinions is limited. Nevertheless, there are ethical concerns associated with behaviourally targeted political advertising. The major ethical concern was related to the invasion of privacy by political actors. Therefore, the study concluded that behaviourally targeted political advertising has a weak impact on the opinions of young adults but has ethical concerns related to privacy and data misuse. It recommended data protection and digital campaign regulations and the promotion of transparent and credible political communication.

title: Assessment of Gender Digital Divide and Participation in Public Discourse Online
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Princess Onyeoma Osife-Kurex, Igbafe A. Alonge
abstract: The study assessed the gender digital divide and participation in online public discourse among internet users in Benin City, Edo State, Nigeria. The objectives of the study were to examine the level of digital access among males and females, identify factors contributing to the gender digital divide, determine patterns of participation in online public discourse, examine challenges limiting women’s participation and assess the implications of the gender digital divide on democracy and public discourse. The study adopted the Digital Divide Theory as its theoretical framework. A descriptive survey research design was employed, while the population comprised internet users in Benin City. A sample size of 400 respondents was selected using a multistage sampling technique involving stratified and simple random sampling methods. Questionnaire served as the instrument for data collection, while data were analysed using frequency tables and simple percentages. Findings revealed that males had greater digital access and participated more actively in online public discourse than females. The study also found that poor infrastructure, high cost of data, lack of digital literacy, cultural restrictions, online harassment, and cyberbullying were major factors contributing to the gender digital divide and limiting women’s participation in online discussions. The study concluded that the gender digital divide negatively affects inclusive democratic participation and reduces women’s visibility and influence in online public discourse. The study recommended improved digital infrastructure, affordable internet access, enhanced digital literacy programmes for women, and stronger measures against online harassment.

title: Evaluation of Development Communication Strategies Employed in the Promotion and Sustainability of Environmental Campaigns in Edo State
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Bobby Eghosa Obayuwana, Gloria Ehimwema Ogono
abstract: The study titled Evaluation of Development Communication Strategies Employed in the Promotion and Sustainability of Environmental Campaigns in Edo State examined how communication strategies influence environmental awareness, participation, and behavioural change among residents in Edo State. The main objective was to evaluate the communication strategies employed in promoting environmental campaigns in Edo State, and the level of audience participation and engagement. Guided by the Development Communication Theory, which emphasises participatory and dialogic communication as drivers of social transformation, the study adopted a survey research design. A sample size of 400 was determined from a population of 5.1 million residents using the Taro Yamane formula. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire administered to respondents purposively selected based on their exposure to environmental campaigns. Descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, were used for analysis, with a benchmark of 3.00 for acceptance. Findings revealed that development communication strategies such as radio, television, and social media are highly effective tools for environmental advocacy, with social media emerging as the dominant platform. However, campaigns conducted in local languages were less frequent, indicating a gap in linguistic inclusivity. Respondents generally perceived campaign messages as clear and persuasive, though some noted that technical language limited understanding. The results further showed that while awareness and attitudinal changes have improved, tangible environmental outcomes, such as reduced pollution and cleaner surroundings, remain minimal due to weak community participation and limited follow-up mechanisms. The study concluded that although development communication has significantly increased environmental awareness in Edo State, its impact on sustained behavioural change is still limited by inadequate grassroots involvement and inconsistent message localisation. It recommended that environmental campaigns should strengthen community-based collaborations, adopt culturally relevant and localised communication approaches, and integrate environmental education into school curricula to foster long-term eco-consciousness.

title: Thematic clusters and emotions on x during Ecuador’s 2024 blackouts
authors: Oscar Molina-Bailon, Juan Ignacio Revestido, Antonia Ramírez-García, Jorge Márquez López
abstract: This study characterizes the conversation on the social network X during the prolonged blackouts that Ecuador endured in late 2024. For this purpose, 3,952 posts published between September and December were analyzed. The messages were grouped by semantic proximity, classified into affective-communicative categories, and their stability was verified; the daily composition was contrasted with the scheduled outage hours using models that respect the interdependence of proportions. The corpus was organized into four discursive functions—psychosocial distress, media framing, informational monitoring, and politicization—each with its own affective profile and shifting presence. The grouping proved consistent throughout the procedure. These profiles broaden the information offered by aggregate polarity and provide useful criteria for the field of crisis communication.

title: Effects of Cost Control Techniques on the Profitability of Listed Manufacturing Companies in Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Franklin Taiye Umaigba, Michael Jimoh Amedu, Doris Esohe Aiworo, Richard Usengbuwa, Ruth Abieyuwa Uhunamure, Endurance Izokun
abstract: The profitability of Nigerian manufacturing firms has come under sustained pressure from rising material, energy and overhead costs, currency volatility and intense competition, prompting renewed interest in cost control as a controllable lever of financial performance. This study examined the effect of cost control techniques on the profitability of listed manufacturing companies in Nigeria, disaggregating cost control into material cost control (MCC), labour cost control (LCC) and overhead cost control (OCC). Grounded in the Contingency Theory of Management Accounting and the Theory of Economies of Scale, the study adopted an ex-post facto design using a balanced panel of ten listed manufacturing firms over the ten-year period 2015-2024 (100 firm-year observations). Data extracted from audited financial statements were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and fixed-effects panel regression, with firm size and leverage as control variables and return on assets (ROA) and net profit margin (NPM) as measures of profitability. The three cost-control dimensions jointly explain approximately 57% of the variation in profitability (adjusted R² = 0.571; F = 27.4, p < .001). The results confirm that the systematic control of costs especially material and overhead costs is a significant driver of manufacturing profitability, corroborating recent Nigerian panel evidence. The study concluded that cost control techniques significantly affect the profitability of listed manufacturing companies in Nigeria over 2015-2024 and recommended prioritising material- and overhead-cost control, institutionalising budgetary control and standard costing and adopting contemporary tools such as activity-based costing and lean manufacturing.

title: Views of Owan West Local Government Residents on the Socio-Cultural Impact of Childlessness on Married Couples
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Johnson Oamien Okaigbuan, Godsent Onobhen Ibhate
abstract: In many African societies, marriage is expected to lead to child bearing and perpetuation of the family and childlessness is a significant reproductive health and social welfare issue. These experiences of stigma, discrimination, psychological distress, marital instability and socio-economic exclusion are common for married couples in Nigeria who experience involuntary childlessness. Although, there has been massive focus on the socio-cultural implications of infertility and reproductive health issues among married couples, there is a dearth of empirical studies on the same in Owan West Local Government Area, Edo State. In this study, the socio-cultural effects of childlessness on married couples were explored focusing on the causes of childlessness and the socio-cultural effects experienced by affected married couples. The study revealed that the childless couples suffer from serious social stigma, emotional trauma, family pressure, marital problems, humiliation, isolation and economic difficulties as a result of the cultural norms associated with marriage and child bearing. Women were also determined to be at a higher risk of being blamed regardless of the medical reason for the infertility. The findings showed that childlessness is not only a medical condition but also a serious socio-cultural problem that impacts on the wellbeing and quality of life of married couples. It suggested raising public awareness, expanding access to reproductive health services, psychosocial support programmes and community-based initiatives to combat discriminatory cultural practices, as well as strengthening social work interventions to mitigate the stigma and foster inclusive family support systems.

title: Arts-Based Storytelling in Science Dissemination and Knowledge Generation: Diverse Perspectives in and about Digital Society
authors: Bieke Zaman, Priscilla Van Even, Jonas Rutgeerts
abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping how scientific knowledge is produced, circulated, and imagined. Yet this shift also amplifies concerns about epistemic narrowing, as digitally mediated, AI driven discourses consolidate dominant narratives and reinforce cultural imperialism. This chapter proposes arts‑based storytelling as a potential response. On the one hand, we discuss the potential of arts-based storytelling as a form of science communication different from the typical one-directional dissemination. On the other hand, we examine arts-based storytelling as a speculative practice of creative imagination and knowledge generation through fabulation. Both practices share similar epistemic and democratic potential: they both set out to construct publics through inclusive forms of engagement and leverage the potential of creative modes of expression to foster plural ways of knowing and challenge hegemonic narratives. The chapter does not consider arts-based storytelling as a universal or flawless approach. We posit it as a complementary epistemic practice that becomes meaningful if practiced in an inclusive way with critical reflexivity towards its own situated nature, which is inevitably entangled with the very systems it seeks to challenge. Embracing this situatedness allows us to view arts‑based storytelling as a continuous negotiation of epistemic inclusion in a digital era.

title: Election Campaigns
abstract: In this chapter we explore the political science of election campaigns. We begin with the puzzle that originally motivated the study of campaigns: whether campaigns matter for explaining electoral behaviour. We then outline findings on the specific effects that campaigns have on turnout, vote choice, and mobilising activists. After this, we explore the implications that advances in technology have had in the development of data-driven campaigning. We conclude the chapter with a discussion of key methodological approaches and ethical considerations when studying campaigns.

title: Perception of Radio Portrayal of Disability among People Living with Disabilities in Ilorin, Kwara State
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Victor Olusegun Babatunde, Oluwajuwonlo Emmanuel Ayanwale
abstract: This study investigated the perspectives of People with Disabilities (PWDs) in Ilorin on radio representation of disability, particularly the radio programmes. A qualitative research design was adopted, using Key Informant Interviews to gather in-depth insights from 15 visually impaired persons in Ilorin. Media Representation Theory was used as an anchor for this study, which focused on how PWDs perceive the representation of disability in radio reports, the prevalent themes and frames in radio coverage, and the consequences of such representation for social inclusion and identity. Findings showed that there is significant improvement regarding the representation of PWDs in media, and in particular in the use of more inclusive themes, frames, and images. While the study did not focus on a particular radio programme but explored the various programmes the informants listen to, it also found that most radio programmes targeted at PWDs are anchored and promoted by PWDs themselves, while programmes handled by non-PWDs often fail to adequately reflect the lived realities of persons with disabilities. However, some non-PWD broadcasters with training in special education were considered more sensitive in their coverage. Despite the progress recorded, informants noted that awareness and representation of disability issues on the radio remain limited. The study finds that although radio has become more inclusive, there is a gap in disability awareness, inclusion of PWD voices, and disability portrayals that can promote social inclusion and minimise stereotypes in society.

title: Measuring Meaning on Video at Scale, from classifier to theory interpreter: From Classifier to Theory Interpreter in AI-Based Humor Annotation
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), has created new opportunities for measuring complex and culturally embedded phenomena. However, existing applications largely focus on textbased data and predefined classification tasks, leaving multimodal and interactional phenomena underexplored. This study proposes a framework for analyzing humor in video data by introducing humor events as the unit of analysis, defined as temporally bounded sequences linking an utterance, its multimodal delivery, and audience laughter. Using a large corpus of Saturday Night Live (SNL) clips, we extract and classify 5,690 humor events with a multimodal generative AI model. To examine how AI can annotate complex cultural phenomena, we compare three prompt strategies: a definition-based prompt, an interaction-oriented prompt, and a theory-informed prompt grounded in sociological theories of humor. Results show that the theory-informed prompt substantially improves performance, particularly for categories requiring contextual and multimodal interpretation. Beyond performance, the study demonstrates that prompt design systematically shapes how cultural phenomena are measured. While aggregate category distributions remain stable across prompts, label assignments at the event level vary in structured ways, indicating that prompts function as measurement frames rather than neutral instructions. The study makes three main contributions. First, it introduces an interactional and multimodal unit of analysis for video-based research, providing a concrete approach to operationalizing meaning in context. Second, it reconceptualizes generative AI not merely as a classifier but as a theory interpreter, capable of operationalizing sociological concepts when guided by theoretical prompts. Third, it shows that prompts themselves constitute measurement frameworks, suggesting that prompt design should be treated as an object of methodological scrutiny—potentially subject to evaluation and review in its own right. More broadly, the findings highlight that cultural phenomena are both structurally patterned and interpretively open, and that AI-based measurement inevitably reflects the analytical frames embedded in prompt design. Although annotating complex cultural phenomena remains challenging, the results suggest that generative AI offers a viable and scalable approach for video-based analysis when guided by explicit category definitions and theoretically informed prompts, providing a significant methodological advance over existing approaches

title: Fund Manager Beta in Tactical Asset Allocation
abstract: We show that realized returns are shaped by two opposing intertemporal forces. They rise with expected short-term returns but fall when risk subsequently increases. Successful timing therefore requires attention not only to favorable return expectations but also to future risk. This logic leads to a two-component specification of manager beta. One raises exposure when near-term opportunities are favorable, while the other lowers exposure when future risk is expected to rise. Market timing is thus represented as a tactical adjustment of portfolio exposure that seeks gains while limiting losses from subsequent risk increases.

title: Gendered Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence among Gen Z Social Media Influencers in Malaysia’s Content Creation Industry: Intellectual Property Challenges and Ethical Imperatives
abstract: This conceptual review examines gender differences in the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) by Generation Z (Gen Z) social media influencers and content creators operating online businesses in Malaysia. Drawing on recent empirical and policy evidence from 2025–2026, it analyses how male and female Gen Z creators differentially integrate AI tools into content production, audience engagement, and monetisation strategies within Malaysia’s rapidly expanding creator economy and high social-media penetration environment (Telenor Asia, 2025). Parallel attention is given to emerging intellectual property (IP) ambiguities surrounding AI-assisted and AI-generated content, alongside ethical concerns including authenticity, disclosure obligations, deepfake risks, cultural representation, and algorithmic bias. Findings synthesised from contemporary studies indicate functional differentiation rather than simple access gaps: male creators more frequently employ AI for technical and coding-oriented tasks, while female creators concentrate on text generation, creative writing, and aesthetic enhancement (Raza et al., 2026). Persistent gendered risk perceptions regarding societal harms further moderate adoption intensity, particularly among younger women (Stephany & Duszynski, 2026). Malaysia’s human-centred copyright framework under the Copyright Act 1987 leaves significant gaps for AI-generated works, exposing creators, especially those building personal brands, to ownership uncertainty and unauthorised replication of likeness or style (Wardi et al., 2025). The paper proposes an integrated ethical-governance and IP-reform agenda tailored to the Malaysian creator ecosystem and calls for gender-responsive AI literacy programmes, mandatory disclosure standards, and updated guidance from the Malaysian Intellectual Property Organisation (MyIPO). Implications for policy, platform design, and future empirical research are discussed.

title: Dual Exposure: Systematic and Systemic Risk
abstract: Systemic risk can be measured by the covariance between an institution’s return and the sector return. This allows systemic risk to be decomposed by decomposing the sector return. When the sector return is separated into a market-driven component and a market-orthogonal residual, systemic risk splits into systematic risk, reflecting exposure to the market-driven component, and net systemic risk, reflecting exposure to the residual. We examine how these two risk dimensions relate to financial sector returns, contemporaneously and intertemporally. Using a sample including the 2008 global financial crisis, we find that including both risks explains substantial variation in financial sector returns.

title: Ethical Challenges of Gamification in Healthcare and Health Promotion: A Systematic Thematic Analysis
abstract: Introduction: the concept of gamification provides possible solutions for the field of healthcare in terms of efficiency, and behavioural change. This work is a trial systematically highlighting the ethical considerations of gamification in healthcare. This research analyses the ethical effects of gamification on healthcare and health approach on a systematic basis. Methodology: the author follows a thematic analysis-based approach to highlight the themes of ethical challenges facing the implementation of gamification in healthcare and health promotion. This paper follows the PRISMA flow diagram for data collection. SPIDER and CASP checklist are used for search strategy and quality appraisal. Results and discussion: seven different themes of ethical challenges are identified in the literature including harm, privacy, manipulation and exploitation, inequality and stereotypes encouragement, data ownership, merging of the real and the virtual world, and the change of power dynamics. Such themes interact with each other in a thematic way that highlights a cause-and-effect relationship. Conclusion: the paper provides an interactive framework of ethical challenges scenarios. The author concludes that the use of different search words presented new themes in comparison to the previous work on the topic and the need for further widening of the scope of research for identification of more themes.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of the Graphic Design Landscape in Malaysia: Implications for Professional Futures and Higher Education Reform
abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into creative workflows has fundamentally altered the graphic design industry worldwide, with particularly pronounced effects in emerging creative economies such as Malaysia. This article examines how AI technologies have reshaped professional practices, labour dynamics, and creative processes within Malaysia’s graphic design sector. Drawing on recent empirical studies conducted among Malaysian design students and practitioners, the analysis explores efficiency gains, authenticity concerns, cultural representation challenges, and shifts in required competencies (Wong et al., 2025; Artificial Intelligence Integration among Design Students in Malaysia, 2025). Evidence indicates that while GenAI tools accelerate ideation and production, they simultaneously raise questions about originality and the preservation of culturally specific visual languages that characterise Malaysian design practice (Abdullah et al., 2025; Azizi & Sannusi, 2025). The discussion then addresses the evolving roles of graphic designers, emphasising hybrid human–AI collaboration, conceptual leadership, and cultural fluency as essential future competencies (Zhou et al., 2025; Lestari, 2026). Designers are increasingly required to function as orchestrators of algorithmic outputs rather than sole executors of visual tasks, a shift that demands both technical fluency and critical judgment. Finally, the article evaluates the responsibilities of Malaysian universities in redesigning academic programmes to prepare graduates for an AI-mediated profession. Recommendations include systematic curriculum integration of AI literacy, ethical frameworks, critical design thinking, and industry-aligned experiential learning (Yang, 2025; Bing, 2025). The paper argues that proactive educational reform is essential to ensure that Malaysian designers retain competitive advantage while safeguarding cultural authenticity and professional identity in an increasingly automated creative landscape.

title: Patient Preferences for Non-Opioid Regimens in Chronic Non-Cancer Pain: A Systematic Review of Discrete Choice Experiments
authors: Ni Wayan Mahahari, Kadek Tania Mediana Putri, Ni Putu Aryati Suryaningsih, Gde Palguna Reganata, Dewa Ayu Putu Satrya Dewi, Kadek Hendra Darmawan
abstract: Chronic non-cancer pain is highly prevalent, and concerns about long-term opioid harms have increased interest in non-opioid therapies. Understanding which treatment attributes patients value is essential for shared decision-making. This systematic review synthesised discrete choice experiments (DCEs) to identify the treatment attributes patients prioritise when choosing non-opioid regimens for chronic non-cancer pain, and to appraise the methodological quality of the underlying studies. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance and a prospectively registered protocol (PROSPERO CRD420251273180), we searched nine databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, EconLit, PubMed and the Cochrane Library). Two reviewers independently screened records and assessed methodological quality using a modified ISPOR Conjoint Analysis Good Research Practices checklist. Attributes were classified using the Sain et al. (2020) framework into outcome, process and cost categories, and synthesised narratively. Seventeen studies (1,540 records identified) met the inclusion criteria, encompassing 109 attributes; 88% were industry-funded. Outcome attributes predominated (67.9%), followed by process (25.7%) and cost (6.4%). Clinical effectiveness was the most influential attribute, identified as the primary priority in 57.1% of studies combining all three categories, with safety acting as a key differentiator and cost as a constraint. Most studies met ISPOR standards (scores 10.5 to 12), though visual aids (71%) and direct patient input (18%) were underused. Patients prioritise clinical benefit when choosing non-opioid pain therapies, informing preference-sensitive decision-making, clinical guidelines and health technology assessment.

title: Patient Preferences for Biologic Therapies in Chronic Disease: A Systematic Review of Discrete Choice Experiments
authors: Kadek Tania Mediana Putri, Ni Wayan Mahahari, Dewa Ayu Putu Satrya Dewi, Ni Putu Aryati Suryaningsih, Putu Yudhistira Budi Setiawan, Kadek Hendra Darmawan
abstract: Introduction: Balancing high efficacy against significant toxicity risks a central challenge in biologic therapy selection for chronic diseases. This systematic review evaluated discrete choice experiments (DCEs) of patient preferences for biologic therapy to identify the treatment attributes that most consistently influence patient choice. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched (PROSPERO CRD420251271716) for Discrete Choice Experiments (DCEs) evaluating patient preferences for biologic therapies. Two reviewers independently screened eligible studies, extracted study characteristics and treatment attributes, evaluated methodological quality using an ISPOR-based quality assessment instrument, and identified the two most important treatment attributes reported in each study. Results: Twenty-four studies (2010-2025), most published after 2020, met inclusion criteria across a range of chronic diseases, most frequently psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Of 173 attributes identified, 61% were outcome attributes, 34% process, and 5% cost. Patients most often prioritized the risk of serious adverse events, followed by treatment response; process features gained importance when efficacy and safety differences were minimal, and cost carried greater weight where out-of-pocket expenditure was higher. Twenty-three of 24 studies achieved the maximum ISPOR score of 9/9 Conclusions: Patient preferences in biologic selection follow a clear hierarchy determined by perceived risk, expected benefit, and treatment context. Incorporating these preferences into shared decision-making might improve treatment alignment and long-term patient adherence. This evidence supports patient-centered care and counseling at the initiation of treatment.

title: Political Memes as Participatory Rhetoric for Voter Mobilisation during Elections
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Osa Director Uhunmwenkpenma, Princess Onyeoma Osife-Kurex
abstract: Political communication during elections has increasingly shifted to digital spaces, with political memes emerging as a dominant form of citizen-generated content. This study examined political memes as participatory rhetoric for voter mobilisation during elections in Nigeria. Anchored on Participatory Rhetoric Theory, Framing Theory and Agenda-Setting Theory, the study adopted the library research method. Findings revealed memes framed candidates as “heroes,” “villains” or “incompetent” and such affective frames recorded the highest engagement and correlated significantly with turnout intention. Thematic analysis also showed that viral memes set the agenda for peer political discussion by foregrounding issues such as youth inclusion and insecurity. Thus, the study concluded that political memes function as participatory rhetorical artefacts that simplify electoral issues, foster in-group solidarity and mobilise first-time and apathetic voters beyond elite-controlled campaign channels. However, the circulation of satirical misinformation within memes poses risks to informed participation.

title: AI Incidents and Marginalized Populations: A Descriptive Analysis of the AI Incident Database (1983–2026) from a Social Work Perspective
authors: Nanyi Deng, Sebastian Douglas, Jemel P. Aguilar, Wen Yin
abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in the institutional core of social work practice, such as law enforcement, healthcare, education, and public administration. Despite this implementation, the social work profession lacks a population-level empirical baseline of documented AI-related harm. This study characterizes the landscape of documented AI incidents, focusing on marginalized populations and the sectors in which social workers practice. Method: We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive analysis of the AI Incident Database (AIID; snapshot as of June 29, 2026), a curated repository of publicly reported AI incidents. The record comprises 1,549 incidents (1983–2026), with three independent post hoc classification systems that provide harm coding for overlapping subsets of these incidents. We report descriptive population proportions with explicit denominators for every reported statistic. Results: Most incidents (83.8%) were dated 2020 or later, though documented incidents date back to 1983, predating large language models by decades. Among the 214 CSET-coded incidents, a subset weighted toward pre-2020 events, 32.7% involved protected characteristics, most often race or ethnicity. Social-work-relevant sectors, including healthcare, law enforcement, education, and public administration, accounted for 23.4% of these incidents. Incidents in these sectors implicated protected characteristics (50.0% vs. 27.4%) and rights violations (40.0% vs. 4.9%) at markedly higher rates than other sectors, and 80.0% involved the public sector. Among incidents classified by intent and deployment timing, discrimination and toxicity incidents were coded as unintentional in 80.7% of cases, and 97.6% occurred after the AI system was already in active use rather than during development or testing. Discussion: Documented AI incidents concentrate on the sectors and populations central to social work's mandate. These findings establish an empirical baseline for AI harm surveillance and ground specific advocacy priorities: mandatory incident reporting in publicly funded services, third-party algorithmic auditing, and algorithmic literacy in frontline practice.

title: A scoping review of threats, enabling technologies, and forms of AI involvement associated with child sexual exploitation and abuse
authors: Chad Hemady, Sara Valdebenito, Chanel Hayre, Franziska Meinck, Professor Deborah Fry
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly implicated in child sexual exploitation and abuse (CSEA), but inconsistent terminology has limited synthesis. This scoping review mapped reported AI-CSEA threats and enabling technologies and examined how AI systems participated in perpetration. English-language sources published from January 2010 to 1 April 2026 were eligible if they concerned children under 18 and where an AI system played a material role in the abuse process. Searches of the ACM Digital Library, CINAHL, Web of Science, EBSCOhost databases, and grey literature identified 48 sources. Three reviewers contributed to screening and data charting, and extracted data were summarised numerically and through qualitative content analysis. Overall, our review found that AI-CSEA nomenclature conflated abusive conduct, production methods and system roles. Five non-exclusive threat domains comprised i) AI-generated CSAM, ii) AI-manipulated CSAM, iii) grooming, iv) sextortion, and v) conversational AI sexual abuse. Six technology groups encompassed: i) generative systems; ii) model adaptation and training data; iii) media manipulation systems; iv) conversational systems; v) immersive and embodied technologies; and vi) access, hosting, and distribution infrastructure. Forms of AI involvement include: i) AI-enabled assistance with person-directed abuse; ii) AI-simulated co-production of user-initiated scenarios; and iii) AI-driven initiation or escalation of sexualised conduct. AI-CSEA largely reflected established forms of abuse reshaped by new modes of production and interaction. Existing act-based classifications of violence against children provide a suitable foundation but require supplementary recording of production route, child linkage, system role and point of steering.

title: Record Linkage Error and Inference in Population Research
abstract: The explosion in digitization of large-scale administrative data and advances in record linkage have opened up new possibilities for studying core topics in population research, including social mobility, early-life determinants of longevity, and shifts in ethnoracial identity. Much attention has been paid to improving record linkage algorithms, but methodological guidance for researchers analyzing linked data is limited. We propose a general framework to explain how different types of linkage errors—false matches and missed matches—impact inference with linked data and introduce a bias-correction method. We then conduct three empirical case studies on canonical topics in population research: social mobility, the education–longevity gradient, and shifts in ethnoracial identification. These case studies demonstrate the settings in which linkage errors do and do not meaningfully impact substantive research findings. We conclude with practical recommendations for researchers performing inference with linked data and provide an accompanying R package implementing the methods introduced in this paper.

title: Educational and Socioeconomic Determinants of Parents’ Knowledge of Child Abuse in Egor Local Government Area of Edo State, Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Egwonor Opoggen, Obehi Destiny Elebhosele
abstract: Despite the enactment of the Child Rights Act and the growing advocacy for child protection in Nigeria, child abuse is a huge public health and social welfare problem. Parents have a key role to play in protecting children but their understanding of what is child abuse may be influenced by their education and social and economic status. The study looked both educational and socioeconomic factors influencing parents' knowledge of child abuse in Egor Local Government Area of Edo State, Nigeria. Specifically, the level of parents' knowledge about child abuse and the effect of educational level and socioeconomic status on parents' knowledge were evaluated. The results showed that parents' awareness of child abuse was moderate but there were significant gaps in their knowledge of child abuse law, such as the Child Rights Act, and of non-physical forms of child abuse. It was reported that parents' knowledge of child abuse was significantly and positively related to their educational level and socioeconomic status was significantly related to their understanding and awareness of child protection issues. The study recommended that there is a need for enhanced parental education and alleviation of socioeconomic inequalities to boost child protection systems in Nigeria. It calls for increased public education initiatives, community outreach parenting education initiatives and policy-level support for prioritising the inclusion of child protection education within adult literacy, health promotion and social welfare initiatives.

title: Administrative Production of Disaster Vulnerability: Explaining Persistent Infrastructure Vulnerability through Administrative Learning in the Himalayan Region
abstract: Public administrations in disaster-prone low- and middle-income countries face a persistent governance question: do institutions learn from one disaster to the next, or does experience fail to translate into revised policy and practice? This study addresses that question through the Administrative Production of Disaster Vulnerability (APDV), a policy-cycle framework tracing how vulnerability is reproduced or corrected across planning, budgeting, maintenance, and reconstruction, applied to Himachal Pradesh, India. PWD infrastructure damage across two successive monsoons (2023, 2025) correlates strongly across eleven districts (Pearson r = 0.819, p = 0.002; Spearman ρ = 0.882, p < 0.001), with Mandi and Shimla the highest-damage districts both years and state-wide damage rising 55.5% despite reconstruction spending. APDV distinguishes chronic vulnerability (Mandi, Shimla), a failure to convert risk into revised practice, from acute vulnerability (Chamba, Una), limited anticipatory capacity. Findings support district-specific resilience planning and identify administrative learning capacity as a distinct governance challenge.

title: The Importance of a Clear and Unambiguous Estimand for Hilbert Problems (or Any Other Empirical Research)
abstract: "Hilbert problems" are a great idea to galvanise research in the scientific study of religion, yet how do we go about answering these – or any other scientific questions of interest – empirically? This "meta-scientific" methodological aspect of research was largely missing from the original Hilbert problems and the 10 year follow-ups. Here, I want to focus on the importance of a clear and unambiguous estimand – the target quantity a study wants to estimate – and how this shapes all aspects of research, from synthesising existing research, data collection, statistical analysis and interpretation of results. At present, this is often vague or left unspecified, yet making progress on these Hilbert problems requires that researchers can clearly and unambiguously answer the question: "What is your estimand?"

title: Cellular automata coupled with Bayesian MCMC reveal the evolutionary history of diffusion processes
authors: Takuya Takahashi, Nico Neureiter, Geneviève Hannes, Peter Ranacher
abstract: Spatial diffusion is a fundamental topic in geographic information science, relevant to various phenomena such as urban sprawl, pathogen dispersal, and the spread of innovation. When studying these processes, we often work with incomplete data. We may know the geographic distribution of the phenomenon at some specific points in time, while the full history of its diffusion is unknown. Alternatively, we may have data for certain regions but not the entire area where the diffusion occurs. We present sBread, a novel Bayesian model which infers the history of a diffusion process from temporally or spatially incomplete data.
