Like a stochastic cellular automaton, sBread uses probabilistic local updating rules to model how the geographic distribution of a phenomenon changes over time through local interactions. However, unlike cellular automata, which focus on forward simulation starting from a known initial state, sBread employs Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample multiple plausible diffusion histories from the posterior distribution, given the observed data. Thus, sBread reconstructs the most likely past histories consistent with any observed data. We apply sBread to both simulated data and a case study on the diffusion of Indo-European languages in South America, which displaced the indigenous languages following European colonisation.

title: Comparative Analysis of Employee Compensation in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, Before and After the COVID-19 Pandemic (2019-2020)
authors: Sohel Sarwar, Robert King, Guelord Gabibulu
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic, which commenced in early 2020, significantly affected worldwide economies, labor markets, and employment conditions. Allegheny County, home to Pittsburgh and its surrounding areas, provides a critical case study examining how the pandemic affected local government employee compensation. Paired t-tests of salary data between 2019 and 2020 (pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic) demonstrate a significant increase in average gross salaries for all employees of Allegheny County. While overall employee gross pays increased, the distribution of salaries became less concentrated, with a greater emphasis on higher-earning individuals. Within specific job categories, Nursing Assistants had a significantly greater salary in 2020; however, Deputy Sheriffs showed no significant change. Nursing Assistants likely worked more overtime to support the healthcare response to the pandemic. Law enforcement officers typically receive paid overtime to provide security for public events such as professional football, baseball, hockey games, and public concerts. With restrictions on these events, law enforcement officers likely faced reductions in their overtime pay in 2020. Forecasting employee salaries from 2023 to 2027 revealed a wide range in the intervals, reflecting increasing uncertainty further in the future. Due to potential variability, the forecasting results were, therefore, inconclusive.

title: Guerreiro Ramos and sociological reduction: dilemmas and prospects for Brazilian Economic Development
abstract: This article examines Alberto Guerreiro Ramos’s contributions to understanding the dilemmas and prospects of Brazilian economic development, em-phasizing the originality and relevance of his thought. The methodological approach is based on a bibliographic review, aiming to identifying the State of the Art on the subject. The analysis is structured around four axes: i) biographical context, ii) theoretical-methodological foundations, iii) critiques of structural obstacles, and iv) proposals for a national-developmental project in Brazil. The study concludes that Guerreiro Ramos’s work rep-resents a landmark in Critical Sociology and Sociology of Development, in Brazil and should be further explored in contemporary economic studies.

title: Intelligence as a Partial Order: Why g Compresses a Structure It Cannot Rank
abstract: The general intelligence factor "g" is one of the most, if not the most replicated constructs in psychology, and its predictive validity is not in question. The question here is its interpretation. The positive manifold is the current popular proof that intelligence is a scalar, a quantity along which people can in principle be ranked. This review argues that such an inference is wrong. Brains that have similar functionality differ significantly in architecture, and the properties they differ on (efficiency, specialization, cost, resilience) are particular trade-offs which form a Pareto front instead of a single optimum. On this front each different architecture that "excels" in different environments is incomparable to the others, as ranking them would require privileging a specific set of abilities to reward, and for human life none is favored. Intelligence, thus, is better described as a partial order rather than a line. Ranking remains legitimate between widely separated scores, where a whole-life average lets a large gap dominate; within a band of equal g, it does not. This account returns a prediction a scalar model cannot make: equally scoring individuals should cross over in performance as demands change. It also names the core assumption whose failure would reinstate g - that for a human life, no environment is privileged.

title: The Value Core of Student Sustainability: Verification Methodology (Author’s English Translation)
abstract: In the context of a deep transformation of the socio-cultural environment and fragmentation of value orientations, the task of moving from a declarative description of youth values to the identification of their stable, behaviorally realizable core is actualized. Existing approaches often fix only normative ideals, ignoring the gap between attitudes and actual practices, which reduces the effectiveness of social design. The purpose of this study is to identify the value core of student youth's resilience, based on the results of an analysis of the degree of interiorization of values among student youth. The methodology of the work is based on the author's four-component empirical model, which evaluates value according to the parameters: "ideal", "significance", "readiness" and "action". The empirical basis was based on data from a mass survey (n = 3864) of students from leading Russian universities. Spearman's correlation analysis was used to identify structural relationships. The criterion for selection to the value core was the high intra-value consistency of all four components and the presence of stable inter-value clusters. It is revealed that the stable core is formed by state-patriotic (patriotism, service to the Fatherland, historical memory) and spiritual and moral values (family, charity, priority of the spiritual), characterized by high internal integration. The values of personal growth and universal norms (rights, justice, health) remain predominantly declarative, demonstrating the gap between ideal and action. Author's English translation of the article published in Russian: Society and Security Insights, 2026, vol. 9, no. 2, pp. 104-121. DOI: 10.14258/ssi(2026)2-06. The Russian original is the version of record. Archived translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21828746

title: Inventory and Evaluation of Metrics for a Sustainability Indicator Framework in the Northeast U.S. Food System
authors: Christopher Donovan, Tessa Lawler, Isabella Loconte, Polly Ericksen, Gillian Galford, Matthew McIntosh
abstract: CONTEXT: Food systems support the nutritional needs and livelihoods of a growing population. Sustainably managing food systems within social and ecological bounds requires accessible and accurate data. Sustainability indicator frameworks provide a structure for curating these data, and regional approaches are particularly relevant for decision making at the state and local levels. OBJECTIVE: To assess data availability, quality, and trends in the Northeast food system, we conducted an inventory and analysis of publicly available datasets representing five dimensions of sustainability. METHODS: Data were sourced from federal, academic, and non-profit repositories, and metrics were selected to best represent the region at the county level. We used correlations and spatial regressions to assess interactions among metrics and trends over time. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: We found key gaps in the Economic, Production, and Social dimensions. Some data were only available at state level, while monitoring for some metrics began recently, precluding analysis of trends over time. We identified 62 metrics to represent the framework indicators, but only 31 were available at the county level with multiple time points. Of these, half were improving, and one third were declining. Trends in the Production and Economic dimensions were neutral to positive, while the other dimensions were mixed. SIGNIFICANCE: Access to data is critical in improving regional food system sustainability. The gaps we identified should serve as a road map in developing monitoring programs. The curation of datasets that are consistent, interoperable, and accessible, is crucial in monitoring food systems and developing policies and interventions to support sustainability.

title: Putting Street Justice into Practice: Insights from London Boroughs
abstract: Street transformations are not merely technical responses to climate, health and liveability goals. They are political interventions that redistribute public space, mobility, environmental quality and decision-making authority. Yet justice rarely appears as an explicit concept in everyday street planning. This paper investigates why justice is invoked as a principle but seldom used as an operational category, how it nevertheless shapes practice, and which institutional and political conditions determine its influence. Conducted within the 32-partner Horizon Europe JUST STREETS programme, the study combines documentary analysis with 10 semi-structured interviews undertaken between October and December 2025 with practitioners working across several London borough contexts. We develop a street-specific framework integrating distributive, procedural, recognition and epistemic justice across streets’ dual functions as links and places and across the transformation project cycle. The findings show that practitioners usually articulate justice through administratively established concepts such as safety, accessibility, health, equality, air quality and inclusion. These concepts connect more readily than justice to statutory duties, departmental responsibilities, funding criteria, technical standards and measurable outcomes. Explicit justice language becomes most salient when practitioners question the inherited allocation of street space, challenge car-centred assumptions or adjudicate between competing claims. Justice is therefore not absent from practice, but operates principally as a normative basis for determining whose needs should receive priority. Its dimensions are, however, unevenly institutionalised. Distributive and recognition concerns shape spatial prioritisation, kerbside reallocation, accessibility and child-centred design. Procedural justice remains largely confined to consultation rather than shared authority, while epistemic justice is constrained by the continuing dominance of professional and quantitative evidence. This unevenness is politically consequential: more specific policy language can enable intervention while obscuring redistribution, normalising inherited inequalities and weakening accountability. We conclude that street justice must be embedded throughout problem definition, design, implementation and evaluation, with explicit scrutiny of benefits, burdens, participation, recognition and evidentiary authority.

title: When Government Uses AI: Experimental Evidence of Selective Trust Decline and Algorithmic Nimbyism
authors: Daniel Juhász Vigild, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Laust Hvas Mortensen, Vedran Sekara
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in government, changing the ways in which citizens relate to public institutions. One important aspect, the impact of AI on trust in public institutions, has been the subject of substantial efforts that document an "AI penalty" on trust in public institutions when they use AI. However, little is known about why or how such a penalty arises. In two preregistered survey experiments (N=6 084) we measure the effect of AI on trust across four real-life use cases of governmental AI. First, we find large differences across the four domains—disclosing AI usage in social services and health care settings decreases trust, while trust is unaffected for policing and unemployment use cases. Second, we experimentally test a specific mechanism (algorithmic nimbyism) that considers personal exposure to the decision-making outcomes as a driver of the negative impact of AI on trust. Despite not finding any causal evidence for the notion of algorithmic nimbyism, we used rich administrative data on survey participants’ medical history and labour force participation to explore heterogeneous treatment effects that revealed descriptive and suggestive evidence of algorithmic nimbyism. Future work could consider further exploring the combination of experimental and observational data to empirically examine explanations of the impact AI has on relations between citizens and public institutions.

title: Predatism and Predocracy: A Conceptual Framework for Emergent Predator-Prey Politics
abstract: This paper introduces the theoretical constructs of predatism and predocracy to describe an emerging authoritarian ideology and its corresponding mode of governance. Predatism is defined as a convergent far-right ideology from the fusion of white nationalism, male supremacism, Christian nationalism, anti-democratic populism, and online conspiracy subcultures into an increasingly unified worldview. This consolidation is argued to be uniquely catalyzed by the contemporary digital ecosystem, in which the dynamics of moral contagion confer a systematic transmission advantage on predator-prey framings, accelerating the migration of disparate fringe conspiracy theories and hate ideologies into the political mainstream. Within this context, distinct grievances coalesce around a shared moral logic, in which the in-group views itself as the collective victim of status theft, justifying a predatory social dynamic which celebrates cruelty and domination as both a righteous self-defense and a seek-to-destroy offense. When this movement captures state institutions, it establishes a predocracy: a system characterized by visible cruelty as a tool of rule, the weaponization of law against opponents, systemic impunity for the in-group, and the spectacular reinforcement of hierarchy through routine public displays of domination. By distinguishing predatism from classical fascism, this paper argues that predocracy is a distinct 21st-century phenomenon driven by the affective mobilization of its online base, the gamification of state violence, and the consumption of out-group anguish as in-group catharsis.

title: Role differentiation as ignition of a collective information engine
abstract: Informational active matter research has shown how measurement-informed decisions produce collective order, so far in systems that reach consensus. We identify a collective information engine that orders by differentiation instead, and construct a minimal instance using anti-coordination games, the simplest game class in which differentiated role information has value. Agents infer their role from a noisy social signal, and role-following action feeds back into that signal, shaping the incentive to follow roles. The schemas prescribing roles are themselves dynamic: resources accrued through coordinated role-play combine with population variability to shape and reinforce the schemas that generated them. The model thereby operationalizes Sewell's duality of schemas and resources, the influential but hitherto qualitative resolution of sociology's structure--agency debate. The engine ignites when a loop gain $\Lambda$---the product of identity persistence, cognitive capacity, and social feedback channel fidelity---exceeds one. For a repertoire of such schemas, roles emerge with increasing gain in a bifurcation cascade whose functional form is fixed by the repertoire's eigenvalue spectrum, ranging from monitorable logarithmic sequences to deceptive spike-then-avalanche onsets. Resource accumulation turns schema competition into a replicator dynamics that, in mean field, selects the cascade type endogenously. Subcritical behavioral covariance reveals that type before onset, enabling early detection, and feedback channel parameters bias which type is selected. For agents interacting on a platform, adaptive platform design then becomes a control lever to throttle emergent coordination, e.g. for mitigating risks from distributional AI. Joining game theory, collective dynamics, and information engines, we open a route to an information thermodynamics of agent populations.

title: 《简繁一对多155组繁本字对照表》的编制与应用 ——兼论“繁本字”概念的理论与实证V2 The Compilation and Application of the "One-to-Many 155 Groups Fanbenzi Mapping Table" — With a Discussion on the Theory and Empirical Evidence of the "Fanbenzi" Concept
authors: 林乐友（1947—），山东济南人，独立学者。首提“繁本字“”五体汉字体系”概念。
abstract: 在社会语言学与文字政策交叉领域，《通用规范汉字表》附表及GB/T 12345-90虽对简繁“一对多”字际关系有所整理，但均存在收字不全、术语混编的问题。为弥补上述缺漏，本文编制了《简繁一对多155组繁本字对照表》。该表以官方96组为种子集，经比对多部字书及区域标准，补充27组区域差异字，筛得同形异音字21组，并经语料共现校验，最终闭合为155组。编制中引入“繁本字”概念（繁本字 = 繁体字 ∪ 传承字），以“四重意涵”（文本之本、本字之本、本有之字之本、文化本位之本）与“三阶证成”（语形、语义、语用）为理论根基，厘清了简化字与多个繁本字之间的音义对应关系。基于0.97亿字语料的简繁转换实验证明，以“繁本字+155组音义规则”为目标层，可将字符级错误率由17.5ppm降至2.8ppm，降幅达84%。本表可供简繁转换软件开发、辞书编纂、汉字教学及书写实践参考使用，也可为未来字表修订提供参考。 英文摘要 Abstract: The appendices of the Table of General Standard Chinese Characters and GB/T 12345-90 have addressed the "one-to-many" relationships between simplified and traditional characters, but both suffer from incomplete coverage and terminological inconsistencies. To address these gaps, this paper presents the One-to-Many 155 Groups Fanbenzi Mapping Table. Starting from the official 96 groups as the seed set, the table was expanded by cross-referencing multiple dictionaries and regional standards, adding 27 groups of regionally variant characters and 21 groups of homographs with different pronunciations, and finally closed at 155 groups through corpus-based co-occurrence validation. The compilation is grounded in the concept of "Fanbenzi" (Fanbenzi = Traditional Characters ∪ Inherited Characters), supported by its "Four Meanings" and "Three Justifications" as theoretical foundations. Each simplified character's corresponding Fanbenzi variants are distinguished by phonetic and semantic contexts. In a simplified-to-traditional conversion experiment conducted on a 97-million-character corpus, using "Fanbenzi + 155 phonetic-semantic rules" as the target layer reduced the character-level error rate from 17.5 ppm to 2.8 ppm, a reduction of 84%. This table may serve as a reference for simplified-traditional conversion software development, lexicography, Chinese character teaching, and calligraphy practice, as well as for future revisions of official character tables.

title: Racializing Surveillance: Flock Camera Deployment, Black Population Geography, and the Limits of the Homicide Rationale in Hampton Roads
authors: Andrew F. Baird, Steven Keener, John Finn
abstract: This study examines the racialized geography of automatic license plate reader (ALPR) surveillance in Hampton Roads, Virginia. We link court-unsealed Flock Safety camera locations to measures from the 2020–2024 American Community Survey and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s 2022–2024 National Vital Statistics System. Population-adjusted negative binomial models with locality-clustered standard errors and Webb wild-cluster bootstrap p-values test associations with racial composition, poverty, age structure, homicide and overdose mortality, and Black/White neighborhood boundaries. Camera counts are consistently higher in areas with larger Black populations and those bordering substantially Blacker communities, net of all covariates. Homicide mortality is not positively associated with cameras in the fully controlled model, whereas overdose mortality is. These findings challenge race-neutral claims that ALPR cameras merely follow serious violence and support theories of racializing surveillance by showing how data-driven public-safety infrastructure can reproduce racial inequalities in surveillance exposure.

title: Against Mechanical Subjectivity: The Misalignment of Generative AI as a Tool for Qualitative Research
authors: Bryce Clayton Newell, Torin Monahan, Lanore Hahn
abstract: Interpretive and constructivist research is under assault from forces within and outside the qualitative research enterprise. Scholars, including those identifying as interpretive or constructivist scholars, have aligned themselves with positivist and metric-oriented scientists in promoting the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI or LLM) technologies in ways that sacrifice human-based knowledge production. We characterize this as the pursuit of mechanical subjectivity: the spurious premise of delegating subjective interpretive analysis and experience to AI machines. In this paper, we outline the ongoing debate in existing research; examine the frictions that GenAI creates with science as a social practice; discuss the implied epistemologies of GenAI tools and their misalignment with interpretive and constructivist research; and address how neoliberal logics shape AI adoption in university contexts. From a Critical Data Studies orientation, we argue that using LLMs for conducting qualitative data coding and analysis, writing up such analyses, or synthesizing ideas and conclusions is incompatible with the epistemological and ontological commitments necessary for conducting interpretive and constructivist research. We contend that mobilizing GenAI tools in ways that fully or partially replace humans in the knowledge production process—or that mediate the generative aspects of knowledge production between human researchers and their data—while claiming an interpretive or constructivist positionality amounts to scholarly malpractice, producing epistemic injustice.

title: Cross-cultural survey research: The impact of translator background and competencies on questionnaire translation and post-editing quality
authors: Ulrike Efu Nkong, Dorothée Behr, Anke Radinger
abstract: Questionnaires in different languages are at the heart of cross-cultural survey research. To ensure their comparability and comprehensibility, translation procedures have continuously been optimized. However, the impact of a translator’s competencies on questionnaire translation and post-editing quality has, to date, not been systematically examined. With the aim to optimize team compositions, this study looks at the very first step of the TRAPD process – initial translations and the translators producing them. In an in-between translation experiment, 16 professional translators and 16 social scientists (with different levels of questionnaire experience) translated an experimental questionnaire containing 45 items partly from scratch and partly neural machine translation output was post-edited (i.e., corrected). To explore how a large language model (LLM) compares, additionally a raw LLM version was generated. After a blind expert assessment of the translations, error counts across different categories were compared and showed that overall error counts were comparable but professional translators, drawing on their translation expertise, produced significantly fewer linguistic errors (linguistic conventions, style and register) in translations produced from scratch. Experience with the questionnaire genre tended to help both professional groups to improve their results. Both professional groups performed similarly when post-editing machine translated text. The LLM-generated translation contained fewer errors overall than the median of human translations.

title: Working Alone? Working from Home and Political Participation
abstract: What are the political consequences of working from home? I study this question in the European context, asking how remote work impacts electoral participation. I test two competing theoretical frameworks: the resource model and the workplace socialisation theory. The resource model suggests that remote work fosters political participation by increasing individuals’ time and civic skills. In contrast, the socialisation hypothesis argues that WFH reduces social interaction and exposure to diverse viewpoints at the workplace, thereby weakening electoral participation. Evidence from cross-country survey data and a causal analysis using Dutch data indicates that WFH reduces electoral participation, with effects that intensify with longer exposure. These effects are driven by diminished exposure to political discussion among work colleagues, supporting the workplace socialisation hypothesis. This study contributes to research on technological change, political socialisation, and the broader societal consequences of remote work, while underscoring the importance of considering democratic implications in the design of future work arrangement policies.

title: Effects of political polarization on non-electoral participation
abstract: Several studies have examined the effects of polarization on election turnout, but the consequences for other forms of participation have remained unexplored. I draw on research on the mechanisms mobilizing non-electoral participation to examine the effects of change in polarization on this form of political engagement, distinguishing institutional and noninstitutional participation. Building on the literatures on respective determinants of both types of participation, I expect polarization to have a positive effect on both types of participation, but I expect that the effect is stronger in the case of noninstitutional polarization. I present longitudinal analyses of the effect of system-level affective and ideological polarization on non-electoral participation as well as protest mobilization in 22 European countries in the period 2002-2019. Results point to a positive effect of polarization on protest participation and mobilization, but show no evidence of an effect of polarization on institutional participation.

title: “Ascending dragon or blasting the dragon vein?”: How Chinese netizens construct environmental meanings in digital publics
abstract: Corporations’ sustainability communication is increasingly challenged by digital publics. Yet research on how netizens contest corporate sustainability narratives, and thereby construct environmental meanings, remains largely confined to Western contexts. This study addresses this gap by examining Chinese netizens’ discursive responses to a controversial fireworks display in the Himalayas staged by international mountaineering brand Arc’teryx. Comments from the seven most popular Weibo posts were selected to compile a corpus (140,584 tokens), and analysed through corpus-assisted discourse analysis, particularly keyword and concordance analysis. Findings show that netizens mobilise multiple meaning systems to express strong disapproval, including scientific ecological knowledge, perceptions of environmental governance failure, spiritual-cultural references, consumer action, and nationalism. These interconnected meaning systems converge around a distinctive feature of Chinese digital environmentalism: a nature-centred view of human-nature relations and harmony. The study extends understanding of digital environmentalism beyond Western contexts by showing that environmental meanings in Chinese digital spaces are place- and culture-based, intertwining ecological concerns with emotion, spiritual wellbeing, perceptions of justice, and national interests.

title: Before You Diagnose Her: AI Companionship as Structural Question, Not Symptom
abstract: AI companionship is surging worldwide, and research on the phenomenon has grown exponentially. However, across the research literature tracking it, from human-computer interaction to communication and the social sciences, a shared pathologizing tendency and its attendant alarmism have set in. This essay argues that the diagnosis has outrun its evidence. The harm literature leans on extreme cases and habitual slippery-slope leaps; it systematically conflates three distinct propositions: that AI companions cause harm, that particular platform designs amplify harm, and that AI companionship as an intimate practice is inherently pathological. The essay further deconstructs the philosophical underpinnings of this pathologizing stance, showing how its ontological assumptions rely on a foreclosed definition of relation. Crucially, such frameworks rarely ask what users' human relationships and social circumstances were before they arrived. Drawing on preliminary observations of Chinese-language public discourse — a field that, over sustained observation, has been almost uniformly female — this essay documents user practices that the deficit frame cannot accommodate — building, theorizing, ethical deliberation, and the organized refusal of the clinical gaze. Connecting these user practices to a longer tradition of female emotional workarounds from romance narratives to fan cultures as exits from inequitable intimate arrangements, I propose structural emotional refuge as an alternative unit of analysis: AI companionship understood as a rational emotional migration from arrangements that extract more than they return. The essay does not answer one totalizing diagnosis with another; it argues for conceptual restraint until the evidence arrives, and for asking where users came from, why they left, and how they understand themselves before writing the answer as psychological problems.

title: Performance Measures and Mean-Variance Efficiency
abstract: While portfolio performance and pricing performance are often treated as separate domains, both rest on the same foundation: mean-variance efficiency. This study makes that connection explicit by examining 11 performance measures drawn from these two domains. We show that these measures share a common basis in the Sharpe ratio, the standard measure of mean-variance efficiency, and can therefore be interpreted within a unified framework. Building on this result, we derive two compact benchmark-relative metrics, the ratio metric and the gap metric, and illustrate their practical relevance using data from the Korean fund industry.

title: Fund Manager Alpha in Tactical Asset Allocation
abstract: This study focuses on the stock picking dimension of tactical asset allocation. To reflect the fact that each manager’s opportunity set is constrained by the fund’s style, we construct a style-matching portfolio and use it to define manager alpha as a time-varying measure of stock picking ability. We then distinguish between this full time-varying measure of manager alpha and the portion left unexplained by factor exposures. The former captures ordinary stock picking ability, whereas the latter captures superior stock picking ability. This distinction forms the basis of our empirical analysis of stock picking ability in the Korean fund industry.

title: Pseudo-Populism as Strategic Political Communication: A Comparative Analysis of Electoral Communication and Voting Behavior in the Philippines, Brazil, India and Türkiye
abstract: The growing prevalence of pseudo-populism has reshaped political campaigns across developing countries, where candidates increasingly employ people-centered rhetoric, anti-elite narratives, and emotionally driven messaging to secure electoral support without consistently advancing policies aligned with the public interest. This study examines the influence of pseudo-populist political messaging on the voting behavior of electorates in developing democracies through a secondary quantitative data analysis. Drawing upon existing datasets and findings from reputable electoral surveys and political behavior studies, the research investigates the relationship between exposure to pseudo-populist appeals and voting preferences while considering the roles of political trust, media consumption, education, and socioeconomic conditions. Rather than assuming that voters are inherently susceptible to populist narratives, the study explores how structural and institutional factors shape citizens' electoral decisions. By synthesizing quantitative evidence from multiple developing countries, the research aims to identify common patterns in voter behavior and assess the broader implications of pseudo-populism for democratic accountability and electoral integrity. The findings are expected to contribute to the expanding literature on populism by providing a comparative perspective on how strategic political communication influences electoral outcomes and by offering insights that may support civic education initiatives, evidence-based policymaking, and the promotion of informed democratic participation.

title: How Much Should We Trust Modern Difference-in-Differences Estimates?
abstract: When do modern difference-in-differences (DID)-style methods work for empirical political science? Scholars exploit the staggered roll-out of policies like election regulation, civil service reform, and healthcare across places to estimate causal effects - often using the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator. However, recent literature has highlighted the TWFE estimator's bias in the presence of heterogeneous treatment effects and tendency to make ``forbidden comparisons" between treated units. In response, scholars have increasingly turned to modern DID estimators that promise greater robustness to real-world data problems. This paper asks how well these modern methods work for for the empirical settings and sample sizes commonly used in political science, with the U.S. states as the running example. In particular, it provides a simulation study of the performance of seven DID methods under either constant or heterogeneous effects, in an N=50 setting that mimics the American federalism natural experiment. I find that many modern methods (1) produce confidence intervals that do not include the true average effect at the specified rate and (2) are underpowered. I show that many cases of coverage problems with modern DID estimators can be addressed using the block bootstrap to estimate standard errors. However, I also show that even where identification and estimation are straightforward, the fifty-state sample poses a power problem without large average effect sizes - at least 0.5 standard deviations. I illustrate the challenges of DID research with the fifty-state panel in the case of estimating the effects of strict voter identification laws on voter turnout.

title: Balancing urbanization, climate change, and biodiversity conservation with nature-based solutions: A case study of Hong Kong
authors: Ashley Bang, Anna Freeman, E.J. Milner-Gulland
abstract: Urban areas face challenges in jointly addressing the global climate change and nature loss crises amidst the pursuit of socioeconomic development agendas. These trade-offs prompt the need to explore solutions for sustainable environmental and societal futures that balance diverse priorities. Nature-based solutions (NbS) are one such approach that can provide synergistic benefits for climate, nature, and society. This study employs geospatial approaches to mapping and identifying such benefits and trade-offs, serving as a foundation to guide further assessment and planning. Using Hong Kong as a case study, we model the carbon storage, road-based disturbance, and climate risk trade-offs under five land use change scenarios for 2030. The results demonstrate the stark losses in climate mitigation benefits when urban areas are expanded at extreme scales, but only moderate losses under current planned development schemes that may be mitigated by the implementation of NbS. Several key areas in Hong Kong are identified where these benefits are maximised, namely Mai Po, Chek Lap Kok, and Sai Kung. NbS opportunities can be further explored in those areas to enhance natural carbon stores, reshape built infrastructure for nature connectivity, mitigate coastal flood risks, among other benefits. The results provides an evidence foundation for implementing NbS to bridge climate and nature policy agendas with competing urbanisation priorities in Hong Kong and other urban areas globally.

title: Child-Focused Reappraisal and Rumination: Associations with Parental Health, Adolescent Academic Achievement, and Parent and Adolescent Gender
authors: Gesine Jordan, Elouise Botes, Samuel Greiff, Ziwen Teuber
abstract: Adolescence is characterized by dynamic biological and emotional changes that influence key developmental tasks (e.g., dealing with academic demands). Parents are critical for their children’s emotion regulation development and offer child-focused emotion regulation strategies in challenging situations. To date, child-focused emotion regulation processes in critical achievement situations are not comprehensively understood as questions remain regarding their associations with parental health and adolescents’ academic achievement. In addition, the roles of parents’ and adolescents’ gender in child-focused emotion regulation have yet to be explored. The current cross-sectional study addressed these gaps by applying single-group and multi-group structural equation modeling, as well as latent mean comparisons in a sample of U.S. parents of sixth–ninth graders (N = 1,304). Higher levels of child-focused reappraisal were related to parents’ lower subjective health issues, whereas child-focused ruminative reflection was negatively associated with adolescents’ academic achievement. Further analyses indicated that the structural paths linking child-focused emotion regulation, parental health issues, and adolescents’ academic achievement differed by parents’ gender, but not by children’s gender. Surprisingly, fathers were more likely to utilize child-focused ruminative reflection than mothers and reported a negative association between self-focused reappraisal and health issues, which was not found for mothers. Parents were more likely to use child-focused ruminative reflection with male adolescents, who also had lower average academic achievement than female adolescents. No significant differences in child-focused reappraisal were observed by parents’ or adolescent’s gender. The results highlighted distinct and context-specific associations between child-focused emotion regulation strategies and family correlates.

title: At The Mercy of Politics? When Policy Change Undermines the Credibility of Public Managers
authors: Mads Pieter van Luttervelt, Mathias Østergaard-Nielsen, Anders Grøn
abstract: Politicians often change policies—sometimes unexpectedly—but how it affects the bureaucracy remains largely unknown. We argue that changing policies can undermine the credibility of public managers in the eyes of the street-level bureaucrats. Testing this argument causally in the real world is challenging as it requires unanticipated policy change that only affects part of the bureaucracy and a pre- and post-change measurement of relevant constructs. To overcome these challenges, we leverage a quasi-experimental design by exploiting that a nationwide reform in Denmark’s education sector was unexpectedly changed for half of the country’s high schools. We find a long-term negative causal effect of policy change on the credibility of public managers, when they showed commitment to the initial policy. The effect is driven by street-level bureaucrats whose policy preferences align with the initial policy. We discuss trade-offs for policy makers and managers when initiating or responding to policy changes.

title: Book Review: A Marxist Critique of the Ruined University, by Krystian Szadkowski and Jakub Krzeski, Springer, 2025.
abstract: This abstract summarizes a review of Krystian Szadkowski and Jakub Krzeski’s A Marxist Critique of the Ruined University (2025), a pivotal theoretical intervention that reconceptualizes the modern decline of higher education. Rather than lamenting the loss of historical academic ideals, the reviewed text posits that the university is experiencing a profound ontological crisis driven fundamentally by the imperatives of global capital accumulation. The review highlights how the authors map the academy's systemic reorganization into a primary node for value reproduction, where knowledge and academic labor are continuously co-opted to serve market interests. To navigate this crisis, Szadkowski and Krzeski deploy a Marxian "integral critique" composed of three dialectical stages: in (diagnosing internal institutional mechanisms and exploitation), against (resisting internal hierarchies), and beyond (identifying emerging social relations). The review traces the book’s eleven chapters through conceptual, foundational, tactical, and reconstructive clusters. It emphasizes the authors' uncompromising dissection of the "Academic Robinson"—a mode of subjectivation marked by hyper-individualization—and the alienating forces of neoliberal metricization that fundamentally transform institutional habitus. Crucially, the review notes that the book avoids deterministic pessimism by offering an affirmative, emancipatory blueprint. By moving beyond mere melancholic observation, the authors envision a post-capitalist "university of the common" anchored in horizontal governance, alternative property relations, and collective social production. Ultimately, the review concludes that this robust analytical toolkit successfully bridges abstract philosophical diagnosis with the urgent material need for transformative praxis and collective solidarity among academic laborers.

title: Bioplastics as a Sustainability Promise: Promises and (Dis)illusionments of a ‘Technological Fix’ in Germany
abstract: Bioplastics have emerged as a beacon of hope for sustainable alternatives to conventional,petroleum-based plastics. They promise sustainability by technically addressing the issues associated with plastics – waste burden, emissions, and dependence on oil. This makes them a ‘technological fix,’ recommending simple technical solutions to complex challenges but overlooking the intricate reality. The article empirically demonstrates that the disappointments with bioplastics are not solely due to technical reasons but stem from neglected societal, social, economic, or ecological factors. These factors range from the material properties of early bioplastics, monocultures and land competition for the use of renewable resources, to their economic competitiveness. From the technological promise of sustainability and the dashed hopes for bioplastics, it follows that the technological fix fails because it is tied to the path dependencies of fossil plastics. Without social innovations in societal use of plastics, departing from these paths is difficult.

title: The Impact of Inflation on Income Distribution in Nigeria. An Empirical Approach (1990–2023)
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Felix I. Ifada, James A. Adesokan
abstract: The study examined the impact of inflation on income in Nigeria for the period of 1990–2023. The study made use of four explanatory variables, which are: external remittance, interest rate, inflation rate, and exchange rate on income in Nigeria. The data were obtained from various issues of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Statistical Bulletin, journals, as well as financial indicators. Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) and Johansen cointegration tests were employed to confirm the stationarity of the series and the long-run relationship among the series. The findings indicate that remittances positively impact economic growth and income distribution, supporting household consumption and investment. Higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing, limiting access to credit, reducing investment, and negatively impacting income distribution. High inflation reduces household purchasing power, particularly affecting low-income earners, thereby worsening income distribution. The study therefore concluded that remittances play a crucial role in boosting real GDP and improving household welfare, emphasising the need for policies that facilitate their inflow. Conversely, high interest rates, inflation, and exchange-rate volatility negatively impact economic growth and exacerbate income inequality. The study therefore recommended that the Central Bank of Nigeria should implement policies to reduce transaction costs and encourage diaspora investments. The apex bank should also promote financial-sector reforms to lower borrowing costs and boost investment. The government should enhance domestic production to stabilise prices and reduce inflationary pressures.

title: Shaping the notion of #wellbeing in the therapy culture context: an analysis through Instagram narratives
authors: Ainara Larrondo-Ureta, Simón Peña-Fernández, Jordi Morales-i-Gras
abstract: Purpose – The aim of this paper is to (1) identify textual and visual themes and sub-themes associated with the #wellbeing hashtag on Instagram, (2) assess their varying levels of engagement and (3) investigate gender bias present in the analysed visual narratives. Design/methodology/approach – This study employs a range of big data analysis techniques to investigate various dimensions of wellbeing on Instagram. Initially, a sample of 9,844 posts was processed using data mining and text analysis methods to identify and categorise significant hashtags, which facilitated the classification of posts into thematic clusters through hierarchical clustering. Engagement was then assessed using non-parametric statistical tests. Additionally, computer vision models were used to analyse and classify visual narratives, grouping images into communities based on visual similarities. Finally, gender representation in the images was examined using object detection models. Findings – The study reveals that the discourse around #wellbeing on Instagram is predominantly feminised and focuses primarily on mental, psychological and spiritual aspects. Therapeutic and positive psychology narratives are the most prevalent and engaging, while physical activity and nutrition play a relatively secondary role. Two major macro-narratives emerge: firstly, mental health and emotional wellbeing, often featuring hashtags related to therapy, self-discovery, spirituality and motivational quotes; secondly, though less prominently, themes and visual narratives concerning physical activity and healthy habits, emphasising exercise and nutrition. Originality/value – The study identifies, for the first time in the academic literature, key themes and subthemes in the textual and visual narratives on wellness on the social media (Instagram), offering evidence for its feminisation. These findings contribute to the academic discussion on the implications of the notion of wellbeing on Instagram in relation to “therapy culture”. This idea can be applied to other social media, as well as to other areas, such as working life, where diverse individualities and groups also coexist.

title: “ChatGPT has helped me more than 15 years of therapy”: AI therapy and moving beyond para-social interaction to conceptualising AI chatbots as a significant other.
authors: Dr Stephanie Alice Baker, Michael James Walsh
abstract: There is a growing body of literature that assesses the risks and ethical challenges associated with AI therapy and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare. Much of this research examines the risks and harms associated with parasocial relationships and projecting sentient qualities onto AI chatbots. This article makes a novel contribution to this literature by examining AI therapy from an ethnographic perspective, examining how people strategically use prompts to reduce the perceived risks associated with AI therapy. Analysing TikTok videos (n = 840) to understand how content creators use AI to support their mental health, our study found that most people use AI therapy for personality analysis and self-improvement rather than medical treatment and diagnosis. Although users demonstrated reflexivity and agency in their therapeutic engagement with AI, we introduce the concept of AI as a ‘significant other’ to highlight the impact of AI therapy.

title: Taxation of the Digital Economy in Nigeria: A Conceptual Review
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Simeon Funminiyi Akinpelu, Igbinosun Friday Ese
abstract: This study examined the taxation of the digital economy in Nigeria through a conceptual review, focusing on challenges, prospects, and policy implications of taxing digital activities including e-commerce, fintech, streaming services, online advertising, and social media commerce. The purpose was to critically analyse how Nigeria’s legal and regulatory frameworks, administrative capacities, and technological tools interact to facilitate revenue mobilisation from digital economic activities. A qualitative conceptual research design was employed, relying entirely on secondary data from academic journals, government reports, Finance Acts, and international frameworks, with data analysed through content and thematic analysis and supported by descriptive statistics from government and global sources. Findings revealed that while Nigeria’s digital economy has expanded rapidly, compliance with tax obligations remains moderate, with informal platforms and cross border transactions limiting effective revenue collection. Legal recognition of significant economic presence is crucial for capturing digital taxes, yet enforcement gaps and limited technological monitoring hinder compliance, with fintech platforms integrated into formal banking systems showing higher adherence than informal social media commerce. The study contributes a structured conceptual framework linking digital activities, regulatory clarity, administrative enforcement, and revenue outcomes, while identifying critical policy and practical gaps. The findings imply that improving technological monitoring, strengthening legal frameworks, and enhancing stakeholder engagement are essential for increasing compliance, offering insights for policymakers and laying the foundation for future research on sustainable digital taxation strategies in Nigeria.

title: Machine-translated ParlSpeech V2 dataset: Full-text corpora of 3.5 million parliamentary speeches from seven countries translated into English
authors: Štěpán Jabůrek, Adam Černý, Christian Rauh, Jan Schwalbach
abstract: Machine-translated ParlSpeech V2 contains complete full-text vectors of more than 3.5 million parliamentary speeches in the key legislative chambers of Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, and Sweden, covering periods between 21 and 32 years. The data include speeches machine-translated into English using open-source OPUS-MT models. Original language speeches from ParlSpeech V2 (Rauh & Schwalbach 2020) are present alongside the English translation. Meta-data include the original information on date, speaker, party, and partially agenda item under which a speech was held. The accompanying release note provides a more detailed guide to the data.

title: Enabling justice in nature-positive transformations: Insights from agricultural, forestry, and health transitions
authors: Aniek Hebinck, Thomas Fransen, Dalia D'Amato, Ben Delbaere, Symke Nieboer, Lara Lebleu, Stella Piipponen-Doyle, Valentina Vaglica, Hans Keune, Opi Outhwaite
abstract: Transformations within the biodiversity nexus are increasingly expected to deliver not only environmental outcomes but also enable justice. Yet, how justice is experienced and shaped within such transformation processes remains unclear. This paper examines how justice is experienced and shaped in practice across three nature-positive transitions in Europe: efforts to make agriculture, forestry, and healthcare more supportive of biodiversity and human wellbeing. Drawing on a relational approach to justice and insights from just transitions, the analysis shows that policy rarely explicitly aims to enable justice. Instead, policies often indirectly aim to promote justice through low-conflict and incremental pathways. Across the cases, procedural dimensions dominate in policy approaches to enable justice, while distributive and recognition dimensions are addressed unevenly and less consistently in the policy frameworks analysed. At the same time, justice appears to be shaped and experienced less by individual policy instruments than by broader structural conditions, including institutional arrangements, property relations, and dominant knowledge frameworks, which influence how policies are implemented and whose interests they serve. Building on these findings, the paper conceptualises justice as a relational and context-dependent phenomenon, produced through interactions between actor framings, institutional arrangements, and transition dynamics. This highlights key tensions between ambition for just transformation and governance approaches that prioritise incremental and low conflict pathways, with important implications for both research and policy.

title: Harm Through the “#RizzCam”: Smart Glasses, Ambient Capture and Invisible Harassment
authors: Milica Stilinovic, Ben Egliston, Wenqi Tan, Marcus Carter, Joanne E. Gray
abstract: In online safety research, harassment is commonly understood as involving overt and unwanted acts that create a hostile environment for individuals or groups. Smart glasses, or wearable digital devices that are often indistinguishable from ordinary eyewear but can record video, audio and location data in real time, enable new forms of online harassment and gender-based harms that may not be recognised by current online safety or platform governance frameworks. Drawing on an interpretive content analysis of 350 point-of-view Instagram videos posted by individuals self-associated with the pick-up artistry (PUA) community, we examine how smart glasses can be used to harass women through what we call ambient capture. Ambient capture includes clandestine recording of people and social interactions within public, semi-private and private spaces. We argue this can constitute harassment when it is targeted at women and shared online without their consent. In our study, we found videos using ambient capture practices to harass women that had gone undetected by Instagram’s content moderation systems. These findings suggest online safety regimes and content moderation approaches should be assessed to ensure they account for the more invisible forms of harassment introduced by smart glasses and other wearable technologies.

title: From science-policy to science-policy-society: enabling transformative change in practice
authors: Aniek Hebinck, Mara de Pater, Anita Lazurko, Gijs Diercks, Dalia D'Amato, Amanda Krijgsman, Heli Saarikoski, Hans Keune, Symke Nieboer, Julia Wittmayer
abstract: Transformative change is widely recognised as necessary to address interconnected, persistent sustainability crises. Yet, despite growing experimentation with co-production and societal engagement, dominant science–policy arrangements remain largely assessment-oriented and geared toward incremental optimisation. While the 2024 IPBES Transformative Change Assessment was a landmark articulating drivers and principles of transformation, less attention has been paid to how science–policy interfaces themselves must reorganise to enable transformative action. This perspective addresses that gap. We argue that enabling transformative change requires reconfiguring the science–policy interface toward a science–policy–society interface embedding collaboration, experimentation, and collective learning. Drawing on insights from transformative research and our own transdisciplinary experiences, we propose three institutional conditions: (1) embracing the contested nature of transformative change as a productive space; (2) shifting research and policy from incremental improvements to transformative futures and emerging alternatives; and (3) institutionalizing reciprocal, action-oriented collaboration that enables sustained experimentation and collective agency. These conditions must be reinforced through institutional reforms in agenda-setting, funding and evaluation logics, and mechanisms ensuring continuity and societal memory. We conclude that institutional reform and transformative practice co-evolve, positioning science–policy–society configurations as enabling infrastructures for sustainability transformations.

title: Accounting for Compositional Bias in Unexpected Event During Survey Designs
abstract: Political events may affect not only people’s political attitudes and behavior but also who responds to surveys. If events change who participates, estimates from event-focused designs may reflect changes in sample compositions rather than genuine opinion change. This is particularly challenging for designs like the Unexpected Event during Survey Design (UESD), which identifies causal effects by comparing respondents interviewed immediately before and after an unexpected event. I develop an analytical framework that extends established UESD best-practices, which successfully address observable differences between these samples, by sensitivity analyses to assess the potential impact of unobserved compositional bias. I illustrate the framework using the 2015 Charlie Hebdo terrorist attacks to estimate rally-around-the-flag effects and demonstrate its broader applicability by replicating 14 published UESD studies on terrorist events and rally-type outcomes. Across cases, political events affect sample compositions, but accounting for observable differences rarely changes estimated effects. Further, unobserved compositional bias would typically need to be implausibly strong to overturn substantive results. The proposed framework provides tools to assess and mitigate compositional bias, which strengthens causal inference in UESD and other event-focused designs.

title: Macroeconomic Volatility and Organizational Performance: A Contingency Theory Perspective from the Nigerian Corporate Sector
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Philip Shakede Sanni, Friday Izen Ohiokha
abstract: Macroeconomic instability has continued to shape the operating environment of firms in Nigeria, creating uncertainty that affects business outcomes. This study examines the effect of macroeconomic volatility on organizational performance in the Nigerian corporate sector, while also considering the role of firm-level characteristics within a contingency theory framework. A longitudinal panel design was adopted, using secondary data obtained from the Central Bank of Nigeria, the World Bank, and financial reports of selected firms listed on the Nigerian Exchange over the period 2010–2024. Panel regression techniques were employed, including fixed and random effects models, with the Hausman test used to determine the appropriate specification. The findings indicate that macroeconomic volatility, particularly inflation, exchange rate fluctuations, and interest rate changes, has a significant negative effect on firm performance, while economic growth exerts a positive influence. The results further show that firm-level factors such as size, liquidity, and leverage significantly moderate this relationship. Firms with stronger financial capacity are better able to absorb macroeconomic shocks, whereas highly leveraged firms are more vulnerable to instability. The study concludes that organizational performance in Nigeria is influenced not only by external economic conditions but also by how firms adjust their internal structures and strategies. By applying contingency theory, the study provides a more nuanced explanation of performance differences across firms. The findings offer useful insights for managers seeking to improve resilience and for policymakers aiming to strengthen the business environment.

title: The Rise and (Partial) Retreat of DEI Claims in Recruiting
authors: Janet Xu, Reuben Hurst, Shanshan Liu
abstract: In recent years, and especially after the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, U.S. employers increasingly affirmed commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Donald Trump's second administration has sought to reverse this shift. Yet how far pro-diversity language actually rose in employers' recruiting, and how much of that rise has since been undone, has not been established. Drawing on the universe of U.S. online job postings between January 2016 and February 2026-371.1 million postings from 2.7 million employers-we find that pro-diversity claims appeared in 7-12% of job postings until mid-2020, then rose 152% to a peak of 25.4% postings on the eve of the 2024 election. They fell 21% thereafter, to 19.9% by February 2026. Declines were sharper among federal contractors but proportionally similar for Democratic-and Republican-leaning employers. The reversal is unprecedented, yet partial: it has undone roughly a third of the post-2020 rise, but pro-diversity claims remain twice as common as they were pre-2020.

title: Gender Bias and Stereotyping in Portrayals of Female Physicists: An International Analysis from 2019-2022
abstract: This research quantifies the presence of pervasive gender biases and discriminatory depictions within the field of physics through the analysis of media representations. Utilizing a dataset spanning 2019-2022 in Mali, India, Peru, and Singapore, the study employs natural language processing techniques to identify instances of biased language, particularly indicative of assumptions of biological determinism (BD) and childhood socialization (CS). Findings reveal more pronounced BD/CS-insinuating diction in lower HDI regions, ranging from 21% in Mali to 0.8% in Singapore. Female physicist representation in academic literature averaged 11.9%, with first authorship rates varying from 0.2% in Mali to 23.2% in Singapore. Negative depictions persisted despite a 27% increase in references to female physicists, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to counteract prejudice and foster inclusive environments within the physics community in order to promote gender equity and harness diverse perspectives in advancing research, development, and scientific innovation.

title: Social network involvement in abortion care-seeking and abortion outcomes among a population-based sample in Nigeria
authors: Selena Anjur-Dietrich, Funmilola Olaolorun, Elizabeth Omoluabi, Philip Anglewicz, Suzanne Bell
abstract: People often engage social networks when navigating structural and local abortion access constraints, but limited research links this involvement to abortion outcomes. This cross-sectional study analyzed PMA2020 data from 1,144 women in Nigeria who had abortions, identified via population-based surveys and abortion-focused follow-ups conducted in 2018. We examined how social network involvement in care-seeking—specifically, participation in selecting method or provider—related to abortion outcomes: medically defined abortion safety, use of preferred method and provider, and success of the initial abortion attempt. Social network involvement was common (63%) and varied across sociodemographic characteristics. Outcomes differed by who participated: when both partners and family/friends participated, women were least likely to have the least safe abortions (23.9% vs. 60.9%, p<0.001) or require multiple attempts (13.7% vs. 19.1%, p=0.009), though equally likely to use preferred care compared to those seeking care alone. Partner-only involvement was also associated with fewer least safe abortions (36.3% vs. 60.9%, p<0.001), while family/friend-only involvement was linked to lower preference fulfillment (36.6% vs. 21.6%, p<0.001) and more repeated attempts (27.8% vs. 19.1%, p=0.038). These findings suggest that social networks have the potential to improve or worsen abortion outcomes, with important variation across person-centered measures of abortion experiences.

title: Irregular Migration Early Warning Systems Based on Digital Migration Intelligence: Evidence from the 2026 Ceuta Crisis
abstract: Irregular migration crises often evolve more rapidly than conventional migration monitoring systems can detect. Although official migration statistics remain indispensable for documenting realised migration flows, they are typically published only after migration events have unfolded, limiting their value for anticipatory migration governance. This study proposes Digital Migration Intelligence as an integrated conceptual and analytical framework for the development of Irregular Migration Early Warning Systems and examines its applicability through the 2026 Ceuta migration crisis. The study combines multilingual Google Trends analyses with evidence derived from Facebook communities and Meta Audience Insights. Rather than relying on isolated search terms, the proposed framework analyses the convergence of multilingual behavioural, communication and demographic digital traces, including destination-related, border-related, environmental, route-related and legal-information searches originating from Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania. The findings suggest that migration-related digital activity intensified several days before the documented escalation of migration pressure. The strongest convergence of multilingual digital indicators was observed in Morocco, while comparable patterns in Algeria and a more limited signal in Mauritania provided additional support for the proposed analytical framework. Facebook communities revealed active communication networks through which migration-related information circulated, whereas Meta Audience Insights contributed complementary demographic evidence on language-specific digital populations. The principal contribution of the study is the development of Digital Migration Intelligence as a multidimensional framework integrating behavioural, communication and demographic digital evidence within a single analytical perspective. The Ceuta case provides a proof of concept illustrating how multilingual digital traces may complement existing migration monitoring by identifying behavioural changes preceding rapidly evolving irregular migration crises. Future research should prospectively evaluate the framework across different migration corridors and assess its integration with artificial intelligence-assisted monitoring systems. Keywords: Irregular Migration, Migration Early Warning Systems; Digital Migration Intelligence; irregular migration; digital demography; Big Data; Ceuta.

title: Impact of Information Technology on Human Resource Management Practices in the Construction Industry in Edo State
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Grace Motunrayo Opia, Monday Osemeke
abstract: This study investigated the adoption and impact of information technology (IT) on Human Resource Management (HRM) practices in the construction industry in Edo State, Nigeria. A descriptive survey design was employed, targeting 500 HR professionals, with a stratified random sample of 222 respondents. Structured questionnaires validated for content and reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0.97) were used to collect data on demographics, IT usage in HR functions, and perceived IT impact. Out of 222 questionnaires, 196 were returned (88.3%). Findings revealed that IT is widely integrated into core HR functions, with payroll management (86.7%), employee records (81.6%), and attendance tracking (79.1%) most supported, and 81.6% of respondents using technology frequently. Regression analyses showed that IT adoption significantly predicts the frequency of HR technology use (R² = 0.425) and improves HRM effectiveness and efficiency (R² = 0.659). Payroll management, performance appraisal, and employee records were the strongest contributors. Despite high adoption, resistance to new technologies persists, indicating a need for training and change management.

title: Global trends of Publications on Online Dating Violence – A Bibliometric Analysis
authors: Yatheesh bharadwaj, Sivaranjini M, Jeevanthi M
abstract: Background: Online Dating Violence (ODV) is increasingly recognized as a distinct form of intimate partner violence, characterized by the use of digital tools to perpetrate control, harassment, or emotional and sexual coercion within romantic relationships. The current aims at Mapping the Global literature in the field of Online Dating Violence by looking at it in the lens of Bibliometric Science. Methodology: The Study used Scopus Database to Conduct the Bibliometric Analysis. Initially, 62576 Documents were retrieved from the database, using systematic Bibliometric Approach. The title focused search was performed. Finally, 352 documents were obtained for the Bibliometric Analysis. To conduct the analysis, R software, VOSViewer, Microsoft excel software were utilised. Results: The Results found out that western Countries have more publications than the east, especially the United States and United Kingdom are two Influential countries in the field of research on Online dating violence.

title: Open Science is an Urgent Necessity in All Areas of Sociology including Public Sociology
abstract: This is a comment on the vision statement for sociology published by Aksoy, Manzo, Birkelund and Raub (2026). It supports their vision of open science in sociology but argues that open science is urgent and should be the first, if not only priority of modern sociology. It discusses recent evidence that sociology is the least reliable of the major social and behavioral science disciplines. It is essentially unreliable as a whole. It also argues that public sociology should not be removed from sociology but simply made transparent and open. Finally, it concludes that sociologists themselves should be humble and honest in public that their discipline is not reliable, rather than defending a failed status quo.

title: Amateur Ensemble Music Making: Between Self and Community, and Experience and Result
abstract: Approximately 14 million people in Germany participate in amateur music-making, much of which takes place within socially structured clubs rooted in volunteerism. This study draws on interviews with 22 ensemble members conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic to explore the interplay between individual and collective dimensions of ensemble participation. Participants’ motivations and experiences were analysed across four interrelated orientations: self, community, experience, and result. While these aspects may appear contradictory, they are in fact complementary, reflecting the complexity of amateur ensemble life. The ensemble offers a space where personal growth and musical achievement occur through shared effort, especially for those who might not pursue music independently. Rehearsals provide emotional and social fulfilment, yet their meaning is often tied to tangible outcomes such as concerts. The unique structure of social clubs facilitates belonging, identity formation, and cohesion, while also presenting challenges related to volunteer roles and diversity. The pandemic highlighted how crucial goal-oriented collaboration is to members’ satisfaction, underscoring the ensemble’s dual role in fostering both community engagement and personal development. Ultimately, amateur music-making in Germany emerges as a dynamic, inclusive practice that bridges individual aspirations with collective purpose.

title: Simulating Strategic Competition in Cyberspace: How Persistent Engagement Generates Cumulative Advantage
abstract: Cyber conflict has become central to international politics, yet traditional strategic frameworks, such as deterrence, struggle to explain competition below the threshold of armed conflict. Cyber Persistence Theory conceptualizes cyberspace as a distinct strategic environment in which security depends on seizing and sustaining initiative through persistent engagement. Yet the theory faces an empirical deadlock: cyber operations are largely classified and intentionally difficult to observe, making initiative challenging to trace empirically; in addition, available measures tend to capture isolated incidents rather than cumulative strategic effects. To address this problem, this study treats cyberspace as a complex adaptive system and develops a nested agent-based model of interstate cyber competition in a network-of-networks characterized by ever-present vulnerabilities, limited resources, and partial visibility. The model bridges micro-level interactions over exploitation and recovery with macro-level outcomes in strategic advantage. The paper formalizes Cyber Persistence Theory by operationalizing initiative as control, shifting the analysis from one-off compromise events to how control is accumulated and retained over time. This enables analysis of mechanisms through which persistent engagement produces compounding gains. The simulations show how hybrid persistent-engagement strategies can outperform pure offense or defense by combining recovery, foreign access, operational tempo, and visibility advantages. The model therefore provides a transparent, mechanism-based test of Cyber Persistence Theory's core logic, showing how persistent engagement can convert maintained initiative into cumulative strategic advantage. More broadly, the study demonstrates the value of agent-based modeling for analyzing strategic tradeoffs in cyber conflict, where direct empirical evidence is scarce and likely to remain so.

title: The mirage of “participation” in vulnerable, hard-to-reach communities through the eyes of the Koome fishing community in Uganda
abstract: Meaningful community participation is vital to successful vaccination, especially in settings characterized by limited communication access and unequal power relations. Uganda’s fishing communities not only represent distinctive challenges and opportunities for participatory health communication initiatives but also experience mixed outcomes from vaccine communication interventions. These settings have historically been itinerant, multi-lingual, marginalized, with limited access to social services; characterized by shared livelihoods and distinct cultural practices, factors which influence both vaccine attitudes and behaviors. Participatory vaccine communication in these vulnerable contexts easily turns tokenistic, which creates a tension between the promise of empowerment and the reality of exclusion. This requires tailored strategies rooted in an understanding of existing power structures. Using Freire’s participatory communication theory, we interrogated how the concepts of power, agency and voice combine to influence the effectiveness of vaccine communication in vulnerable communities. We report findings from 29 in-depth interviews and two gender-specific Focus Group Discussions. Key findings revealed gender dynamics evident in divergent budget priorities and the absence or disengagement of men from vaccine decisions; partial or inaccurate vaccine information leading to mis-or dis-information or mistrust; multigenerational discourses of vaccine experiences, and perceptions about health worker-patient communication at health facilities. The findings provide a window into the quality of participation from message design to delivery highlighting possible causes of channel mistrust and vaccine hesitancy. This study highlights the potential for structural transformation through dialogue and the need for a nuanced appreciation of local communication contexts and their impact on vaccine communication.

title: Cohesive Subgroups in Friendship Dynamics
authors: Stepan Zaretckii, Tom A.B. Snijders, Marijtje A.J. van Duijn, Christian Steglich
abstract: This study examines whether friendship dynamics differ within and outside inferred cohesive subgroups using longitudinal friendship data from 83 classrooms in 14 Dutch secondary schools. Cohesive subgroups are inferred from observed friendship networks using a Latent Membership Stochastic Actor-Oriented Model (LM-SAOM). Friendship change is then modeled using SAOMs in which shared membership in inferred cohesive subgroups is included as a binary dyadic covariate. The results show that students are more likely to maintain existing friendships and create new ones with classmates with whom they share latent group membership, beyond well-established tendencies toward reciprocity, transitive closure, and sex homophily. Moreover, reciprocity, transitive closure, and sex homophily contribute more strongly to friendship dynamics among classmates who do not share latent group membership. These findings suggest that cohesive subgroups may provide a shared social context that stabilizes friendships among groupmates, underscoring the importance of cohesive subgroups for friendship dynamics.

title: Environmental sustainability, healthiness and cost of supermarket retailer food and non-alcoholic beverage categories: an observational analysis of retail transaction data from Yorkshire and the Humber, UK (2022)
authors: Emma Wilkins, Mariana Dineva, Mark Alan Green, Mark Gilthorpe, Alexandra Johnstone, Michelle Morris
abstract: Background Changing our food system to address the dual challenge of population and planetary health requires greater understanding of the environmental sustainability of food products, and how these interplay with healthiness and food cost. Large scale transaction data from supermarket retailers can be used to better understand these factors, and how consumer behaviours contribute to environmental footprints. Methods We used anonymised loyalty card transaction data for 2022 from a major UK supermarket retailer for customers living in the Yorkshire and the Humber region (UK) (>160 million sales). These data were linked with product-level nutrition data to derive a binary indicator of product healthiness (High Fat Salt and/or Sugar (HFSS) status). The sales data were also linked with global estimates for greenhouse gas emissions (GHGE), land use, water use per kg. We described environmental impacts (GHGE, land and water use, and a composite of these domains) of food categories according to the Living Costs and Food Survey categories (n = 64), operationalised as unit metrics (per kg) and sales footprints (accounting for the weight of each product sold). We explored the interplay between product healthiness, cost per kg and environmental impact using visualisation methods. Findings For the composite index, the food categories with the highest sales footprints were Beef, Cheese and Curd, Milk, Ready Meals and Chocolate. Category rankings were substantively different when operationalised as impact per kg versus sales footprints, and for GHGE, land use and water use separately. Products that were less healthy and high environmental impact per kg had a median cost per kg that was 350% higher than healthier and low impact products, but there was wide variability in food cost across all levels of healthiness and impact. Fruits and vegetables tended to have favourable profiles across healthiness, sustainability and cost domains. Interpretation Sales footprints and unit metrics (e.g. per kg) provide different lenses, which are both needed to understand the sustainability of our food system at a product level, and should be considered in data-focussed policy to drive population and planetary health. Policy should support initiatives to minimise discretionary food consumption, particularly chocolate, and increase fruit and vegetable consumption to improve both human and planetary health. Funding This work was part of the FIO-Food project, funded through the Transforming the UK Food System for Healthy People and a Healthy Environment SPF Programme, delivered by UKRI, in partnership with the Global Food Security Programme, BBSRC, ESRC, MRC, NERC, Defra, DHSC, OHID, Innovate UK and FSA (FIO-Food award: BB/W018021/1).
