title: Religious Racism, Black LGBTQI+ Christianity, and Human Rights: An Intersectional Dialogue Between Brazil and the United States
abstract: The discourse on religious racism in Brazil has predominantly centered on violence against Afro-Brazilian religions, such as Candomblé and Umbanda. This essay argues that the analytic power of the category "religious racism" is significantly amplified when examined through an intersectional lens that connects race, religion, sexuality, gender, and belonging. Moving beyond a framework of simple religious intolerance, it explores how racialized religious hierarchies affect Black subjects whose religious identities are internally contested, with a specific focus on Black LGBTQI+ Christians and, more precisely, Black LGBTQI+ Pentecostals. The Brazilian case is placed in a critical dialogue with U.S. scholarship on Black Christianity, Black Pentecostalism, LGBTQI+ religious identities, and affirming congregations. This comparison is not predicated on the assumption of identical phenomena but rather on what each context illuminates in the other. Drawing on Brazilian legislation, human rights instruments, research on Afro-Brazilian communities, jurisprudence, and the author’s previous ethnographic research on an inclusive Pentecostal congregation, the essay proposes that religious racism functions as a form of racialized exclusion that operates through the regulation of religious legitimacy, sacred space, bodies, theological belonging, and access to justice. The U.S. literature provides a vital comparative vocabulary for understanding how racial identity and Christian belonging can coexist with sexual marginalization. The essay concludes that the protection of religious freedom requires more than formal state neutrality; it demands the institutional recognition of historically racialized religious practices and the intersectional subjects who inhabit them. In this sense, the struggle against religious racism is simultaneously a struggle over religion, race, citizenship, dignity, and human rights.

title: Equal Returns, Unequal Outcomes: How Education Reproduces the Racial and Gender Earnings Gap
abstract: Education is widely assumed to function as "the great equalizer" — a mechanism through which inequality of birth is overcome. This study tests that assumption by examining whether the returns to education close racial and gender earnings gaps or reproduce them. Using pooled data from the General Social Survey (2016–2024, N = 6,151) and a survey-weighted interaction model, I distinguish between equal returns (credentials raising earnings by the same proportion for all groups) and equalizing returns (credentials closing the gap between groups). I introduce the concept of credential suppression: the labor market suppression of a credential's value by suppressing the value of the person who holds it, along lines of race and gender. Results show that Black men with bachelor's degrees earn amounts statistically indistinguishable from white men with only a high school diploma. Returns to education are not significantly differential for Black men and, where differential for white women and Black women, are not compensatory enough to overcome baseline penalties of 49 to 67 percent. The earnings gap persists within the same fields of study and survives controls for family background. For Black men, a bachelor's degree would need to return 2.5 times what it returns for white men to reach parity. It returns less. These findings challenge the premise underlying both the Supreme Court's decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) and Executive Order 14173 (2025), which ended affirmative-action requirements for federal contractors: that neutral treatment of credentials produces neutral outcomes. Equal returns do not equalize. They reproduce the gap at every education level.

title: “Anti-Genderism” and Euroscepticism: A Cross-National Analysis
abstract: The Anti-Gender Movement (AGM) has emerged as a potent illiberal movement in reaction to socially progressive issues such as LGBTQ+ rights, feminism, adoption by heteronormative families, abortion, euthenasia, and surrogacy. Despite increasing attention to this transnational radical right movement, little is known about the relationship that these views have with perceptions of the EU, which institutionally supports many of these liberal issues. Using two cross-national datasets, the Voices of Central Europe (VoCE) survey of ten Central and Eastern European countries and European Social Survey (ESS) with merged panel data from the CRONOS-2 follow-up survey covering nine countries in Europe, this study tests whether anti-gender beliefs are related to perceptions of the EU and compares them to similar Eurosceptic benchmarks from nativist and populist ideologies. The results from the multilevel models show in both cases that anti-gender beliefs are related with strong negative attitudes towards the EU. In the VoCE dataset, there are strongly associated preferences for anti-democratic forms of government and perceptions of significant threat from Western countries, as well as perceptions that the EU is threatening that it “dictates” laws to their country. The results from the ESS dataset demonstrate that anti-gender beliefs are strongly associated with a lower trust in the EU Parliament, a preference for decisions to be taken at the national level over the supranational level, and preferences to leave the EU, though, to a smaller extent than those with nativist or populist attitudes. The results testify to the AGM’s opposition to not only progressive cultural values, but also the EU’s liberal democratic “social contract.”

title: An Open Two-Corpus Dataset of Animal Harm Incidents and Criminal Judgments in China (AHID-CN)
abstract: China has no anti-cruelty statute, so there is no offense category, court statistic, or government database that records harm to animals. AHID-CN makes this harm countable through two deliberately separate sub-corpora. An incident corpus documents 30 publicly reported animal-harm events through archived sources, extracted claims, and coded institutional responses. A judgment census identifies 490 animal-harm criminal judgments (about 409 unique cases) from CAIL2018, a frozen corpus of 2.68 million Chinese criminal judgments published up to 2018, using a documented search protocol in which every automated exclusion was manually re-examined. The dataset ships as five CSV tables with full field documentation under CC BY-SA 4.0 on Zenodo. It supports research on how existing criminal law stretches to cover harms it was not written for, on the co-occurrence of animal abuse with interpersonal violence, and on what public reporting captures that the judicial record misses.

title: ‘What does "fairness” mean for you?': Using data visualizations to promote interdisciplinary dialogue about key terms in AI Ethics.
authors: David Moats, Francien Dechesne, Judit Varga, Tjitske Holtrop, Ludo Waltman, Nees Jan van Eck
abstract: The task of making Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning systems, fair, accountable and transparent is a necessarily interdisciplinary one, involving contributions from computer science, philosophy, sociology and law. But in this emerging field it is frequently acknowledged that key terms like ‘fairness’, ‘accountability’, ‘transparency’, ‘discrimination’ and ‘bias’ are used very differently by these different disciplines. This paper presents a workshop exercise intended to facilitate discussions about the divergent uses of key terms in AI Ethics, FairML and related interdisciplinary spaces. It uses a simple data visualization technique to highlight different uses of key terms in a given corpus of scientific papers and also provides a platform and protocol to guide the discussion. We argue that data visualizations can play an important role in this task, but they need to acknowledge the multivalence of key terms, rather than glossing over them, and they need to be deployed as part of a process of collective inquiry and managed dialogue (they do not speak for themselves). Our goal is to both promote awareness and understanding of different uses of words and, hopefully, generate new ideas and thinking through more productive dialogue between disciplines.

title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

title: Salient Shock, Imperceptible Impacts: Germans' Immigration Attitudes and the 2022-2023 Energy Price Spike
authors: Niloufar Davis, William Matthew Halm, Hanno Hilbig, Daniel Hopkins
abstract: Prior research finds that personal economic experiences typically have limited political impacts but can shape attitudes under certain conditions. Here, we explore a likely case: in Germany, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine led to a dramatic spike in energy prices and an influx of Ukrainian refugees, both widely covered by news media. We use an online panel of German citizens (2022-2024) to assess the energy shock's impacts on immigration attitudes. Living in areas with larger natural gas price increases (and so higher residential heating costs) is associated with heightened economic distress. Yet we find no systematic evidence that these shocks shifted immigration attitudes over the subsequent 20 months, with minimum detectable effects of 0.10 to 0.18 standard deviations across our five attitude indices. Although extant research documents sizable political responses to some economic shocks, even a large, salient economic shock need not generate exclusionary immigration attitudes.

title: The functional and structural diversity of rhythmic communication across species
authors: Gabriela-Alina Sauciuc, Jennifer N. Schneider, Lara Sophie Burchardt, Michael D. Greenfield, Gerlinde Höbel, Nao Ota
abstract: Research on the rhythmic communication (RC) of nonhuman animals is undergoing a period of great effervescence and expansion. Here, we synthesize this rapidly growing literature with the aim of mapping RC forms and usage contexts in an unprecedented diversity of taxa, spanning insects, fish, frogs, birds and mammals. We see this as a first large-scale effort toward charting the functional and structural traits of RC in order to identify taxon-specific and shared motifs and, thus, preliminary evolutionary trends. Our synthesis shows that all the covered taxa use RC in reproductive contexts and suggest that RC undergoes an increasing functional complexification as a function of socio-cognitive complexification. By contrast, structural complexity fluctuates less at cross-taxonomic level, such that, at the production level, within each studied class or order, some species exhibit highly complex RC forms and rhythmic coordination, while others exhibit the simplest forms of RC. However, based on the current data, it remains unclear if species with complex RC structures also possess sophisticated RC perception. The chapter also reveals considerable theoretical and methodological heterogeneity in the study of animal RC and the need for cross-talks between taxon-specialized researchers toward harmonizing key terms, concepts and measures to improve data comparability.

title: The developmental trajectory of rhythmic abilities in humans and singing primates
authors: Gabriela-Alina Sauciuc, Teresa Raimondi, Chiara De Gregorio
abstract: Rhythmicity is a composite competence that spans perceptual, motor, and socio-cognitive abilities. This is highly salient when adopting a developmental perspective, as we do in this chapter that reviews data from humans and other singing primate taxa with a close (gibbons) or remote (indri lemurs) phylogenetic relatedness to our species. The findings we review show that rhythmicity develops as an interplay between innate maturational processes and socio-ecological influences and that its underlying mechanisms have distinct developmental trajectories. Generally, however, the human data show that perceptual skills emerge earlier than motor ones. Moreover, both the human and nonhuman data show that rhythmic proficiency improves as (possibly innate) behavioural rhythms are brought under increased motor — and likely also cognitive — control. We surmise that developmental primate data are essential for understanding the underlying mechanisms and adaptive benefits of human rhythmic competence and the human-definitory forms of communication and cooperation that it enables. As this kind of data is exceedingly scarce, a substantial task of future research will be to reduce this gap. We also identify substantial gaps in current developmental research with human children, including the need to go beyond auditory rhythms and investigate rhythms broadcasted in other modalities as well, to increase the cross-cultural representativeness of the samples and to examine longitudinally the relationships between elements of the rhythmic composite.

title: Moving the Body and the Mind - Links between Emotion and Rhythmic Communication and the underlying Neurobiological Mechanisms
abstract: Rhythmic patterning is a widespread structural trait of animal (including human) communication. Concomitantly, a key role of communication is to convey and/or induce emotion. The expression and modulation of emotion is also hypothesized to be a key mechanism for the evolution of rhythmic synchronization in humans. Despite the centrality of both rhythm and emotion to human and nonhuman communication, a systematic treatment of the link between them is currently lacking. In this chapter we bridge these two areas of research by reviewing findings from human and animal studies. These studies show how emotional states can be encoded and decoded through rhythmic parameters and how rhythmic parameters modulate the emotional states of receivers. Taken together, this review of literature demonstrates that the main rhythmic parameter currently evaluated in emotion research is frequency rate, which in all the surveyed taxa is reliably associated with levels of emotional arousal. We discuss a range of neurobiological mechanisms that could mediate the link between rhythm and emotion. We also identify several avenues for future research that address current limitations, such the overwhelming focus on acoustic modality and frequency rate, while other communication modalities and rhythmic parameters remain understudied.

title: How animals produce rhythm – an overview of ethological mechanisms for rhythmic communication
abstract: Animals communicate with a staggering diversity of rhythmic signals, yet behind all this diversity lies a small number of ethological mechanisms. In this chapter, we provide a quick review of how animal produce rhythmic signals based on these mechanisms, which span tremulation, percussion, bodily displays, stridulation, tymbalation, aerodynamic sound production (including vocalisation), as well as the production of luminescent, chromogenic and electric rhythms. We point out that these ethological mechanisms which underlie the production of communicative rhythms appear to be derived from rhythmic praxic behaviours that initially evolved to implement vital functions such as breathing, feeding, locomotion, defense or procreation. Based on the findings reviewed by the chapter, we identify three important areas for future research for advancing our understanding of the evolution of rhythmic communication. First, there is a massive research gap when it comes to quantifying how rhythmic signals unfold and interact across perceptual and behavioural modalities. Second, there is a need to understand how behavioural rhythms relate to — and are constrained by — their underlying neuromuscular substrates. Third, very little is known about the relationship between communicative rhythms and the praxic behaviours in which they putatively originated.

title: Saskatchewan's Patients First Health Care Plan: A Health Reform Analysis Through the Lens of Urban Baseline Normativism
abstract: Saskatchewan’s Patients First Health Care Plan, launched in March 2026, promises universal attachment to a primary care provider by 2028, primarily through expansion of the Patient Medical Home (PMH) model, independent nurse practitioner (NP) contracts, and incremental scope-of-practice changes. Emerging after a prolonged access crisis, the plan assembles a suite of instruments that had already been piloted or partially implemented, favouring rapid scaling over fresh policy design. Using Kingdon’s Multiple Streams Framework, this health reform analysis shows how converging problem, policy, and politics streams opened a window for a low‑risk, evidence‑referencing response rather than a structural redesign of primary care. It introduces Urban Baseline Normativism to argue that PMH funding criteria, NP contract parameters, and unchanged physician‑delegation rules for nursing procedures may reflect the organisational and physician‑supply conditions of Swift Current, the flagship PMH pilot site, and then extended province‑wide as if those baseline capacities were ubiquitous. This produces a reform architecture in which expanded roles for NPs, pharmacists, and paramedics remain tethered to unevenly available physician resources, and in which attachment targets can be met in aggregate while rural and remote communities continue to face structural barriers to primary care. The analysis concludes that without recalibrating implementation criteria and delegation rules for low‑capacity settings, Patients First may be more likely to reproduce than to correct the urban‑normative assumptions embedded in Saskatchewan’s primary care system, yielding geographically uneven.

title: Ten months of continuous coordinated-behaviour monitoring on Facebook: the VERA-AI Alert system and its empirical yield
authors: Fabio Giglietto, Giada Marino, Anwesha Chakraborty, Nicola Righetti
abstract: What does a coordination detector find when it is seeded once and then left to follow its own detections for ten months? Evidence on coordinated behaviour and influence operations comes almost entirely from retrospective case studies selected for their political salience. We report ten months (October 2023 – August 2024) of continuous monitoring by VERA-AI Alert, which wraps coordinated link-, message- and image-text-sharing engines in a recursive discovery loop, promotes recurring accounts into a watched pool, and alerts analysts in quasi-real time; we document the implementation in full. From a seed of 1,225 accounts anchored in fact-checked political and health misinformation, the deployment discovered 14,832 coordinated accounts forming 207 communities across 11 operational categories. Entertainment is 4.5% of the fact-checked URLs the seed was built from and gambling one URL in a thousand, yet entertainment/fan communities came to hold 36.4% of all discovered accounts and five gambling operations a further 6.3%. Matching on account identifiers, 0.26% of those entertainment accounts and 0.11% of the gambling ones had been on the seed watched list, against 3.92% of the political ones: new populations the loop reached, not the seed under new names. Political, entertainment and commercial coordination are thus not parallel ecosystems but spaces connected by sparse brokerage, and research scoped to political content cannot observe the bridges between them. Most detected coordination is low-intensity (80.7% sporadic or weak); the structure departs from a marginal-preserving null on all five metrics (p ≤ 0.001); and a strict filter recovers a 19-community core, matching a prior, separate analysis of the same data. The deployment ran on CrowdTangle; reproducing it now needs four things of a data-access route — programmatic export, scheduled unattended execution, a live engagement baseline, and identifiers that resolve to platform content — that no route available to us supplies together. Code and data: https://github.com/GiaMa/VeraAI-Global-CSB-Alert (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21225024).

title: BURIAL, MOURNING, AND THE SOCIAL ORGANIZATION OF CARE IN THE 2026 BUNDIBUGYO VIRUS DISEASE OUTBREAK IN THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO A desk-based qualitative synthesis
abstract: Background Burial is among the most epidemiologically consequential and socially sensitive components of Ebola response. During the 2026 outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, public-health agencies documented confrontations with burial teams, rumours about empty or opened coffins, questions about why families could not see or touch the dead, and delays in safe and dignified burial operations. These events were often described as community resistance. This paper instead examines burial as a moral, relational and practical process through which families care for the dead, organise grief, negotiate authority and restore social order. Methods We conducted a desk-based qualitative synthesis of outbreak-specific materials available up to 5 August 2026, including World Health Organization and Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reports, infodemic monitoring, key-message guidance, Red Cross reporting, social-science syntheses and a 2026 contextual note on funeral practices in Ituri. These were triangulated with peer-reviewed studies of safe and dignified burial, burial workers, gendered caregiving and community feedback from earlier Ebola outbreaks. Sources were coded for the social stages of burial, family authority, ritual obligations, gendered labour, conflict points, operational delays, adaptations and behavioural consequences. Findings Burial was not a single technical act but a sequence extending from end-of-life care and body preparation to viewing, transport, prayer, interment and continued mourning. The legitimacy of safe burial depended on whether families could identify the body, understand each procedure, retain recognised roles and participate in decisions about clothing, burial place, religious observance and commemoration. Conflict concentrated around rapid removal without explanation, limited visual access, uncertainty about testing and decontamination, delays in burial-team arrival, the presence of unfamiliar responders and procedures perceived as disrespectful. Women and relatives of the same sex as the deceased appeared especially exposed through caregiving and body preparation, although the available outbreak data could not quantify gender-specific risk. Locally recruited teams, family liaison, safe visual confirmation, ritual substitution, timely response and grief-sensitive communication were the most consistently supported adaptations. Interpretation Dignity and infection control are not competing objectives. A burial becomes epidemiologically effective when it is socially recognisable as a burial and when families have defensible reasons to trust what is happening to the body. Safe and dignified burial should therefore be managed as a negotiated care pathway, with timeliness, family participation, body-identification assurance, gender-sensitive risk assessment and family satisfaction treated as operational performance indicators.

title: TRUST, RUMOURS, AND RESPONSE LEGITIMACY IN THE 2026 BUNDIBUGYO VIRUS DISEASE OUTBREAK IN THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO A desk-based qualitative synthesis
abstract: The 2026 outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo developed into a major public-health emergency in a setting marked by armed insecurity, population mobility, weak routine health services and previous experience of externally led Ebola responses. Alongside the epidemiological emergency, response agencies documented doubts about whether the outbreak was real, suspicions that it was being used for financial or political purposes, concerns about treatment and isolation, and confrontations around the handling of the dead. These narratives raise a central operational question: under what conditions do communities consider an epidemic response credible, fair and morally legitimate? We conducted a desk-based qualitative synthesis of publicly available materials relating to the outbreak, identified up to 5 August 2026. The outbreak-specific corpus included World Health Organization and Africa Infodemic Response Alliance social-listening reports, disease outbreak notices and situation reports, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies community-feedback reporting, the Social Science in Humanitarian Action Platform rapid synthesis, operational statements and selected media accounts. These materials were triangulated with peer-reviewed research on institutional trust, community feedback and the atmosphere of mistrust during the 2018–2020 Ebola epidemic in eastern DRC. The available evidence identified several connected narrative clusters: claims that Ebola was invented or exaggerated; the recurrent idea that “Ebola is a business”; allegations of political manipulation or external intervention; suspicion of medicines, disinfectants, experimental products and treatment centres; uncertainty about how patients could recover without a licensed treatment; and rumours concerning burials, bodies and empty coffins. These narratives were not expressions of biomedical ignorance alone. They interpreted the outbreak through prior experiences of corruption, unequal resource distribution, inadequate routine services, coercive authority and limited transparency. Operational reports linked these concerns to delayed care-seeking, resistance to referral and isolation, incomplete contact tracing, burial tensions and hostility towards responders. Local volunteers, survivors and trusted community intermediaries appeared capable of improving credibility, although the available evidence did not support a representative ranking of trusted institutions. Trust should be treated as part of outbreak-control infrastructure rather than as an attitudinal outcome of communication. Response legitimacy is produced through the conduct of the response: transparent explanation of case figures and procedures, fair and visible use of resources, respectful treatment of patients and families, locally credible messengers, practical opportunities for community participation, and demonstrable adaptation to feedback.

title: Disrupting Workplace Gender Inequality from Below: Relational Mechanisms of Feminist Organizing in a Dutch Union-Based Women's Network
authors: Elise Jantine van der Mark, Raisa Mulder
abstract: Workplace gender inequality remains a pertinent issue in the Netherlands. Existing organizational responses have predominantly focused on top-down strategies such as awareness training and diversity policies, which may insufficiently engage with the everyday workplace dynamics through which gendered inequalities are reproduced. Collective, bottom-up organizing that challenges these dynamics has received substantially less attention. We draw on feminist relational theory, the Gender@Work (G@W) framework and feminist conceptualizations of power to specify the relational mechanisms through which collective feminist organizing carries a shift in consciousness into access to resources, informal norms and formal rules. Twelve in-depth interviews with participants in FemForce, a Dutch union-based women's network, provide the empirical basis, supplemented by document review and expert interviews. Where the G@W framework establishes that its quadrants interact, this study specifies how that interaction is carried relationally, showing this transmission to be collective rather than individual, and uneven across participants. It extends existing insights in four directions: consciousness-raising is relationally produced through affective conditions that must be actively co-produced; feminine authority transforms not through visibility alone but through the embodied mode in which it is practiced and the institutional location from which it is exercised; the union context actively politicizes experience rather than merely hosting it; and feminist organizing has a cumulative, diffusive logic through which transformation travels beyond its original space into everyday workplace and social life.

title: The Political Ecology of Constructed Scarcity: Climate Variability and Development Policy in Southwest Timor
authors: Isnan Fauzi, Mario Arnesto Onggang, Lommi Dida Kini, Adeodatus Carmelo Daniel, Priska Manek
abstract: In dryland Indonesia, water and agricultural scarcity is predominantly framed as a consequence of climate change, justifying state-led interventions in irrigation, hybrid seed promotion, and commodity agriculture. This study challenges that framing by examining how scarcity is co-produced through the interaction of climatic variability and development policy in Southwest Timor. Focusing on Atoin Meto communities in Kolbano, it combines multi-decadal spatial analysis of temperature, precipitation, and drought indices with qualitative evidence from interviews and focus group discussions across three ecologically distinct villages. The spatial record confirms genuine climatic intensification: sustained warming since 1949, a precipitation deficit below long-term averages over the past decade unprecedented in 120 years, and structural drying extending beyond El Niño cycles. Yet these stresses do not explain who experiences water shortage, who loses crops, or who abandons farming. Drawing on the political ecology of constructed scarcity, the analysis shows that climatic exposure becomes consequential scarcity through three interrelated domains: material redistribution, where road-led settlement reconfiguration displaced communities from their water sources and dismantled indigenous forest custodianship; institutional reconfiguration, where coercive agricultural mandates, hybrid seed promotion, and technocratic extension eroded local seed sovereignty and epistemically displaced indigenous ecological knowledge; and socio-economic restructuring, where market integration, rice dependency, and extractive mining narrowed livelihood diversity and pushed youth into precarious migration. The study contributes to political ecology by demonstrating that what appears as climate vulnerability is substantially the accumulated legacy of spatial dispossession and epistemic displacement and by treating indigenous knowledge systems as constitutive elements of adaptive capacity whose institutional erasure is itself a mechanism of scarcity production.

title: Business Process Re-engineering and Organisational Performance: Evidence from Commercial Banks in Edo State, Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Joshua Adeyemi Awotade, Elody Saidu Mamman, Mubaraq Ayomide Bada
abstract: This study examined the effects of process cycle time reduction and automation of banking processes on operational efficiency and service quality among selected commercial banks in Edo State, Nigeria. A cross-sectional survey design was adopted, and data were collected from 215 valid respondents using a structured questionnaire. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression with SPSS version 29. The findings revealed that process cycle time reduction had a positive and significant effect on operational efficiency and service quality. Automation of banking processes also had a positive and significant influence on both outcomes and emerged as the strongest predictor of organisational performance. The regression models explained 64.8% and 69.1% of the variance in operational efficiency and service quality, respectively. The study concludes that sustained process redesign and digital automation significantly enhance organisational performance by improving internal operational efficiency and customer service delivery. It recommends sustained investment in process optimisation, digital automation and continuous process improvement to strengthen organisational competitiveness and long-term performance.

title: Silent archival of World Development Indicators: data unavailability for retired WDI series through the World Bank API
abstract: The World Bank publishes over 1,000 time series in its World Development Indicators (WDI) catalogue, yet individual series are periodically retired. Using WDI's own archival metadata, we document that 1,338 currently unlisted series codes are absent from the public API and bulk-download catalogue, and that none of 40 retired series queried returned data through the World Bank's official API. We treat this as a silent-archival phenomenon: series disappear from the catalogue without public notice, release of a cessation report, or an archival dataset. We characterize the scale of the phenomenon, the metadata signals that identify retired series, and the resulting implications for reproducibility of economic research that relies on WDI time series.

title: PARIDAD DE GÉNERO EN LAS CANDIDATURAS Y VOTO CIUDADANO EN LAS ELECCIONES PARA GUBERNATURAS EN MÉXICO (2021-2024).
abstract: This study analyzes gender parity in Mexican gubernatorial candidacies (2021–2024). Through a comparative analysis of 32 elections, it examines whether regulatory balance in nominations (47% female) has translated into substantive equality in electoral outcomes. Findings reveal a persistent disparity: despite legal compliance, three out of every five votes favored male candidates. Although the electoral gap narrowed between 2021 and the 2022–2024 period, results demonstrate that formal parity is insufficient without transforming civic culture and eradicating gender stereotypes among the electorate. It is concluded that institutional engineering requires complementary policies to ensure substantive representation.

title: From Clicks to Credibility: Exploring the Use and Evaluation of News on Social Media Platforms among University Students in Ogun State, Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Oladipo AROWA, Ayoola Olalekan AJASA, Dasola Zainab OWOLABI
abstract: This study examines how university students in Ogun State, Nigeria, use and evaluate news obtained through social media, with particular attention to usage patterns, credibility judgements and digital literacy. Guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology and the Uses and Gratifications Theory, the study employed a quantitative survey design involving 676 respondents drawn from a population of 5,305 students across Mountain Top University and Anchor University. Stratified random sampling was used, while data collected through structured questionnaires were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including regression analysis. The findings showed that social media use had a weak and statistically insignificant influence on the news-consumption habits of Mountain Top University students but had a moderate and statistically significant influence among Anchor University students. No significant difference was found in the patterns of social media use between students of the two universities. The study concludes that students’ credibility evaluations are influenced more by digital literacy, trust and institutional context than by frequency of social media use alone. It recommends university-led media-literacy programmes that encourage fact-checking and responsible engagement with digital news.

title: Adaptive Grit: Persistence With Plasticity as a Dynamic Process Theory of Goal Pursuit Under Changing Conditions
abstract: Grit theory established perseverance and consistency of interest as individual differences relevant to long-term achievement, but subsequent research has raised questions about the construct’s structure, overlap with conscientiousness, incremental validity, and limited attention to contextual change. Traditional grit measures and theory provide limited guidance for determining when continued persistence becomes maladaptive. This paper introduces Adaptive Grit, a domain-general process theory defined as persistence with plasticity: the capacity to pursue meaningful goals through flexible persistence while continuously adapting to changing personal, social, and environmental contexts. Unlike trait models that treat adaptability as a parallel dimension, Adaptive Grit positions adaptation as the regulatory function of goal pursuit. Individuals identify meaningful goals, pursue and monitor them, evaluate whether their strategies support adaptive functioning, develop habits and environmental scaffolds, and determine whether observed or anticipated benefits outweigh current costs. The model permits four disciplined responses: persist, adjust, pause/disengage, and re-engage, while allowing strategies, pacing, expectations, environments, supports, or goals to change in response to feedback. By treating psychological and emotional wellbeing as indicators of adaptive functioning rather than acceptable costs of achievement, Adaptive Grit seeks to support sustainable goal pursuit without equating relentless endurance with success. Keywords: adaptive grit, grit, persistence, plasticity, self-regulation, goal adjustment, environmental scaffolding

title: A conceptual framework for information experience: evidence from serodiscordant couples in Malawi
abstract: This paper presents a conceptual framework for information experience grounded in a phenomenological study of how serodiscordant couples in Malawi experience HIV and AIDS information. Using Van Manen's hermeneutic phenomenology, in-depth interviews were conducted with 21 serodiscordant couples and 3 separated individuals. Analysis revealed that the life-world, comprising the lived body, lived space, lived others, and lived time, constitutes the overarching context within which information is experienced. A fifth life-world existential, spirituality, is proposed to account for the role of God and ancestral spirits as information sources. The study identifies four stages of information experience: anticipating, interacting with, acting on, and reflecting on information. These stages are non-linear, recursive, and mediated by continuous evaluation against religious, cultural, moral and social criteria. The framework extends existing information experience theory to populations facing stigmatised, life-threatening illness in low-resource settings.

title: How Well Can We Estimate Public Opinion Country-Year Trends from Multiple Survey Projects? A Monte Carlo Simulation
authors: Piotr Koc, Tomasz	Żółtak, Marco Steenbergen
abstract: Systematic studies of aggregate trends in public opinion hold great promise for the study of political behavior, representation, and comparative politics. Recently, several approaches have emerged to facilitate these studies. But how solid is the methodological footing of these approaches? While their methodological properties have been examined in a limited number of simulation studies, those have focused on isolated aspects of the data generating process. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of two key methodological frameworks, based on polytomous and dichotomized item response solutions, across several dimensions: richness of the data, number of countries, and the nature of differential item functioning (DIF). We find that the polytomous approach yields credible intervals that are too small, that both approaches have difficulties with severe DIF, and that dichotomization increases uncertainty relative to polytomous items. We show these results while paying attention to the full distribution of the latent variable of public opinion---both its center and its tails. Aside from showing the difficulties with extant approaches, we also show how they can be adapted to yield better estimates and comparisons of public opinion across countries.

title: Penggunaan metode Research and Development dalam penelitian Bahasa Indonesia di perguruan tinggi
abstract: Research is one of Tri Dharma of Higher Education pillars and become an integral part of the activities at the college. This has implications for the demands of college to have research centers and research institutions are adequate. Answering the demands of university-based research, then as a lecturer required mastery of qualified research methods. Methods of research and development is one of the research methods of Borg and Gall were introduced in this paper as a systematic method and can be applied in Indonesian language studies in college. Recommendations from this paper that the Association of Indonesian Language and Literature Lecturer (ADOBSI) expected to facilitate Indonesian language lecturers to develop the study of language, literature and teaching as an effort to create a sustainable professional development and as a means of discussion and collaboration to do the various research in languages, literature and teaching in Indonesia Keywords: Research, Research and Development Method, Indonesian Language, Higher Education

title: Monitor Digital Working Society – Brief report on the fourth wave of surveys: AI is becoming increasingly embedded in everyday work: Rising usage, greater degrees of autonomy and growing concerns.
authors: Frank Marcinkowski, Birte Keller, Marco Lünich, Florian Golo Flaßhoff
abstract: This brief report presents key findings from the last of four representative survey waves of the Monitor Digital Working Society, conducted as part of the research project Opinion Monitor Artificial Intelligence 3.0. The analysis is based on responses from 1,607 participants surveyed in July 2026, including 915 employed and 692 non-employed respondents. At the end of the survey series, interest in AI has returned to the elevated level observed in summer 2025 following an interim decline, while respondents’ self-assessed knowledge remains stable at a higher level than in the first wave. At the same time, assessments of the societal consequences of AI have become more critical: fewer respondents believe that the benefits outweigh the risks, while risk-oriented and ambivalent assessments have become more prevalent. In the workplace, the risk–benefit assessment of AI for respondents’ own occupations remains stable and slightly benefit-oriented. Evaluations of specific working conditions have become somewhat more positive, while personal job insecurity has increased noticeably. Most strikingly, occupational AI use has risen to the highest level recorded across the survey series. Growth is particularly pronounced for generative, recommendation-based, analytical, and decision-related functions. Employees also report greater freedom of use, decision-making authority, and opportunities to participate in shaping AI use, although a majority still have no influence over the introduction of AI in their workplace. Overall, the findings point to an ongoing normalization of AI: as its use becomes more widespread, both its concrete benefits and associated scope for action, as well as potential risks for employment and society, are becoming more visible and are assessed in increasingly differentiated ways.

title: ‘Some say vaccines kill children; others say they are expired’: Understanding community-driven narratives that exist alongside expert-driven vaccine communication in fishing communities in Uganda’
abstract: Public health communication in low and middle-income countries often relies on a unidirectional, expert-driven model that overlooks the socio-cultural complexities of underserved populations such as fisher folk along the islands of Lake Victoria. This paper presents the dual narratives between official health messaging and community-driven discourses in the geographically peripheral fishing communities of Koome Island, Uganda. Drawing on qualitative data from the VAnguard project, we explore how mobile populations create a dual communication landscape where institutional instructions competed with deep-seated local fears about vaccines. We mapped and consulted key stakeholders and conducted ethnographic research to understand community dynamics, local beliefs and misconceptions. Drama skits co-created with communities provided deeper insights into local beliefs, guiding culturally sensitive data collection and message design. By centering community members as co-producers of vaccine knowledge, the research sought to connect the ‘periphery’ of local island life to the ‘center’ of national public health policy. Participants reported receiving vaccine information from both the static clinics and outreach programmes. They also revealed that there was widespread misinformation fueled by poor communication. Participants repeatedly expressed fear that modern vaccines, particularly for COVID-19, Yellow Fever and the Human Papilloma Virus, were intended to kill people or cause long-term infertility. These fears were compounded by participants’ concerns about the improper storage of vaccines during transportation by boat and on-site, and some believed that children were sometimes given expired vaccines. Other barriers such as perceived poor health-worker and patient relationships further reinforced these negative narratives. This research argues that for social change to occur in these contexts, communication ought to move from a one-way dissemination toward a two-way communication model. By acknowledging and integrating community-driven narratives into the design of health communication, this can foster a more equitable dialogue that respects peripheral voices and enhances the legitimacy of preventive public health approaches.

title: From Monetary Entrepreneurship to Inclusive Growth in Nigeria: The Role of Multi-Stakeholder Governance and Institutionalisation in Digital Complementary Currencies
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Joshua Adeyemi Awotade, Monday Osemeke
abstract: This study analyses how monetary entrepreneurship, multi-stakeholder governance and institutionalisation shape the inclusive-growth outcomes of digital complementary currencies in Nigeria. Adopting an interpretivist approach and a qualitative multiple-case design, the study compares three settings: the state-driven eNaira, fintech-driven platforms and community-driven financial institutions. Data were obtained from semi-structured interviews and documents and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings demonstrate that monetary entrepreneurship is a multi-actor and co-produced endeavour involving state, market and community actors operating within a particular institutional context. Multi-stakeholder governance mediates system design, coordination and adoption, while institutionalisation influences legitimacy, sustainability and long-term impact. The study concludes that inclusive growth is an ecosystem outcome arising from the interaction of innovation, governance and institutional development, rather than from technological innovation alone. It recommends coordinated governance and institutional alignment in using digital financial systems to support financial inclusion and inclusive development.

title: Notified Bodies in the AI Act: regulatory intermediaries with a de facto gatekeeping role
abstract: This paper examines the significant yet underexplored role of notified bodies within the EU AI Act. These conformity assessment entities, once designated by national authorities and notified to the European Commission, are tasked with determining whether high-risk AI systems meet legal requirements to enter the EU market or put into service. Positioned between state regulators and providers of high-risk AI systems, notified bodies function as de facto gatekeepers, with the authority to allow or deny market access. Drawing on gatekeeping theory and regulatory governance literature, the paper conceptualises notified bodies as regulatory intermediaries who wield gatekeeping power despite not being state actors. The paper analyses their functions, accountability, and overall role, highlighting tensions arising from their quasi-public responsibilities and private nature. The paper argues for stronger safeguards to ensure legitimacy, transparency, and fundamental rights protection

title: Urban Baseline Normativism in Health Policy Design: A Framework for Understanding Rural Health Reform Challenges
abstract: Abstract Context: Health policy instruments are often designed around service configurations, densities, and utilization patterns typical of urban settings, treated as the baseline against which jurisdictions are judged. When rural communities cannot meet thresholds calibrated to urban conditions, the disadvantage is often read as a local implementation failure rather than a distinct structural feature of the instrument. This article introduces urban baseline normativism (UBN), a framework identifying when such assumptions become embedded in health policy design. Methods: This conceptual study develops UBN through theoretical literature on policy instruments, problem definition, and administrative classification, illustrated through purposively selected Canadian health-policy cases. The illustrations are not a representative sample and carry unequal evidentiary weight. They are used primarily to probe and demonstrate four proposed mechanisms rather than establish prevalence or causal effect. Findings: Four mechanisms operate across the policy cycle: majoritarian amplification at agenda-setting, baseline invisibility at formulation, structural dependency at implementation, and reform reproduction at evaluation. These are illustrated through physician licensure, nurse-practitioner contracting, trauma designation, perinatal surgical closures, and primary-care incentive payments, alongside boundary conditions specifying where UBN is weaker. Conclusions: UBN offers a diagnostic for identifying embedded urban assumptions, informing more deliberate, rural-responsive policy design and evaluation.

title: Internal Dispossession as Epistemic Injustice: A Concept Analysis of American Indian Identity Appropriation
abstract: Across the academy and health professions, individuals and organizations claim American Indian identity they do not hold, capturing positions, grants, and the authority to speak for Native peoples. This harm has been described across separate literatures—federal law, internal colonialism, internalized colonialism, and identity appropriation—but was never named or theorized as a single concept. This article reports an evolutionary concept analysis of internal dispossession, drawing on literature from 1887 to 2026 across five bodies of work and grounded in autoethnographic and public-record evidence, selected under a sovereignty-consistent citational criterion. Internal dispossession is defined as the harm produced when the authority of a sovereign people to define its own belonging is relocated onto individuals, institutions, and markets through identity appropriation, eroding the nation's capacity to define itself and displacing individual citizens. The concept is constituted by five attributes; arises from three antecedents—settler colonialism, the confusion of race with political status, and incentive structures with weak verification—and operates through interlocking relational, structural, and epistemic harms that continue the colonial logic of taking and turn, over time, inward upon the people. Understood as epistemic injustice, internal dispossession names the newest form of colonial dispossession and gives nursing analytic language to protect the integrity of its Indigenous workforce data, its health-equity funding, and the Indigenous health knowledge base—an analytic tool transferable to other settler-colonial contexts where belonging is constituted politically rather than racially.

title: Does automatic gratuity help or hurt servers? An examination of a casual restaurant’s POS data
abstract: Restaurants use automatic gratuities to protect servers from low tips, but these charges may also reduce voluntary tipping. After analysing transaction data from a casual dining restaurant, we found that automatic gratuity policies reduce voluntary tipping while increasing total service payments to servers. Implications for restaurant managers and directions for future research are discussed.

title: The Paradox of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Malaysian Art and Design Undergraduate Education: Overreliance, Erosion of Critical Thinking and Originality, Intellectual Property Ambiguities, and Pathways for Institutional Regulation
abstract: The rapid normalisation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools among undergraduate art and design students has created a dual-edged transformation in creative higher education. While GenAI accelerates ideation, visualisation, and iterative refinement, emerging evidence from 2025–2026 indicates that overreliance risks diminishing critical thinking, homogenising original expression, and complicating intellectual property (IP) ownership and attribution (Thinking Skills and Creativity, 2026; Xianwen, 2026). In the Malaysian context, where art and design programmes at public and private universities are integrating these tools amid uneven policy development, students increasingly treat GenAI as a default collaborator rather than a constrained aid (Wong et al., 2025; Nik Harun et al., 2026). This article synthesises recent empirical and conceptual literature to examine these effects. Drawing on studies conducted between 2025 and 2026, it analyses how normalised AI use fosters cognitive offloading, aesthetic standardisation, and authorship ambiguities, with particular attention to culturally specific challenges around local visual languages and authenticity (Mustaffa Halabi et al., 2025; ResearchGate, 2025). The discussion advances a regulatory framework tailored to Malaysian undergraduate programmes, emphasising structured AI literacy that pairs technical competence with critical verification, process-oriented assessment that prioritises decision-making evidence, mandatory disclosure of prompts and transformations, and human-centred pedagogy that positions AI as subordinate to student authorship (Chen et al., 2025; Nik Harun et al., 2026). Recommendations include curriculum redesign, institutional guidelines aligned with national higher education priorities on integrity and employability, and explicit safeguards for cultural originality. The article concludes that balanced regulation can preserve the distinctive human capacities central to art and design education while preparing graduates for an AI-augmented professional landscape.

title: Flood Disaster and Its Socio-Economic Effects on Livelihoods in Benin Metropolis, Edo State, Nigeria
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Afenge Kingsley Izevbekhai, K. A. Eghafon
abstract: This study examined flood disaster and its socio-economic effects on livelihoods in Benin Metropolis, Edo State. The study specifically examined the factors responsible for flooding and the extent of the social and economic disruption caused by flooding in Benin Metropolis. A qualitative method was employed, using in-depth interviews and observation. The study population comprised people affected by flooding in Benin Metropolis, while 36 household heads were purposively selected as key informants. The data generated were transcribed, analysed and presented descriptively in relation to the study objectives and the cultural ecology and political economy theories. The findings established that flooding occurs mainly because of blocked drains, poor waste-management practices, indiscriminate land use, population growth and selective governmental intervention. These factors contribute to the frequency and intensity of flooding in the study area. Flooding was also found to cause considerable disruption to the socio-economic lives and livelihoods of residents. The study recommends that the government urgently develop and implement a comprehensive policy for mitigating flooding in Benin Metropolis.

title: Trust us, “we love our horses”! A qualitative frame analysis of equestrian industry animal welfare policies
authors: Erica Cheung, Daniel S. Mills, Beth Ventura
abstract: Promotion of positive welfare for performance horses requires understanding the horses’ experience as well as human motivations for their care and training practices. However, an area given less scientific consideration has been the role of the activities of horse sport governing bodies, which set welfare standards for the industry or discipline and reflect that organisation’s attitudes toward horses. Governance may be an important influence in maintaining or reforming equestrian cultural norms that influence horse welfare. The present study uses frame analysis to explore how horse sport governing organisations frame messages about horses and their welfare. We sought to answer the question: what are horse sport governing bodies doing to promote a good life for performance horses? A total of 5 frames were interpreted within the categories of the horse, horse welfare, and the performance horse industry. Horses were framed in one of two ways: as a willing participant, and/or as a sentient being. Horse welfare was framed as high priority, but also left up to individuals to tangibly realise in practice. Finally, the performance horse industry was framed as guardians of horses and their welfare, and as a trusted entity. We conclude that these frames may function as strategies to secure legitimacy, social licence to operate, and a positive social identity for equestrian culture, rather than as enforceable policy. Drawing on non-ideal ethics and agent-based theories of change, we suggest that improvement in performance horse welfare may require independent oversight and tangible, equine-centric policies that include the equestrian industry as a collaborative partner in this endeavor.

title: A Comparative Analysis of New Technology Adoption in Agriculture and Manufacturing Sectors in Nigeria and Selected Countries
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Felix I. Ifada, Uma K. E.
abstract: This study investigates the importance of new technology in Nigeria’s agricultural and manufacturing sectors. Data were obtained mainly from online sources, libraries, and textbooks, while the analysis employed descriptive statements, tables, and charts. The comparative analysis shows that the adoption of new technology in agriculture and manufacturing has improved production possibilities in selected countries, including the United States of America, China, and Brazil, particularly in the production of crops such as maize, wheat, and rice. Nigeria’s agricultural production, however, remains comparatively low. The study recommends the aggressive adoption of modern technology, improved technological know-how, and the mechanisation of the agricultural and manufacturing sectors. It also recommends that the government provide an enabling environment and adequate facilities to encourage unemployed youths to participate in agriculture and improve food production.

title: Brand Loyalty vs Brand Switching: A Study of Mobile Phone Preferences in Young Pakistani Adults in South Punjab
abstract: This paper studies the mobile phone preferences in Pakistani Young Adults and what factors influence brand loyalty and brand switching among young Pakistani consumers. GenZ have unique characteristics in their behaviour from their older counterparts. In current era of AI and Internet smartphone has become an essential part of our life that connect us with the rest of the world as world has now become a global village. The smartphone industry is growing rapidly with new innovations and features every year or so. Pakistan as a developing country is filled with smartphones that are cheaper and has better features made possible by Chinese manufacturers. Young adults and Adults can now afford better smartphones at competitive prices. Data in this study was collected by the help of cross-sectional survey that include 70 smartphone users as subjects. Using Literature review we found that even though the purchase of a mobile phone is subjective there are some factors that influence the customers i.e. young adults, to switch brands. Study Indicated that Infinix has most loyal customer base as compared to other smartphone users and Apple is the most popular brand, The studies shows that the things that influence consumer switching behaviour of smart phones includes product quality as the primary factor. The study further reveals that customer satisfaction has positive affect on customer switching brands. Moreover, switching cost also played an important role.
